lessons.title: What Mobile App Development Is
lessons.content:
Think about the last hour of your day. Maybe you paid a shop with bKash, checked a Pathao ride, scrolled Facebook, asked a friend on Messenger about tomorrow's class test, and set an alarm for Fajr. Every one of those was a mobile app: a program somebody designed, wrote, tested and published so that it would run well on a small glass rectangle in your pocket. This course is about becoming the person who builds those programs.

What it is: Mobile application development is the craft of building software that runs on smartphones and tablets. It sounds like normal programming, and partly it is: you still write functions, classes, loops and data structures. But a phone is a very special kind of computer, and almost every lesson in this course is really about one question: what changes when the computer is small, battery powered, always moving, and always in somebody's hand?

Why it matters in Bangladesh: For many people in Bangladesh, the phone is the first and only computer they own. A rickshaw puller may never touch a laptop, but he may receive money on Nagad, watch videos and call his family on IMO or WhatsApp. Banks, mobile financial services, ride sharing, food delivery, e-commerce like Daraz and Chaldal, government services and online classes all reach people mainly through phones. That makes mobile skills some of the most useful and most hired skills for a CSE graduate here, both in local companies and in remote work for foreign clients.

What makes mobile different, part 1, the screen: A phone screen is small and you control it with fingers, not a mouse. A finger is fat compared to a mouse pointer, so buttons must be big enough to tap. There is no hover, so you cannot hide important information behind a mouse-over. The screen can rotate, and phones come in many sizes, from small budget phones to large tablets. Your interface must adapt to all of them. Lessons 8 and 9 teach how.

What makes mobile different, part 2, the battery: A desktop is plugged into the wall; a phone lives on a battery that must last a whole day. Every time your app wakes the processor, turns on GPS, or keeps the radio busy downloading, it drinks battery. Because users hate apps that drain their phone, both Android and iOS put strict limits on what apps may do in the background. A good mobile developer treats battery like money: spend it only when it buys something real.

What makes mobile different, part 3, the network: On a laptop at home you usually have stable Wi-Fi. A phone moves: from home Wi-Fi to 4G on the road, to weak 2G in a village, to no signal at all inside a lift or on a launch in the river. Requests fail halfway. Speeds change every minute. Mobile data also costs money, and many users buy small data packs. So mobile apps must handle slow and broken networks gracefully, show cached data, and avoid wasting megabytes. Lessons 15 and 18 go deep on this.

What makes mobile different, part 4, the operating system is the boss: On a desktop, a program you start usually keeps running until you close it. On a phone, the operating system decides. If memory is low, it may silently kill your app while it is in the background. If the user switches to another app, yours is paused. If the user rotates the screen, Android may destroy and recreate your screen. Your app must survive all of this without losing the user's half-typed message. This is the app lifecycle, covered in lesson 7.

What makes mobile different, part 5, sensors and personal data: A phone carries a camera, microphone, GPS, accelerometer, gyroscope, fingerprint sensor and more. It also stores the most private data people have: photos, contacts, messages, location history, money. This gives apps superpowers, like scanning a QR code to pay or showing the nearest pharmacy, but it also brings responsibility. Phones protect this data with permissions: the app must ask, and the user can say no.

What makes mobile different, part 6, the sandbox and the store: Each app lives in its own sandbox, a private area of storage and memory that other apps cannot read. Apps are not usually downloaded from random websites; they are installed from an app store such as Google Play or Apple's App Store, which reviews them, and they must be digitally signed by the developer. Updates go through the store too, which means you cannot fix a bug instantly; users must download the new version.

Kinds of mobile apps: Native apps are written specifically for one platform with its own tools, for example Kotlin for Android or Swift for iOS. Cross-platform apps are written once in a framework like Flutter or React Native and run on both. Hybrid apps put a web page inside an app shell. Progressive Web Apps are websites that behave somewhat like apps. Each has trade-offs in speed, cost and access to phone features; lesson 3 compares them carefully.

The layers of a mobile app: Picture a building. At the bottom is the hardware: processor, memory, radio, sensors. Above it sits the operating system kernel (Linux for Android, a kernel called XNU for iOS), which manages memory, processes and drivers. Above that is the platform framework: ready-made code for windows, buttons, notifications, location and so on. Your app sits on top and uses that framework. If you use Flutter, there is one more layer: the Flutter engine, which draws your widgets on the screen itself. Knowing these layers helps you understand error messages later.

The main jobs inside an app: Almost every real app does the same five jobs. It shows a user interface (UI). It reacts to user input like taps and typing. It keeps track of state, meaning the current data on screen. It talks to a server over the internet, usually through a REST API returning JSON. And it stores some data on the phone so it works offline and starts quickly. The middle of this course takes these jobs one by one.

The language of this course: We will mostly use Flutter with the Dart language for examples, because one codebase runs on Android and iOS and the code is short and readable. We will also show small Kotlin snippets so you see how native Android does the same thing, and talk about iOS at the concept level. The ideas, such as lifecycle, state, lazy lists, async code and offline sync, are the same on every platform. Learn the idea once and the syntax becomes easy.

A tiny taste of code: Here is the smallest Flutter app, written inline: void main() { runApp(const MaterialApp(home: Text('Assalamu Alaikum'))); }. The main function starts the program, runApp hands a widget to Flutter, and MaterialApp sets up a basic app with Text on the screen. In Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, a similar screen is a function marked @Composable that calls Text("Assalamu Alaikum"). Do not worry about the details yet; lessons 4, 5 and 8 build this up slowly.

Real-life example 1, a ride sharing app like Pathao: Open the app and many lessons appear at once. The map uses location and sensors (lesson 20). The list of nearby bikes is fetched from a server through an API (lesson 15). The screen moves from "choose destination" to "confirm ride" to "driver on the way" using navigation (lesson 10). If you switch to Messenger and come back, the ride is still shown, thanks to good lifecycle and state handling (lessons 7 and 11). When the driver arrives, a push notification pops up even if the app is closed (lesson 21). Your payment details are protected by security rules (lesson 22).

Real-life example 2, a school attendance app in a char area: Imagine a teacher in a riverside upazila where the network comes and goes. She opens an attendance app each morning. The app saves attendance in a local SQLite database on the phone (lesson 17), then quietly uploads it when the network returns (lesson 18). The interface is in Bangla with large buttons because many teachers use cheap phones with small screens (lesson 24). The app is small in size, because downloading a 200 MB app on a slow connection is painful (lesson 23). Good mobile development is not just code; it is understanding the user's real life.

What a mobile developer actually does: A typical day may include building a new screen from a designer's mockup, connecting it to an API, fixing a crash reported from a particular phone model, writing tests, measuring why a list scrolls slowly, and preparing a new release for the store. You work with designers, backend developers, testers and product managers. The Software Engineering course taught you process; here you apply it to a product that lives in millions of pockets.

Course map: Lessons 1 to 3 explain the platforms and approaches. Lessons 4 and 5 set up tools and the Dart language. Lessons 6 and 7 explain how Android and iOS run apps. Lessons 8 to 13 build interfaces, navigation, state, architecture and smooth lists. Lessons 14 to 18 handle async code, networking, storage and offline sync. Lessons 19 to 22 cover permissions, sensors, notifications, background work and security. Lessons 23 to 25 cover testing, accessibility with Bangla localisation, and publishing your app to the stores.

What this course does not repeat: HTTP methods, REST design, JSON format and web security are taught deeply in Web Engineering, so here we only recap them and focus on the mobile side. Usability principles, user research and design rules are the heart of Human Computer Interaction, so we only touch them when building screens. SQL itself comes from DBMS, and threads and processes come from Operating Systems.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Beginners think a phone app is just a small website, and then ignore battery, lifecycle and offline use. Another mistake is testing only on one expensive phone; real users have older and cheaper phones. Exams often ask: list the challenges or constraints of mobile development; compare native, cross-platform and hybrid apps; explain the role of an app store; or explain why mobile apps need permissions. A good answer names the constraint and gives a concrete example of how it affects the code.

Recap: Mobile development is software development under special conditions: small touch screens, limited battery, unreliable networks, an operating system that can pause or kill your app, rich sensors, private data, sandboxing and app stores. Apps are built natively, cross-platform, hybrid or as web apps. Almost every app shows UI, handles input, manages state, talks to servers and stores data locally. Keep the image of a real Bangladeshi user, with a budget phone and a weak signal, in your mind through the whole course.
key_points: Mobile development means building apps for phones and tablets, under special limits that desktops do not have.
Key constraints: small touch screens, limited battery, unreliable and costly networks, an OS that can pause or kill apps.
Phones have rich sensors and private data, so apps must ask permission and protect user data.
Each app runs in its own sandbox and is usually installed and updated through a signed app store package.
Apps can be native, cross-platform (Flutter, React Native), hybrid (WebView) or Progressive Web Apps.
Almost every app does five jobs: show UI, handle input, manage state, talk to servers and store data locally.
This course uses Flutter/Dart for most examples, with small Kotlin snippets and iOS concepts for comparison.
lessons.tip: Keep a cheap or older Android phone (yours, a sibling's or a parent's) as your test device for the whole course. If your app feels smooth there, it will feel smooth almost everywhere.
lessons.task: Pick three apps on your phone, for example bKash, a ride sharing app and a news app. For each one, write which of the five jobs (UI, input, state, network, local storage) you can see it doing, and one thing it does when the internet is off.

quiz.q: Why do Android and iOS put strict limits on what apps can do in the background?
options: To protect battery life and system resources
Because background code cannot use the internet at all
To force developers to use Flutter
quiz.explain: Background work wakes the processor, radio and GPS, which drains the battery, so the OS limits it to keep the phone usable all day.

quiz.q: What is an app sandbox?
options: A test server used before publishing
A folder on the developer's computer
A game engine for children's apps
A private area of storage and memory for each app that other apps cannot read
quiz.explain: The sandbox isolates each app so one app cannot read another app's private files or memory.

quiz.q: Which of these is a cross-platform framework where one codebase runs on Android and iOS?
quiz.explain: Flutter lets you write one Dart codebase that builds apps for both Android and iOS.

quiz.q: A user switches from your app to Messenger. Later the OS needs memory. What may happen to your app?
options: It is moved to the SD card
It may be killed while in the background
quiz.explain: Mobile operating systems may kill background apps to free memory, so apps must save state and restore it later.

quiz.q: Why is testing only on one new flagship phone a mistake?
options: Flagship phones cannot run debug builds
Real users have many older, cheaper and smaller phones where the app may behave differently
App stores reject apps tested on flagship phones
quiz.explain: Users have a wide range of devices, screen sizes and speeds, so testing on varied and lower-end phones catches real problems.

lessons.title: The Two Platforms: Android and iOS
lessons.content:
Walk into any mobile phone market in Dhaka, such as Bashundhara City or the shops around Motijheel, and you will see two worlds. On most shelves are Android phones from Samsung, Xiaomi, Realme, Walton, Symphony, Vivo, Oppo and others, at every price from a few thousand taka to well over a lakh. In one corner, behind glass, are iPhones, made only by Apple. These two worlds are the two mobile platforms that matter today: Android and iOS. Before you build an app, you need to know how each one is put together and how they differ.

What a platform is: A mobile platform is the full package an app runs on: the operating system, the libraries and frameworks that apps call, the programming languages and tools used to build apps, the rules apps must follow, and the store where apps are sold. When we say "build for Android", we mean build something that fits this whole package, not just the kernel underneath.

A short history of iOS: Apple released the first iPhone in 2007. At first, outside developers could not install their own native apps; then Apple released a software development kit and opened the App Store in 2008. The operating system was later named iOS. Apple designs both the hardware and the software, and it decides which devices get new versions. For years apps were written in Objective-C; in 2014 Apple introduced Swift, a modern, safer language that is now the main choice for new iOS apps.

A short history of Android: Android started as a small company that Google bought in 2005. In 2007 Google and many phone and chip companies announced the Open Handset Alliance, and the first Android phone went on sale in 2008. Google releases the core of Android as open source, called the Android Open Source Project (AOSP). Phone makers take this code, add their own changes and apps, and ship it on their own hardware. That is why a Samsung phone and a Xiaomi phone both run Android but look and behave a little differently.

The Android software stack, bottom layer: At the bottom is the Linux kernel. It handles the low-level jobs you studied in Operating Systems: process scheduling, memory management, drivers for the display, camera, Wi-Fi and so on, and security features. Each Android app runs as a separate Linux user, which is one of the ways the sandbox is enforced: the kernel simply does not let one user's process read another user's private files.

The Android software stack, middle layers: Above the kernel is a Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL), a set of standard interfaces so that the upper layers can talk to the camera or sensors without caring which company made the chip. Next are native libraries written in C and C++, such as the graphics libraries and SQLite. Then comes the Android Runtime (ART). Android apps written in Kotlin or Java are compiled into a bytecode format called DEX, and ART runs that bytecode, using a mix of ahead-of-time and just-in-time compilation to turn it into machine code for the phone's processor. Older Android versions used a runtime called Dalvik; ART replaced it.

The Android software stack, top layers: On top of the runtime sits the Java API framework, the huge set of building blocks your app uses: the Activity manager, the window and view system, the notification manager, the location manager, the package manager that installs apps, content providers for sharing data, and more. Google also provides Jetpack, a large family of libraries (for lifecycle, navigation, databases with Room, background work with WorkManager, and the Compose UI toolkit) that make modern Android development easier and more consistent across versions. At the very top are apps, both system apps like the dialer and your own.

The iOS layers: Apple describes iOS in layers too, though in less public detail. At the bottom is the core operating system, built on Darwin, which includes the XNU kernel shared with macOS. Above it are core services such as networking, file access, databases and location. Above that are media layers for graphics, audio and video. At the top is the user interface layer, historically called Cocoa Touch, with the UIKit framework; since 2019 Apple also offers SwiftUI, a declarative way to build interfaces. Swift apps are compiled ahead of time into native machine code for the iPhone's ARM processor.

Languages: For native Android, Google recommends Kotlin, a concise, null-safe language that runs on the same runtime as Java and works smoothly with old Java code. Java is still supported and many older apps use it. For native iOS, Swift is the main language, with Objective-C in older code. Cross-platform frameworks add other languages: Dart for Flutter, JavaScript or TypeScript for React Native, C# for .NET MAUI. Underneath, all of them must eventually run on the platform's runtime or call its native APIs.

Development tools: Android apps are usually built in Android Studio, Google's official IDE, which runs on Windows, macOS and Linux and includes an emulator, a layout editor, a profiler and the Gradle build system. iOS apps are built in Xcode, which runs only on macOS. This matters a lot to students in Bangladesh: you can develop Android apps on any ordinary laptop, but to build and publish an iOS app you need access to a Mac, either your own, a friend's or a cloud Mac service. Flutter developers often write and test on Android first and then build the iOS version on a Mac.

Fragmentation versus control: Because many companies make Android phones, Android has huge variety: different screen sizes, chips, amounts of RAM, camera hardware, custom skins, and many versions of Android in use at the same time, because not every maker updates old phones. This variety is called fragmentation. It means you must test on several devices and handle features that may be missing. Apple controls a small set of iPhone and iPad models and pushes updates directly, so most iPhones run a recent iOS version. Your testing matrix is smaller, but Apple's rules for apps are also stricter.

API levels and versions: Each Android release has a number called the API level. In your project you set a minimum SDK, the oldest Android version your app supports, and a target SDK, the version whose newest behaviour rules your app has been tested against. If you set the minimum too high, users with old phones cannot install your app; if too low, you must write extra code to support old behaviour. Google Play also requires apps to target a fairly recent API level, so you must update your target regularly. iOS has a similar idea with the deployment target.

Sandboxing on both platforms: On both Android and iOS each app gets its own private storage directory and runs in its own process with limited rights. To touch anything outside, such as the camera, contacts, photos or precise location, the app must declare what it wants and ask the user at runtime. iOS also requires the developer to write a short reason string for each sensitive permission, which the user sees in the system dialog. Lesson 19 covers permissions fully.

Distribution and openness: Android lets users install apps from outside the Play Store, called sideloading, if they allow it in settings. Some companies in Bangladesh distribute internal apps to field staff this way, for example as an APK file. iOS traditionally allowed installation only through the App Store, TestFlight for beta testing, or enterprise and developer channels, though rules have started to change in some regions because of new laws. For a normal student project, assume Android allows sideloading and iOS requires the official channels.

Market in Bangladesh: Android phones make up the large majority of smartphones in Bangladesh, mainly because they are available at every price point. iPhones are a small but valuable group: their users often spend more on apps and subscriptions. That is why many Bangladeshi startups launch on Android first, and add iOS later or build both at once with a cross-platform framework. In countries like the USA or Japan, iOS has a much larger share, so a product aimed at foreign users may need iOS from the start.

Design languages: Each platform has its own look and feel. Google's design system is Material Design, with its cards, floating action buttons and bottom sheets. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines describe iOS conventions such as navigation bars with a back button at the top left and swipe-from-the-edge to go back. Users expect apps to follow their platform's habits. The Human Computer Interaction course discusses design guidelines in depth; here, just remember that the two platforms have different expectations.

Real-life example 1, a mobile banking app: A bank in Dhaka builds a mobile banking app. Most customers use Android, so the Android version must work from older budget phones up to new flagships, which means testing many screen sizes and API levels. The iOS version serves fewer users but must pass Apple's review, which checks things like privacy explanations and login flows. Both versions use each platform's secure storage for login tokens: the Android Keystore and the iOS Keychain. The core features are the same; the platform details differ.

Real-life example 2, a university club app: You and your friends build an event app for your CSE club. Everyone in the team has a Windows laptop and Android phones. You can build, run and even share the Android version as an APK the same week. For iOS you would need a Mac and an Apple developer account to put it on friends' iPhones in the normal way. This is why many student teams choose Flutter: they write one codebase, test on Android daily, and borrow a Mac for a few hours near the end to build the iOS version.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students sometimes say Android "is Linux" in the same sense as Ubuntu; in fact it uses the Linux kernel but has a very different user space and app model. Another mistake is thinking Swift code runs on a virtual machine like Java; it is compiled to native code. Exams often ask you to draw the Android architecture stack and explain each layer, compare Android and iOS on openness, languages, tools and fragmentation, or explain the meaning of minimum and target SDK.

Recap: Android and iOS are the two main platforms. Android, from Google, is open source, built on the Linux kernel with a HAL, native libraries, the ART runtime and a large Java API framework, and runs on phones from many makers, which causes fragmentation. iOS, from Apple, runs only on Apple hardware, is built on Darwin and the XNU kernel, and uses UIKit and SwiftUI. Kotlin and Swift are the recommended native languages, Android Studio and Xcode the main tools, and Xcode needs a Mac. Both sandbox apps and guard sensitive data with permissions.
key_points: A platform is the whole package: OS, frameworks, languages, tools, rules and app store.
Android stack: Linux kernel, HAL, native libraries, Android Runtime (ART) running DEX bytecode, Java API framework, apps.
iOS is built on Darwin and the XNU kernel, with UIKit and SwiftUI for interfaces; Swift compiles to native code.
Native languages: Kotlin (or Java) for Android, Swift (or Objective-C) for iOS.
Android Studio runs on Windows, macOS and Linux; Xcode runs only on macOS, so iOS builds need a Mac.
Android has fragmentation (many makers, sizes, versions); Apple controls fewer devices and pushes updates directly.
Minimum SDK sets the oldest supported Android version; target SDK sets which newer behaviour rules apply.
lessons.tip: Draw the Android stack from memory as five boxes (kernel, HAL, native libraries plus ART, framework, apps) and write one job next to each box. This single diagram answers many exam questions.
lessons.task: Open Settings, then About phone on an Android phone (yours or a family member's). Write down the Android version, the maker, the RAM and the screen size. Ask two friends for theirs. Compare the three and note how fragmentation would affect an app you build.

quiz.q: What does the Android Runtime (ART) do?
options: It runs app bytecode (DEX) by compiling it to machine code
It reviews apps for the Play Store
quiz.explain: Kotlin and Java code is compiled to DEX bytecode, and ART runs it using ahead-of-time and just-in-time compilation.

quiz.q: Which tool is required to build an iOS app in the normal way, and where does it run?
options: Xcode, which runs only on macOS
quiz.explain: Xcode is Apple's IDE for iOS and runs only on macOS, so iOS builds need access to a Mac.

quiz.q: What is fragmentation in the Android world?
options: Breaking an app into small files
A memory error in the kernel
Splitting the screen into two apps
Many device makers, screen sizes and Android versions in use at the same time
quiz.explain: Because many companies make Android phones and not all are updated, apps must handle a wide variety of devices and versions.

quiz.q: In an Android project, what does the minimum SDK decide?
options: The oldest Android version on which the app can be installed
How many users can download the app
quiz.explain: The minimum SDK is the lowest API level the app supports; devices running older versions cannot install it.

quiz.q: Which language did Apple introduce in 2014 as the modern choice for iOS apps?
quiz.explain: Swift was introduced by Apple in 2014 and is now the main language for new native iOS apps.

lessons.title: Native, Cross-Platform, Hybrid and PWA
lessons.content:
Imagine you run a small restaurant in Mirpur and you want to deliver food to customers in two neighbourhoods across the river. You could hire two separate delivery teams, each knowing its own area perfectly. You could hire one team with a clever map that works in both areas. Or you could just put your menu on a Facebook page and let people order through it. Each choice costs different money and gives different quality. Building a mobile app for Android and iOS gives you exactly the same kind of choice, and picking the right one is one of the first big decisions in any app project.

The four approaches: There are four main ways to build a mobile app. Native: write a separate app for each platform with that platform's own language and tools. Cross-platform: write one codebase in a framework that produces real apps for both platforms. Hybrid: write a web app with HTML, CSS and JavaScript and wrap it inside a thin native shell. Progressive Web App (PWA): build a website that can be installed and can work offline, with no app store needed. Let us see how each one actually runs on the phone, because the trade-offs come from that.

Native apps, how they run: A native Android app is written in Kotlin or Java, compiled to DEX bytecode and run by the Android Runtime. Its buttons and lists are the platform's own UI components, or Jetpack Compose. A native iOS app is written in Swift, compiled to machine code, and uses UIKit or SwiftUI. Nothing sits between your code and the platform. When Google or Apple releases a new feature, such as a new kind of widget or a new camera API, native developers can use it on day one.

Native apps, strengths and costs: Native apps usually give the best performance, the smoothest feel, the most natural platform behaviour, and full access to every device feature. The cost is that you build and maintain two apps: two codebases, two teams or one team that knows two languages, two sets of bugs, and features that may arrive on one platform before the other. For a large company like a big bank this cost is acceptable. For a three-person startup in Dhaka, it can be heavy.

Cross-platform apps, the idea: A cross-platform framework lets you write most of your app once and produce real installable apps for Android and iOS, often from the same codebase. The two most widely used today are Flutter, from Google, using the Dart language, and React Native, started by Meta, using JavaScript or TypeScript. They solve the same problem in very different ways.

How Flutter runs: Flutter does not use the platform's buttons and text fields at all. It brings its own rendering engine and draws every pixel of the interface itself, much like a game engine draws a game. Your Dart code is compiled ahead of time into native ARM machine code for release builds. During development it runs in a just-in-time mode that enables hot reload, where you save a file and see the change on the phone in about a second. Because Flutter draws everything itself, an app looks the same on Android and iOS unless you choose platform-specific widgets.

How React Native runs: React Native runs your JavaScript in a JavaScript engine inside the app. Your components, such as View and Text, are translated into real native views on each platform, so a React Native button on iOS is an actual iOS view. Older versions of React Native passed messages between JavaScript and native code over an asynchronous bridge; the newer architecture lets JavaScript call native code more directly, which reduces overhead. The big attraction is that web developers who know React can move into mobile quickly.

Other cross-platform tools: Kotlin Multiplatform lets you share business logic, such as networking, data models and validation, written in Kotlin, while keeping native UI on each platform, or sharing UI too with Compose Multiplatform. .NET MAUI from Microsoft uses C#. Each has a different balance between how much code is shared and how native the result feels. You do not need to learn them all; understanding one well, plus the general idea, is enough for most jobs.

Cross-platform, strengths and costs: The main win is one codebase and one team, which can cut development time a lot, often far below the cost of two native apps. Bugs are fixed once, features ship to both platforms together. The costs: app size is larger because the framework or engine ships inside the app; you depend on the framework to support new platform features, sometimes with a delay; and for special hardware or platform features you still write some native code. In Flutter, these bridges are called platform channels and plugins.

Plugins and platform channels: Suppose your Flutter app needs the camera. The Flutter team and community publish plugins, packages that contain Dart code plus native Kotlin or Swift code that actually calls the camera API. Your Dart code calls the plugin, a message is sent across a platform channel, the native side does the real work and sends the result back. Most common needs, like camera, location, storage and notifications, already have plugins on pub.dev, Flutter's package site. Only rare needs force you to write native code yourself.

Hybrid apps, how they run: A hybrid app is a web application placed inside a native app shell that shows a WebView, a full browser component without the address bar. Tools such as Apache Cordova, Ionic with Capacitor, and similar frameworks provide plugins so JavaScript can call native features like the camera. You get an installable app built mostly with web skills. Many simple business apps, especially ones that mostly show forms and content, were built this way.

Hybrid apps, strengths and costs: Hybrid apps reuse web code and web developers, and can even share code with the company's website. But everything is drawn by a browser engine, so heavy animations and long lists can feel slower than native or Flutter, and the app may not feel like a true native app. Performance depends partly on the phone's WebView, which can vary between devices. Both stores also have policies against apps that are just a thin wrapper around a website with no real app value, so a hybrid app should offer genuine app features.

Progressive Web Apps, how they work: A PWA is a website that uses modern web features to behave like an app. A web app manifest, a small JSON file, gives the app a name, icon and colours so users can add it to their home screen. A service worker, a script that sits between the page and the network, can cache files and data so the app opens offline and loads fast. On many platforms PWAs can also show notifications. Web Engineering covers service workers and the web side in depth; here we care about the comparison.

PWAs, strengths and costs: There is no store review, no installation size worry, and updates are instant: you change the website and every user gets the new version on next load. One codebase runs on Android, iOS and desktop browsers. But PWAs have the most limited access to device features, and support differs by browser and operating system; on iOS, PWA support has historically been more limited than on Android. You also lose the discoverability of the app stores, where many users search for apps.

A comparison in words: Think of four questions. How fast and smooth? Native first, then Flutter and React Native close behind, then hybrid and PWA. How much device access? Native full, cross-platform almost full through plugins, hybrid partial, PWA least. How much code do you write for two platforms? Native two codebases; the others mostly one. How easy are updates? PWA instant, the others through store releases. No approach wins on every question; you choose based on what matters most for this app.

How to choose, a simple checklist: If the app needs heavy graphics, deep hardware use, or the very latest platform features, and the budget allows two teams, choose native. If you need a good-looking app on both platforms quickly with a small team, choose a cross-platform framework like Flutter. If you already have a strong web app and the mobile app mostly shows content and forms, a hybrid app or PWA may be enough. Also consider your team's existing skills: a team of JavaScript experts may move faster with React Native.

The decision is not forever, but changing is expensive: Switching approach later usually means rewriting most of the app, so teams try to decide well at the start. A common middle path is to build the main app with a cross-platform framework and write one or two performance-critical screens natively, or to keep a website or PWA for occasional visitors and an installable app for regular users. Another middle path is sharing only the business logic, as Kotlin Multiplatform allows. Real projects often mix approaches; the exam answer should still explain the reasons behind each choice clearly.

Real-life example 1, a Dhaka startup: A small team wants to launch a tutoring marketplace that connects students with home tutors in Dhaka and Chattogram. They have three developers, six months, and users on both Android and iOS. They choose Flutter. One codebase gives them both apps; plugins handle maps, image upload and notifications; and the same team builds features once. A year later, if a particular feature needs special native work, such as a video calling SDK, they add a small amount of Kotlin and Swift through platform channels.

Real-life example 2, a government information service: A public office wants citizens to check service status and download forms. Most visits are short, many users have old phones with little storage, and they do not want users to install anything. A PWA fits: one website, fast, cached for weak networks, installable to the home screen for those who want it. If later they need fingerprint login and offline document scanning, they could build a native or cross-platform app for that part.

Common mistakes and exam questions: A common mistake is thinking cross-platform means zero native knowledge; in reality you still need to understand Android and iOS for permissions, signing, lifecycle and debugging. Another mistake is saying Flutter apps use native buttons; they do not, Flutter draws its own. Exams often ask you to compare native, hybrid and cross-platform approaches with advantages and disadvantages, define a PWA and its parts, or recommend an approach for a given scenario with reasons.

Recap: Native apps use each platform's own language and UI and give the best performance and full access, at the cost of two codebases. Cross-platform frameworks such as Flutter, which draws its own UI from AOT-compiled Dart, and React Native, which maps JavaScript components to native views, give one codebase with near-native results and plugins for device features. Hybrid apps run web code inside a WebView shell. PWAs are installable, offline-capable websites with the least device access but instant updates. Choose based on performance needs, device access, budget, team skills and update needs.
key_points: Four approaches: native, cross-platform, hybrid (web inside a WebView shell) and Progressive Web App.
Native apps use Kotlin/Swift and platform UI: best performance and full access, but two codebases.
Flutter draws every pixel with its own engine and compiles Dart ahead of time to native code for release.
React Native runs JavaScript and maps components to real native views on each platform.
Plugins and platform channels let cross-platform code call native features like the camera.
PWAs use a web app manifest and service worker to be installable and work offline, with limited device access.
Choose by performance needs, device access, budget, team skills and how quickly updates must reach users.
lessons.tip: When an exam gives a scenario, answer in the same order every time: who are the users, which device features are needed, what is the budget and team, then which approach and why. A structured answer scores well.
lessons.task: Pick three apps you use, for example a bank app, a news site you have added to your home screen, and a game. Guess whether each is native, cross-platform, hybrid or PWA, and write one clue for each guess (feel, offline behaviour, store or no store, app size).

quiz.q: How does Flutter show buttons and text on the screen?
options: It draws them itself with its own rendering engine
It uses the platform's native buttons
It opens a WebView and renders HTML
It asks the user's browser to draw them
quiz.explain: Flutter brings its own rendering engine and paints every pixel itself, so it does not use native platform buttons.

quiz.q: What is a hybrid mobile app?
options: An app written twice in Kotlin and Swift
A website with no installation at all
A web app running inside a native shell's WebView
An app that runs only on tablets
quiz.explain: Hybrid apps (for example with Cordova or Ionic with Capacitor) run HTML, CSS and JavaScript inside a WebView in an installable shell.

quiz.q: Which part of a PWA lets it cache files so it can open offline?
quiz.explain: A service worker sits between the page and the network and can cache resources for offline and fast loading.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of building fully native apps for both platforms?
options: Native apps cannot use the camera
Native apps cannot be published to stores
You maintain two separate codebases, often with two skill sets
quiz.explain: Native gives the best performance and access, but you build and maintain one app per platform.

quiz.q: In Flutter, how does Dart code use a device feature like the camera?
options: Dart talks directly to the camera hardware
It cannot; Flutter apps have no camera access
Through a plugin that sends messages over a platform channel to native code
quiz.explain: Plugins contain native Kotlin/Swift code; Dart calls them through platform channels and receives the result.

lessons.title: Tools and Your First Project
lessons.content:
A tailor in Islampur needs more than cloth to make a shirt: scissors, measuring tape, a sewing machine, chalk and a table. If any tool is missing, the work stops. Building a mobile app is similar. Before you write a single screen you need the right toolkit on your laptop, a phone or emulator to run the app, and a clear picture of what files a project contains and how they turn into something a phone can install. This lesson sets up that workshop and walks through your first project.

What an SDK is: SDK means Software Development Kit. It is a bundle that contains everything needed to build software for a platform: libraries your code calls, compilers and build tools, command-line utilities, documentation, and often an emulator. The Android SDK contains platform libraries for each API level, build tools, and the platform tools such as adb. The Flutter SDK contains the Dart compiler, the Flutter framework and engine, and the flutter command. Xcode includes the iOS SDK. An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is the editor that ties these together with buttons for build, run and debug.

The usual setup for this course: Install Android Studio, which downloads the Android SDK and gives you an emulator manager. Install the Flutter SDK and add its bin folder to your system PATH so the flutter command works in a terminal. Then run flutter doctor. This command checks your setup and prints a list: Flutter found, Android toolchain found, licences accepted, a connected device or not, and so on. Anything with a cross or warning tells you what to fix. You can write Flutter code in Android Studio or in Visual Studio Code with the Flutter and Dart extensions. On a Mac you would also install Xcode for iOS builds.

Creating your first Flutter project: In a terminal, type flutter create hello_dhaka. The tool generates a full project with a sample counter app. Move into the folder and type flutter run. Flutter builds the app, installs it on the connected phone or running emulator, and starts it. You will see a screen with a number and a plus button; each tap increases the number. That sample is worth reading line by line, because it already shows widgets, state and a button handler.

The Flutter project layout: Inside the project you will see a few important items. The lib folder holds your Dart code, and lib/main.dart contains the main function where the app starts. The pubspec.yaml file describes the project: its name, version, the Dart SDK range, the packages it depends on, and assets such as images and fonts. The android and ios folders contain real native projects that Flutter uses to build the final apps; you only edit them for things like permissions, app icons or signing. The test folder holds tests. Running flutter pub get downloads the packages listed in pubspec.yaml.

Adding a package: Suppose you need to make HTTP requests. You add a line under dependencies in pubspec.yaml, for example http followed by a version constraint, or simply run flutter pub add http, which edits the file for you. Then you import it in Dart with import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;. Packages come from pub.dev. Before adding one, check that it is maintained, popular, and supports both Android and iOS. Every package you add increases app size and adds code you did not write, so add only what you need.

The native Android project layout: If you open a pure Kotlin Android project, the key parts are different. The AndroidManifest.xml file declares the app's package identity, its components such as activities, and the permissions it needs. The kotlin or java source folder holds your code. The res folder holds resources: layout files, images in drawable folders, the app icon in mipmap folders, and values such as strings.xml, colors and themes. Gradle build files, written in Kotlin script or Groovy, set the applicationId, the minimum and target SDK, version numbers and library dependencies.

Why resources live outside the code: Android keeps text, images and layouts in the res folder instead of inside code so the system can pick the right version automatically. For example, values/strings.xml holds the default English text and values-bn/strings.xml holds Bangla text; on a phone set to Bangla, Android picks the Bangla file. Drawables can have versions for different screen densities. This idea of qualifiers, choosing resources by language, screen size or night mode, returns in lessons 9 and 24.

Emulator or real phone: An emulator is a program on your laptop that pretends to be a phone. Android Studio's Device Manager creates Android Virtual Devices with any screen size and API level, which is great for testing many configurations. But an emulator needs a fair amount of RAM and CPU, and hardware virtualization enabled in the BIOS; on an older 8 GB laptop it can be slow. Apple's equivalent, the iOS Simulator, runs on a Mac. A real phone gives true speed, real sensors and real network behaviour, and costs nothing extra if you already have one.

Running on a real Android phone: Go to Settings, About phone, and tap Build number seven times to unlock Developer options. In Developer options, turn on USB debugging. Connect the phone with a USB cable and accept the prompt that asks whether to trust this computer. Now flutter devices or Android Studio will list your phone. Newer Android versions also support wireless debugging over Wi-Fi. Many students in Bangladesh do all their development this way on budget laptops, and it works very well.

adb, the Android Debug Bridge: adb is a command-line tool that talks to connected Android devices. adb devices lists them. adb install app-release.apk installs an APK. adb logcat streams the system log, where your app's print messages and crash stack traces appear. adb shell opens a shell on the device. You will use logcat constantly when debugging, and lesson 23 returns to it. Flutter's own flutter logs command shows a filtered view of the same information.

Hot reload and hot restart: In debug mode, Flutter runs your Dart code on a virtual machine with just-in-time compilation. When you save a file, hot reload injects the changed code into the running app and rebuilds the widgets, usually in about a second, while keeping the current state: if your counter shows 7, it still shows 7 after the reload. Hot restart reloads the code and resets the state to the start. Changes to native code, to pubspec dependencies with native parts, or to the main function's startup logic usually need a full stop and rebuild.

Debug, profile and release builds: Flutter has three build modes. Debug mode includes assertions, debugging support and hot reload, but it is slower and larger; never judge performance in debug mode. Profile mode is optimised like release but keeps some tools for measuring performance. Release mode compiles Dart ahead of time to native code, removes debugging aids and is what users get. Native Android has debug and release build types too, and the release build is typically shrunk and optimised by the R8 tool.

What the build produces, Android: An APK (Android Package) is the file a phone installs. It is basically a zip archive containing the compiled DEX code, the resources, the manifest, any native libraries, and a signature. For publishing on Google Play, new apps are uploaded as an Android App Bundle (AAB), and Google Play generates optimised APKs from it for each device, so a phone downloads only the code and resources it needs, such as images for its own screen density. Commands: flutter build apk for an APK, flutter build appbundle for an AAB.

What the build produces, iOS: For iOS the build produces an app bundle that is packed into an IPA file for distribution. iOS requires code signing even for installing on your own test device, using certificates and provisioning profiles tied to an Apple developer account. Xcode can manage much of this automatically. Lesson 25 explains signing on both platforms in detail; for now just remember that every installable mobile app is signed by its developer.

The build pipeline in one picture: Your Dart or Kotlin source, plus resources and the manifest, go into the build system (Gradle for Android, Xcode's build system for iOS, with Flutter driving both). The compiler turns code into DEX or machine code. Resources are compiled and packed. Everything is zipped, signed and aligned into an APK, AAB or IPA. Then it is installed on a device or uploaded to a store. When a build fails, the error message usually tells you which step broke: Dart analysis, Gradle dependency resolution, Kotlin compilation or signing.

Real-life example 1, a student's laptop in a hostel: Rafi has a laptop with 8 GB RAM and a mid-range Android phone. The emulator makes the laptop slow while Android Studio is open, so he uses VS Code with the Flutter extension and runs the app on his phone over USB. Hot reload lets him change colours and padding in seconds. When he wants to test a small-screen phone, he borrows a cousin's old phone. He has a complete professional setup without buying anything new.

Real-life example 2, a small software firm: A company in Banani builds apps for clients. Developers write code in Android Studio, run tests on several emulators with different screen sizes and API levels, and keep a shelf of real test phones: a low-end Android, a mid-range one, a flagship and an iPhone. A shared Mac builds the iOS versions. Their continuous integration server runs flutter test and builds release artifacts automatically on every merge, so nobody needs to build release files by hand.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Beginners often measure speed in debug mode and think Flutter is slow; always test performance in profile or release mode. Another mistake is editing generated files that the build system overwrites. Others forget to run flutter pub get after editing pubspec.yaml, or forget to accept the USB debugging prompt on the phone. Exams may ask: what an SDK and an IDE are, the difference between an emulator and a real device, APK versus AAB, hot reload versus hot restart, or the role of the Android manifest and the res folder.

Recap: An SDK bundles libraries and tools for a platform; an IDE such as Android Studio, VS Code or Xcode ties them together. flutter doctor checks your setup, flutter create makes a project, and flutter run installs and starts it. A Flutter project has lib/main.dart, pubspec.yaml, and native android and ios folders; a native Android project has the manifest, source, res resources and Gradle files. Use real phones with USB debugging and adb, or emulators. Hot reload keeps state, hot restart resets it. Builds come in debug, profile and release modes, and produce APK, AAB or IPA files that are always signed.
key_points: An SDK bundles a platform's libraries, compilers and tools; an IDE ties them together for editing, building and debugging.
flutter doctor checks setup, flutter create makes a project, flutter run builds and installs it on a device.
Flutter projects: lib/main.dart for code, pubspec.yaml for packages and assets, android/ and ios/ native projects.
Native Android projects: AndroidManifest.xml, source code, res resources (layouts, strings, drawables) and Gradle build files.
Real phones need Developer options and USB debugging; adb installs apps and shows logs with logcat.
Hot reload injects code and keeps state; hot restart resets state; never judge speed in debug mode.
Android builds produce APKs (installable) and AABs (for Play publishing); iOS produces signed IPAs.
lessons.tip: Run flutter doctor every time something strange happens with builds. Half of all setup problems (missing licences, wrong PATH, device not detected) are printed right there in plain words.
lessons.task: On an Android phone, unlock Developer options by tapping Build number seven times, then look through the list of options without changing anything risky. Write down three options that look useful for an app developer (for example USB debugging, show layout bounds, or a profile rendering option) and guess what each is for.

quiz.q: Which file in a Flutter project lists the packages the app depends on?
quiz.explain: pubspec.yaml describes the project, including its dependencies and assets; flutter pub get downloads them.

quiz.q: What is the difference between hot reload and hot restart?
options: Hot reload only works on iOS
Hot reload keeps the current app state, hot restart resets it
Hot restart is faster than hot reload
quiz.explain: Hot reload injects changed code and rebuilds widgets while keeping state; hot restart starts the app state over.

quiz.q: Why should you not measure performance in debug mode?
options: Debug mode only runs on emulators
Debug mode includes extra checks and JIT code, so it is slower than release
quiz.explain: Debug builds favour developer tools and hot reload over speed; use profile or release mode to judge performance.

quiz.q: What format are new apps uploaded to Google Play in, so Play can create optimised APKs per device?
quiz.explain: New Play apps are published as AABs; Google Play generates device-specific APKs from the bundle.

quiz.q: Which command shows the Android system log, including your app's crash stack traces?
quiz.explain: adb logcat streams the device log where print output and crash traces appear.

lessons.title: Dart Essentials for App Developers
lessons.content:
When you move to a new city, you do not need to learn every word of the local dialect on the first day. You need the words for food, directions, money and help. Then you can live there and learn the rest along the way. Dart, the language of Flutter, is like that. If you know C, C++, Java or Python from earlier courses, most of Dart will feel familiar. This lesson teaches the survival vocabulary: the pieces of Dart you will meet in every Flutter app, with a few features that are special to Dart and important on mobile.

What Dart is: Dart is a programming language created by Google. It is object-oriented, with classes and objects like Java, and it is statically typed, meaning every variable has a type that the compiler checks before the program runs. Dart can be compiled in two ways: just-in-time on a virtual machine during development, which allows hot reload, and ahead-of-time to native machine code for release, which makes apps start fast and run smoothly. Dart can also compile to JavaScript and WebAssembly for the web, but in this course we care about mobile.

The main function and printing: Every Dart program starts at main. A tiny program is: void main() { print('Hello, Sylhet'); }. The word void means main returns nothing. Statements end with a semicolon, blocks use curly braces, and comments start with // like in C. When you run this in a Flutter app, print output appears in the debug console and in logcat.

Variables and types: You can write the type explicitly, as in int age = 20; or String city = 'Khulna';, or let Dart infer it with var, as in var price = 120; where Dart decides price is an int. Common types are int for whole numbers, double for decimals, num for either, String for text, bool for true or false, and the collection types List, Map and Set. There is also dynamic, which turns off type checking for that variable; avoid it unless you truly need it, because it hides mistakes until runtime.

final and const: A final variable can be set only once, but its value can be decided while the program runs, for example final now = DateTime.now();. A const variable must be known at compile time, for example const pi = 3.1416; or const appName = 'BazarList';. In Flutter you will see const in front of widgets, such as const Text('Hello'). This tells Dart the widget never changes, so it can be created once and reused, which saves work during rebuilds. A good habit: use final by default, const when possible, and var only for values that really change.

Strings and interpolation: Dart strings can use single or double quotes; Flutter style prefers single quotes. You can put variables inside strings with a dollar sign: 'Hello $name' or, for expressions, 'Total: ${price * qty} taka'. Multi-line strings use triple quotes. Strings are immutable, meaning methods like toUpperCase() return a new string. This small feature makes UI code much cleaner than joining strings with plus signs.

Null safety, the problem: In many languages any variable can secretly be null, meaning it points to nothing. If you call a method on null, the program crashes with the famous null pointer error. This is one of the most common crashes in mobile apps. Dart solves this with sound null safety: by default, a variable cannot be null, and the compiler refuses to compile code that might put null into it.

Null safety, the tools: If a value may be missing, you add a question mark to the type: String? nickname; means nickname can hold a String or null. Before using it, you must handle the null case. The ?. operator calls a method only if the value is not null: nickname?.length gives null instead of crashing. The ?? operator gives a default: nickname ?? 'Guest'. The ! operator tells the compiler you are sure it is not null: nickname!.length; if you are wrong, the program throws an error at that point, so use ! rarely. The keyword late means a non-null variable will be set later, before it is first used.

Null safety, a worked example: Suppose an API returns a user whose phone number may be missing. You write class User { final String name; final String? phone; }. To show it on screen you write Text(user.phone ?? 'No phone added'). The compiler forces you to think about the missing case at the moment you write the code, instead of discovering it from a crash report after release. That single habit removes a whole family of bugs.

Functions: A function has a return type, a name and parameters: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }. A one-line body can use the arrow syntax: int add(int a, int b) => a + b;. Functions are objects in Dart, so you can store them in variables and pass them to other functions. Anonymous functions, often called lambdas, look like (x) => x * 2. In Flutter you pass functions all the time, for example onPressed: () { print('tapped'); } on a button.

Named and optional parameters: Flutter code uses named parameters everywhere, which is why widget code reads so clearly. You declare them in curly braces: void greet({required String name, String title = 'Bhai'}) { print('Salam $title $name'); }. You call it as greet(name: 'Karim'). The required keyword forces the caller to pass it, and a default value covers the rest. Optional positional parameters go in square brackets. When you read Padding(padding: EdgeInsets.all(8), child: Text('Hi')), padding and child are named parameters of the Padding constructor.

Classes and constructors: A class groups data and behaviour. Example: class Product { final String name; final int price; const Product(this.name, this.price); int priceWithVat() => (price * 1.15).round(); }. The constructor shorthand this.name assigns the parameter directly to the field. Named constructors give extra ways to build an object, such as Product.free(this.name) : price = 0;. Factory constructors can return an existing object or build one from data, and you will often write factory Product.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) to create objects from API data in lesson 15.

Inheritance, interfaces and mixins: Dart supports single inheritance with extends, and every Flutter screen you write starts this way, for example class HomeScreen extends StatelessWidget. Every class also acts as an interface, so another class can implement it and must then provide all its methods. Mixins, added with the with keyword, let a class reuse a bundle of methods without inheriting from it; Flutter uses a mixin when an animated widget needs a ticker, for example. You studied these ideas in OOP; Dart just has its own keywords.

Collections: A List is an ordered list: var marks = [72, 85, 64];. A Map stores key-value pairs: var stock = {'rice': 50, 'dal': 20};. A Set holds unique items. Lists have handy methods: marks.where((m) => m >= 80).toList() keeps high marks, marks.map((m) => m + 5).toList() adds grace marks, and marks.fold(0, (sum, m) => sum + m) adds them all. Dart also lets you use if and for inside list literals, which Flutter uses to build children: [Text('Title'), if (isLoggedIn) Text('Welcome'), for (var item in items) Text(item)].

Control flow and enums: if, else, for, while, break and continue work just like in C and Java, and for (var m in marks) loops over a collection directly. An enum names a fixed set of choices, which is perfect for screen states: enum LoadState { loading, success, error }. A switch on an enum makes the code read like a decision table: switch (state) { case LoadState.loading: ... }. Modern Dart can also check that a switch covers every enum value, so if you later add a new state such as empty, the compiler points to every place you forgot to handle it. You will use this pattern in lesson 15.

The cascade operator: Sometimes you call several methods on the same object. The cascade .. lets you write it neatly: var buffer = StringBuffer()..write('Dhaka')..write(' ')..write('Metro');. Each .. call works on the same object and the whole expression returns that object. It is not essential, but you will see it in Flutter code, especially when configuring paints and controllers.

A first look at asynchronous code: Mobile apps constantly wait for slow things: the network, the disk, the camera. Dart represents a value that will arrive later with a Future. A function marked async can use await to wait for a Future without freezing the app: Future<String> loadName() async { await Future.delayed(Duration(seconds: 1)); return 'Nadia'; }. Dart runs your code on a single main thread with an event loop, and await lets other work, like drawing the screen, continue while waiting. Lesson 14 explains this properly, along with Streams and isolates.

Real-life example 1, a bazar list model: Imagine a shopping list app for a family. You define class Item { final String name; final int qty; final bool bought; const Item({required this.name, this.qty = 1, this.bought = false}); }. The list is final items = <Item>[Item(name: 'Alu', qty: 2), Item(name: 'Peyaj')];. To count what is left you write items.where((i) => !i.bought).length. Named parameters make the creation readable, default values save typing, and null safety guarantees every item has a name.

Real-life example 2, safe profile data: A student portal app receives a profile where the blood group and the guardian's phone may be missing. With String? bloodGroup and String? guardianPhone, every place that shows them must decide what to display when they are null, such as 'Not given'. Before null safety, an app like this could crash on the profile screen for exactly the students whose data was incomplete, often the newest admissions. Null safety turns that hidden runtime crash into a visible compile-time decision.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Beginners overuse the ! operator to silence the compiler, which brings the crashes back. Others use dynamic or var everywhere and lose type checking. Some forget that final objects can still change inside: a final List can still have items added; only the variable cannot point to a new list. Another confusion is final versus const. Exams and interviews often ask: what is null safety and why is it useful, the difference between final and const, named versus positional parameters, and what a Future represents.

Recap: Dart is a statically typed, object-oriented language that compiles just-in-time for development and ahead-of-time to native code for release. Use final by default, const for compile-time constants, and avoid dynamic. Sound null safety makes types non-null by default; use ?, ??, ?. and late carefully and ! rarely. Functions are objects; Flutter relies heavily on named parameters and passed-in callbacks. Classes have short constructor syntax, named and factory constructors, and support extends, implements and mixins. Lists, maps and sets come with where, map and fold. Futures with async and await handle slow work.
key_points: Dart is statically typed and object-oriented, compiled JIT in development (hot reload) and AOT to native code for release.
Use final for values set once, const for compile-time constants (also on widgets), var only for changing values.
Sound null safety: types are non-null by default; String? allows null, handled with ??, ?. and checks.
The ! operator forces non-null and crashes if wrong, so use it rarely; late means set before first use.
Named parameters in curly braces, with required and defaults, are used everywhere in Flutter widgets.
Classes support this.field constructors, named and factory constructors (like fromJson), extends, implements and mixins.
A Future represents a value arriving later; async and await wait for it without freezing the app.
lessons.tip: Use DartPad in a browser (dartpad.dev) to try every snippet in this lesson. No install, works on a phone too, and you see results in seconds.
lessons.task: On paper or in DartPad, write a class Student with a required name, a required roll number and an optional email (String?). Create three students, one without email, and print each one's email or 'No email' using the ?? operator.

quiz.q: What does the type String? mean in Dart?
options: A string that must be a question
A variable that can hold a String or null
A string that cannot be changed
A string loaded from the internet
quiz.explain: The question mark makes the type nullable, so the variable can be a String or null and must be checked before use.

quiz.q: What is the difference between final and const?
options: final can be set once at runtime; const must be known at compile time
const can be changed later; final cannot
quiz.explain: A final value is decided once while the program runs; a const value must be a compile-time constant.

quiz.q: What does nickname ?? 'Guest' return when nickname is null?
quiz.explain: The ?? operator returns the right-hand default when the left value is null.

quiz.q: Why is overusing the ! operator a bad habit?
options: It throws an error at runtime if the value is actually null, bringing crashes back
quiz.explain: ! tells the compiler a value is not null; if that is wrong, the program fails at that point.

quiz.q: In greet({required String name, String title = 'Bhai'}), how do you call it for Karim?
quiz.explain: Named parameters are passed by name; title uses its default value.

lessons.title: Android App Components and Intents
lessons.content:
Think of a big hospital like Dhaka Medical College Hospital. It has different kinds of staff: doctors who meet patients face to face, lab technicians who work quietly in the background, a notice board where announcements are posted, and a records office that shares files with other departments when asked properly. Staff talk to each other with request slips: "Please do a blood test for this patient". An Android app is organised in a surprisingly similar way. It is built from four kinds of components, and they communicate with messages called intents. Even if you write Flutter, your app lives inside these Android pieces, so you must understand them.

Why apps are made of components: On a desktop, a program usually has one entry point, main, and the program controls everything from there. Android was designed differently. The system, not your app, decides when parts of your app start and stop, and other apps can start parts of your app. For example, when you tap "Share" in the gallery and choose WhatsApp, the gallery starts one specific screen inside WhatsApp. To make this possible, an app is split into components that the system knows about and can start individually.

Component 1, Activity: An Activity is a single screen with a user interface that the user interacts with. An email app might have one activity for the inbox, another for reading a message and another for composing. Each activity is a Kotlin or Java class that extends an Activity base class, usually AppCompatActivity or ComponentActivity. The activity that appears when you tap the app icon is called the launcher activity. Activities have a lifecycle, a set of callbacks the system calls as the screen appears, goes to the background and is destroyed; lesson 7 covers that in detail.

One activity or many: Older apps used one activity per screen. Many modern apps use a single activity that hosts many screens, swapping fragments or Compose destinations inside it, because moving between screens inside one activity is lighter and easier to animate and share data across. Flutter goes even further: a Flutter app on Android normally has one activity, FlutterActivity, which hosts a FlutterView. Every Flutter screen and route you create lives inside that one view, drawn by the Flutter engine. Android sees just one activity.

Component 2, Service: A Service is a component that does work without a user interface, such as playing music while you use other apps or syncing data. A started service runs a task until it finishes or is stopped. A bound service offers an interface that other components connect to, like a little server inside the phone. Because background work drains battery, newer Android versions strictly limit background services. Long, user-visible work like music playback or navigation must run as a foreground service, which shows a persistent notification so the user knows something is running. For most deferrable tasks, Google recommends WorkManager instead; lesson 21 explains this.

Component 3, BroadcastReceiver: A BroadcastReceiver responds to announcements broadcast by the system or other apps. The system broadcasts events such as the device finished booting, the battery is low, airplane mode changed, or the timezone changed. Your receiver's onReceive method runs briefly when a matching broadcast arrives. Receivers should do very little work and finish quickly; for longer work they schedule a job. To save battery, newer Android versions do not deliver most implicit broadcasts to receivers declared only in the manifest; apps register many receivers in code while they are running instead.

Component 4, ContentProvider: A ContentProvider manages a set of app data and offers it to other apps through a standard interface, a bit like a mini database server with URLs. Data is addressed with content URIs that start with content://. The Contacts app exposes contacts through a provider, and the media store exposes photos and videos. Other apps read this data through a ContentResolver, using query, insert, update and delete, and only if they hold the right permission. Your own app rarely needs to write a provider unless it shares data with other apps.

The manifest, the app's identity card: Every component must be declared in AndroidManifest.xml (except receivers registered in code). The manifest also lists the permissions the app needs, such as android.permission.INTERNET or CAMERA; hardware or software features it requires; the app icon and label; and intent filters, which say what kinds of requests each component can handle. When you install an app, the system reads the manifest to know what the app contains. In Flutter, you edit android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml for permissions and app settings.

The Application object and Context: Besides the four components, each app process has one Application object, created before any component, which lives as long as the process lives. Many Android APIs also ask for a Context, an object that gives access to the app's resources, files, preferences and system services. Activities and the Application are both contexts. A classic beginner bug is storing an activity's context in a long-lived object; when the screen is destroyed, the old activity cannot be freed, causing a memory leak. When something lives longer than a screen, give it the application context instead.

Intents, the request slips: An Intent is a message object that asks the system to perform an action, usually starting an activity or service, or delivering a broadcast. It can carry an action (what to do), data (a URI to act on), a MIME type, a category, and extras (a small bundle of key-value data). There are two kinds: explicit and implicit. Understanding the difference is one of the most common exam questions on Android.

Explicit intents: An explicit intent names the exact component to start, usually inside your own app. In Kotlin: val intent = Intent(this, DetailActivity::class.java); intent.putExtra("productId", 42); startActivity(intent). The system starts DetailActivity, which reads the extra with intent.getIntExtra("productId", -1). Explicit intents are like a slip addressed to a specific doctor by name.

Implicit intents: An implicit intent does not name a component. It describes what you want, and the system finds an app that can do it. For example, Intent(Intent.ACTION_DIAL, Uri.parse("tel:999")) asks for a dialer with the number filled in, and Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, Uri.parse("https://example.com")) asks to open a web page. If several apps can handle it, Android shows a chooser. This is how your app can reuse the phone's camera, maps, browser and dialer without building them.

Intent filters, how matching works: An app announces which implicit intents it can handle with intent filters in its manifest. A filter lists actions, categories and data patterns. A browser declares it can VIEW URIs with the http and https schemes. A launcher activity declares the MAIN action with the LAUNCHER category, which is how the home screen knows which activity to start when you tap the icon. When an implicit intent is sent, the system compares it with all installed apps' filters and picks the matches.

The share sheet, a worked example: Suppose your Flutter recipe app wants to share a recipe. On Android, a sharing plugin creates an implicit intent with action ACTION_SEND, type text/plain, and the recipe text as an extra, then wraps it in a chooser. Android finds every app with a filter for ACTION_SEND and text/plain, such as Messenger, WhatsApp, Gmail and IMO, and shows them. The user picks one and that app's sharing activity starts with your text. You wrote none of their code; the intent system connected you.

Getting results back: Sometimes you start another activity to get something back, such as picking a photo or scanning a QR code. Modern Android uses the Activity Result API, where you register a callback, launch the request, and receive the result when the other activity finishes. The older startActivityForResult method is deprecated. In Flutter, plugins such as image pickers hide this and simply return a Future that completes with the chosen file.

Tasks and the back stack: When activities start one another, Android keeps them in a stack called a task. Opening the inbox, then a message, then the compose screen pushes three activities. Pressing back pops the top one and shows the one below. When you share from the gallery into WhatsApp, the WhatsApp share screen may join the gallery's task, so back returns you to the gallery. Launch modes and intent flags can change this behaviour, but the default stack model is what you need for now. Lesson 10 covers navigation inside an app.

Security of components: If a component can be started by other apps, it is called exported. An exported activity or provider is a door into your app, so it must check what it receives and should not leak private data. Newer Android versions require developers to state explicitly whether components with intent filters are exported, to avoid accidental open doors. Keep components private unless other apps truly need them, and protect providers with permissions.

The iOS picture, briefly: iOS does not use the same four-component model. An iOS app has an application object and one or more scenes with view controllers or SwiftUI views. Apps communicate through URL schemes, universal links, share sheets with app extensions, and system services, all more tightly controlled by Apple. The goal is the same: let apps cooperate without breaking each other's sandbox.

Real-life example 1, a food delivery app: When a restaurant's order arrives, the server sends a push notification, received by a service from the push library. Tapping the notification fires an intent that opens the order details activity, or in a single-activity app, the order screen. The "Call rider" button sends an implicit ACTION_DIAL intent with the rider's number. "Open in maps" sends an implicit VIEW intent with a geo or map URL, and Google Maps opens. Every one of these steps is components and intents working together.

Real-life example 2, an NGO field survey app: Field workers in Sunamganj collect household data. The app uses a BroadcastReceiver registered while it runs to notice when connectivity returns, then schedules work to upload pending surveys. It uses an implicit intent with the camera to take a photo of a damaged house. It does not export any of its activities, because survey data is private. When a worker taps the app icon, the system starts the launcher activity declared in the manifest.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Beginners forget to declare a new activity in the manifest and get a crash saying the activity is not found. Some do long work inside a BroadcastReceiver, which is killed quickly. Others export components carelessly. Many confuse explicit and implicit intents. Typical exam questions: name and explain the four Android components with examples; what is an intent; explicit versus implicit intents with code; what is an intent filter; and what is the role of the manifest.

Recap: An Android app is built from four component types the system can start individually: activities (screens), services (work without UI), broadcast receivers (react to system events) and content providers (share data). All are declared in AndroidManifest.xml along with permissions and intent filters. Intents are request messages: explicit ones name a component, implicit ones describe an action and let the system find a matching app through intent filters. Activities form a back stack within a task. A Flutter app normally runs inside a single FlutterActivity.
key_points: Android apps are built from four components: Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver and ContentProvider.
An Activity is one screen with UI; a Flutter app usually runs inside a single FlutterActivity.
Services do work without UI; long user-visible work runs as a foreground service with a notification.
BroadcastReceivers react briefly to system events; ContentProviders share data through content:// URIs.
AndroidManifest.xml declares components, permissions, features and intent filters.
Explicit intents name the component; implicit intents describe an action and the system finds a matching app.
Activities form a back stack in a task; exported components are doors into your app and must be protected.
