lessons.tip: Make a four-row table with the components, and fill in for each: what it is, a real app example, and one lifecycle method or key fact. Reviewing that table before the exam covers the most common Android theory question.
lessons.task: On your phone, open the gallery, pick a photo and tap Share. Count how many apps appear in the share sheet. Write one sentence explaining, in terms of implicit intents and intent filters, why exactly those apps appear.

quiz.q: Which Android component represents a single screen with a user interface?
quiz.explain: An Activity is a single screen the user interacts with; services, receivers and providers have no UI of their own.

quiz.q: What is an implicit intent?
options: An intent that names the exact class to start
An intent that only works inside one app
An intent sent by the kernel
An intent that describes an action and lets the system find an app that can handle it
quiz.explain: Implicit intents, like ACTION_VIEW or ACTION_SEND, are matched against other apps' intent filters.

quiz.q: Where must you declare a new Activity so the system knows it exists?
quiz.explain: All activities must be declared in the manifest; otherwise starting them causes a crash.

quiz.q: Which component would you use to react briefly when the device finishes booting or the battery gets low?
quiz.explain: BroadcastReceivers respond to system-wide broadcast announcements such as boot completed or battery low.

quiz.q: Why does long-running, user-visible background work need a foreground service?
options: It allows the app to skip permissions
It is required to use Kotlin
The visible notification tells the user something is running and the system allows it to continue
quiz.explain: Foreground services show a persistent notification; newer Android versions restrict hidden background services to save battery.

lessons.title: The App Lifecycle
lessons.content:
Imagine you are filling in a long online admission form on your phone. Halfway through, your mother calls. You talk for five minutes, then open Facebook to check a message, then return to the form. If the form is empty again, you will be furious. Whether it is still filled or not depends on how the app handled its lifecycle. On a phone, your app does not simply run from start to finish. It is started, paused, hidden, sometimes killed and recreated by the operating system, and it must handle every step gracefully.

Why mobile apps have a lifecycle: A phone has limited memory and battery, and the user switches apps constantly. The operating system therefore manages apps actively. The app on screen gets full priority. Apps the user left recently are kept in memory in case they come back, but they are not allowed to use much processor time. When memory runs low, the system kills background app processes, starting with the least important ones. The app is not asked for permission; it is just told, through lifecycle callbacks, what is happening so it can save its work in time.

Process importance on Android: Android ranks processes roughly like this. The foreground process holds the activity the user is interacting with. A visible process holds something the user can see but is not using, such as an activity partly covered by a dialog. A service process runs a started service. Cached processes hold activities that are no longer visible; they are the first to be killed when memory is needed. So the moment your app goes into the background, it becomes a candidate for being killed.

The Activity lifecycle callbacks: An Android activity has six main callbacks that the system calls in order. onCreate runs once when the activity is created; here you set up the UI and initialise data. onStart runs when the activity becomes visible. onResume runs when it comes to the foreground and the user can interact with it. onPause runs when it loses focus, for example when another activity comes in front. onStop runs when it is no longer visible. onDestroy runs before the activity is destroyed. There is also onRestart, called before onStart when a stopped activity comes back.

A worked sequence, opening and leaving: The user taps your app icon: onCreate, onStart, onResume. The app is now running in the foreground. The user presses the home button: onPause, onStop. The activity is hidden but still in memory. The user returns through the recent apps screen: onRestart, onStart, onResume. If, instead, the user presses back on that screen, the activity usually finishes: onPause, onStop, onDestroy. Writing these sequences from memory is a common exam question, so practise them.

A worked sequence, rotation: By default, when the user rotates the phone, Android treats it as a configuration change and recreates the activity so it can load layouts and resources suited to the new orientation. The sequence is onPause, onStop, onDestroy, then a brand new instance runs onCreate, onStart, onResume. Any data stored only in the old activity object's fields is lost unless you saved it. The same recreation happens for other configuration changes, such as changing the system language, switching dark mode, or resizing in multi-window mode.

What to do in each callback: In onCreate, build the UI and restore saved state. In onStart and onResume, start things that are needed only while visible, such as camera preview, animations or location updates. In onPause, stop things that should not run when the user is not looking, and keep it fast, because the next activity cannot fully appear until your onPause finishes. In onStop, release heavier resources and save data that must not be lost. In onDestroy, do final cleanup, but do not rely on it for saving data, because if the process is killed, onDestroy may never be called.

Saving state, the Bundle: To survive recreation, Android gives each activity a chance to save small pieces of UI state into a Bundle, a key-value container, in onSaveInstanceState. When the activity is recreated, the same Bundle arrives in onCreate. For example: outState.putString("draftText", editText.text.toString()). Many standard views, such as text fields with IDs, save their own state automatically. The Bundle is meant for small data, like a text draft, a scroll position or a selected tab, not for large lists or images.

Process death, the hidden trap: Here is the case many developers never test. The user leaves your app, and while it is in the background the system kills the whole process to free memory. Later the user returns through the recent apps screen. Android creates a new process and recreates the activity, passing the saved Bundle, so it looks to the user as if the app was never closed. But every in-memory object, every static variable and every cached list is gone. If your code assumes they still exist, the app crashes or shows empty data. Developer options include a setting to not keep activities, which helps you test this.

ViewModel and lifecycle-aware components: Recreating everything on rotation would be painful, so Android Jetpack offers the ViewModel class. A ViewModel holds screen data and survives configuration changes: when the activity is recreated after rotation, the new instance gets the same ViewModel back, with data intact and without reloading from the network. A ViewModel does not survive process death, though; for that, it can use a SavedStateHandle that saves small values into the same saved-state mechanism. Lifecycle-aware components can also observe the lifecycle themselves and start or stop work automatically.

State in Jetpack Compose: If you build the Android UI with Compose, the same rules apply with different tools. A value created with remember { mutableStateOf(0) } survives redraws of the UI, but it is lost when the activity is recreated on rotation. A value created with rememberSaveable is written into the saved-state Bundle automatically, so it survives rotation and even process death, as long as it is small and of a type that can be saved. A common pattern is: rememberSaveable for small UI details like an expanded card or a typed search query, and a ViewModel for the real screen data.

Multi-window and pausing: On large phones and tablets, two apps can be shown side by side. Then an activity can be visible but not focused, so onPause has been called while the user can still see it. This is why the rule is to stop work in onStop, not onPause, when the work is related to visibility, such as a video that should keep playing while visible. Thinking in terms of visible versus focused, instead of simply running versus not running, keeps your app correct on both phones and tablets.

The iOS app states: iOS describes the whole app with a small set of states. Not running: the app has not been launched or was terminated. Inactive: the app is in the foreground but not receiving events, for example briefly during an incoming call alert. Active: in the foreground and receiving events, the normal running state. Background: no longer on screen but still executing code for a short time, for example to finish saving. Suspended: in memory but not executing code at all. The system can terminate suspended apps at any time without notice to free memory.

iOS callbacks at concept level: iOS informs the app of these transitions through methods on the app delegate or, in apps with multiple windows, the scene delegate, with names like did become active, will resign active, did enter background and will enter foreground. SwiftUI offers a scenePhase value that is active, inactive or background. The advice is the same as on Android: save user data and release shared resources when entering the background, because you may never get another chance before being terminated.

The Flutter app lifecycle: A Flutter app is one activity on Android and one view controller on iOS, and Flutter turns the platform signals into one enum, AppLifecycleState. The main values are resumed (visible and responding to input), inactive (in the foreground but not receiving input, for example during a phone call overlay or while switching apps), paused (not visible, in the background), and detached (the engine is running without any view). Newer Flutter versions also have a hidden state between inactive and paused. You listen to these with WidgetsBindingObserver or the AppLifecycleListener class.

A Flutter example: To pause a video when the app goes to the background, you add a lifecycle observer to your screen's state class and implement didChangeAppLifecycleState(AppLifecycleState state) { if (state == AppLifecycleState.paused) { controller.pause(); } }. You register the observer in initState with WidgetsBinding.instance.addObserver(this) and remove it in dispose with removeObserver(this). Forgetting to remove observers or dispose controllers causes memory leaks.

Widget lifecycle inside Flutter: Separately from the app lifecycle, every StatefulWidget's State object has its own lifecycle. initState runs once when it is inserted into the tree; set up controllers and subscriptions there. build runs every time the UI must be redrawn, so it must be fast and free of side effects. didUpdateWidget runs when the parent rebuilds it with new configuration. dispose runs when it is removed forever; release controllers, timers and stream subscriptions there. Lesson 8 shows these in a real widget.

Real-life example 1, a mobile banking transfer: A user starts sending 5,000 taka on a bank app, types the account number, and then gets a phone call. The app receives inactive, then paused. A well-built app keeps the typed account number (saved state), but for security it may ask for the PIN again when resumed after a long time, and it never keeps the PIN in saved state. If the process is killed, the app restores the form from saved state when the user returns, and shows the login screen again if the session has expired.

Real-life example 2, a Ludo game on a slow phone: Two cousins are playing a Ludo game on an old phone with 2 GB of RAM. One switches to the camera to take a photo. The camera needs lots of memory, so Android kills the game's process. When they return, a badly written game starts from zero and they lose the match. A well-written one saved the board state when it was paused, either in saved state or in local storage, and restores the exact positions. This is the difference users notice and rate on the Play Store.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Doing heavy work in onPause, which slows down switching. Saving data only in onDestroy. Keeping important data only in memory and never testing process death. Forgetting that rotation recreates the activity. Leaking listeners by not unregistering them in the matching callback, such as registering in onStart but never unregistering in onStop. Exams ask you to draw the activity lifecycle diagram, list callbacks for a given scenario like rotation or an incoming call, explain process death, or list iOS app states.

Recap: Mobile apps live inside a lifecycle controlled by the operating system, which pauses, stops and kills apps to protect memory and battery. Android activities move through onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop and onDestroy, with onRestart on return; rotation and other configuration changes recreate them. Save small UI state in a Bundle, keep screen data in a ViewModel that survives rotation, and test process death. iOS apps move between not running, inactive, active, background and suspended. Flutter exposes AppLifecycleState values like resumed, inactive, paused and detached, and its State objects have initState, build and dispose.
key_points: The OS pauses, stops and kills background apps to save memory and battery; apps must save work in time.
Activity callbacks in order: onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroy, plus onRestart on return.
Rotation and other configuration changes destroy and recreate the activity by default.
Save small UI state in a Bundle (onSaveInstanceState); a ViewModel survives rotation but not process death.
Process death: the app is killed in the background and recreated later with saved state but empty memory.
iOS states: not running, inactive, active, background, suspended; suspended apps can be terminated without notice.
Flutter's AppLifecycleState includes resumed, inactive, paused and detached; State objects use initState, build and dispose.
lessons.tip: Draw the activity lifecycle as a loop with arrows and practise three scenarios on it: home button and return, rotation, and back button. If you can trace these three without looking, you can answer almost any lifecycle question.
lessons.task: Open any form-like app on your phone (a notes app or a message box), type a sentence, then rotate the phone, press home, open three other apps, and come back. Note whether your text survived each step. Then guess which lifecycle events happened at each step.

quiz.q: Which callbacks run, in order, when a user opens an activity from the launcher?
quiz.explain: A new activity goes through onCreate, then onStart (visible), then onResume (interactive).

quiz.q: What happens to an activity by default when the user rotates the screen?
options: It is destroyed and recreated as a new instance
quiz.explain: Rotation is a configuration change, so Android destroys and recreates the activity to load suitable resources.

quiz.q: What does a ViewModel survive?
options: Process death without any extra saving
quiz.explain: A ViewModel survives configuration changes, but not process death; SavedStateHandle helps for small values.

quiz.q: In iOS, what is true about an app in the suspended state?
options: It is actively running code in the foreground
It is waiting for a phone call
It is in memory but not running code, and may be terminated without notice
quiz.explain: Suspended apps stay in memory without executing; the system may terminate them at any time to free memory.

quiz.q: Where should a Flutter State object release controllers and stream subscriptions?
quiz.explain: dispose runs when the State is removed permanently, so resources must be released there to avoid leaks.

lessons.title: Building UI I: Imperative vs Declarative, Widgets
lessons.content:
Picture the scoreboard at a cricket match in Mirpur Sher-e-Bangla stadium. In the old days, a person stood behind the board and changed the numbers by hand: take down the 4, put up a 5, change the overs, change the wickets. If he forgot one plate, the board showed a wrong score. A modern digital scoreboard works differently: a computer simply knows the current score and redraws the whole board from it. Nobody edits individual numbers. These two scoreboards are a perfect picture of the two ways to build mobile user interfaces: imperative and declarative.

The UI is a tree: Every screen you see is made of nested pieces. A screen contains a top bar and a body; the body contains a column; the column contains a picture, a title, a price and a button; the button contains a label. This nesting forms a tree, with the screen as the root and small elements as leaves. On Android the classic pieces are called views and view groups, on iOS views, and in Flutter widgets. Whatever the name, building UI means describing this tree and keeping it in sync with your data.

The imperative style: In the traditional Android approach, you describe the initial tree in an XML layout file, such as a LinearLayout containing a TextView with id score and a Button. In code you find the views and change them step by step: val scoreView = findViewById<TextView>(R.id.score); button.setOnClickListener { runs += 4; scoreView.text = "Runs: $runs" }. You are the man behind the scoreboard: whenever data changes, you must remember every view that depends on it and update each one by hand. Classic iOS UIKit works the same way.

The trouble with imperative UI: In a small screen this is fine. In a large screen, one piece of data, say whether the user is logged in, may affect ten views: the greeting, the menu, the profile picture, three buttons and so on. Each code path that changes the data must update all ten. Miss one and the screen shows a contradiction, like "Welcome, Rahim" next to a "Log in" button. These bugs are common, hard to find and get worse as the app grows.

The declarative idea: Declarative UI flips the approach. You write a function that says: given the current state, this is what the screen should look like. In short, UI = f(state). When the state changes, you do not touch any view; you just change the state, and the framework calls your function again to get the new description and updates the screen efficiently. You are the computer behind the digital scoreboard. Flutter, Jetpack Compose on Android, SwiftUI on iOS and React Native all follow this idea.

What declarative looks like: In Flutter the same score example becomes: Text('Runs: $runs') inside the build method, and the button does setState(() { runs += 4; });. In Jetpack Compose it is Text("Runs: $runs") inside a @Composable function, with runs held in a state variable. In SwiftUI it is Text("Runs: \(runs)") inside a view's body. In every case you never write "find the text view and change it". You describe; the framework updates.

Why the framework does not redraw everything: It might seem wasteful to rebuild the description of the whole screen on every change. The trick is that the description is made of cheap, lightweight objects, and the framework compares the new description with the old one and changes only the parts that differ on the real screen. This comparing is often called diffing or reconciliation. You get the simplicity of "redraw everything" with the cost of "update only what changed".

Flutter's core idea, everything is a widget: In Flutter, a widget is an immutable description of part of the UI. Text, Image, Icon and ElevatedButton are widgets, but so are layout helpers like Padding, Center, Row and Column, and even invisible things like GestureDetector and Theme. You build screens by composing small widgets inside each other, not by inheriting from big classes. Want space around text? Wrap it: Padding(padding: EdgeInsets.all(16), child: Text('Hello')). This composition style is the heart of Flutter.

StatelessWidget: A StatelessWidget has no data of its own that changes over time. It receives its configuration from its parent through constructor parameters and turns it into a widget tree in its build method. Example: class PriceTag extends StatelessWidget { final int price; const PriceTag({super.key, required this.price}); @override Widget build(BuildContext context) { return Text('৳$price'); } }. If the parent passes a new price, Flutter builds a new PriceTag. Most widgets in a well-built app are stateless.

StatefulWidget and State: When part of the UI must change by itself, for example a counter, a checkbox or a form, you use a StatefulWidget. It is split into two classes: the widget, which is immutable configuration, and a State object, which lives longer and holds the changing data. You change data inside setState: setState(() { count++; });. Calling setState marks this widget as dirty, and Flutter calls its build method again in the next frame. The State object keeps its data across rebuilds.

The counter app, read slowly: The template from flutter create has class MyHomePage extends StatefulWidget and a State class with int _counter = 0;. The method _incrementCounter calls setState(() { _counter++; }). The build method returns a Scaffold, the basic Material page structure, with an AppBar, a body with Center and Column containing two Text widgets, the second showing '$_counter', and a FloatingActionButton whose onPressed is _incrementCounter. Tap the button, the state changes, build runs, and the new number appears. That is the whole declarative loop in twenty lines.

BuildContext: Every build method receives a BuildContext. It is a handle to this widget's position in the tree. You use it to look up things provided higher in the tree, such as Theme.of(context) for colours and fonts, MediaQuery.of(context) for screen size, or Navigator.of(context) to move between screens. Because it represents a location, using a context from the wrong place, for example after the widget has been removed, causes errors. You will meet context constantly.

The three trees in Flutter: Behind the scenes Flutter keeps three related trees. The widget tree is your cheap, immutable description, rebuilt often. The element tree holds the long-lived instances that link each widget to its place on screen and keep State objects. The render tree holds RenderObjects that do the real layout and painting. When you rebuild, Flutter compares new widgets with the elements and updates render objects only where needed. You do not manage these trees yourself, but knowing they exist explains why rebuilding is cheap and why State survives rebuilds.

Keep build methods pure and small: Because build can run many times per second, for example during an animation, it must not start network requests, write files or do heavy calculations. Put those in initState, in event handlers, or in separate state management classes. Split large build methods into smaller widget classes; this makes code readable and lets Flutter rebuild only the parts that changed. Mark widgets const when their inputs never change, so Flutter can reuse them.

Common Material building blocks: Scaffold gives a page with app bar, body, floating action button, drawer and bottom navigation slots. AppBar shows the title and actions. Text and Icon show content. Image.asset and Image.network show pictures. ElevatedButton, TextButton and IconButton handle taps. Card groups content with a shadow. ListTile is a ready-made row with leading icon, title and subtitle. With these and Row, Column and Padding you can build most screens. Lesson 9 covers layout in depth.

Jetpack Compose in a little more detail: In Compose, UI pieces are Kotlin functions marked @Composable instead of classes. A function like @Composable fun Greeting(name: String) { Text("Salam, $name") } emits UI when called. State is held with remember { mutableStateOf(0) }, and when a state value changes, Compose re-runs only the composable functions that read it; this is called recomposition. Layout uses Column, Row and Box, and styling uses a chain of modifiers such as Modifier.padding(16.dp).fillMaxWidth(). The vocabulary differs from Flutter, but the mental model, describe UI from state and let the framework update, is the same.

Themes and styling: Hard-coding a colour like a specific green in fifty places makes a redesign painful. Both Flutter and Compose provide a theme: a central set of colours, text styles and shapes. In Flutter you set ThemeData in MaterialApp and read it with Theme.of(context).colorScheme.primary or Theme.of(context).textTheme.titleLarge. Supporting dark mode then becomes mostly a matter of giving a second theme. A consistent theme also helps accessibility, which lesson 24 covers, because contrast and text sizes are controlled in one place.

Mixing old and new: Real projects are rarely pure. Many Android apps were written with XML views and are moving to Compose one screen at a time; Compose and views can live together in the same screen. Flutter can be added to an existing native app as a module for a few screens, called add-to-app. So a job may require you to read both imperative and declarative code. Understanding why declarative UI was invented helps you work in both.

Real-life example 1, a cricket live score card: An app shows a live score card for a Bangladesh match. The state is one object: runs, wickets, overs, current batsmen and the last six balls. The build method describes the card from that object. When the server sends a new ball, the code replaces the state object and calls setState or its state manager. The runs, wickets, over count and the little circles for the last six balls all update together. No risk of showing 6 wickets on one line and 5 on another.

Real-life example 2, tap to see balance: Many mobile wallet apps in Bangladesh hide the balance until you tap. In declarative style, the state is a bool showBalance and maybe the balance value. The build method says: if showBalance, show Text('৳ 2,450'), else show a button 'Tap for balance'. Tapping sets showBalance to true and, after a few seconds, a timer sets it back to false. The screen always matches the state, and there is no code path that can leave the old text visible by mistake.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Beginners call setState for data that does not affect the UI, or forget to call it, so the screen does not update. Some create controllers or start requests inside build, which repeats them on every rebuild. Others build one giant widget with hundreds of lines. Exam questions ask: compare imperative and declarative UI with examples; explain UI = f(state); difference between StatelessWidget and StatefulWidget; what setState does; or what the widget, element and render trees are.

Recap: A screen is a tree of UI elements. In the imperative style, used with XML layouts and classic UIKit, you find views and change them by hand, which leads to inconsistency bugs in large screens. In the declarative style, used by Flutter, Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI, you describe the UI as a function of state and the framework updates the screen by comparing descriptions. In Flutter everything is a widget; StatelessWidget depends only on its inputs, StatefulWidget keeps a State object and rebuilds when setState is called. Keep build methods pure, small and fast.
key_points: Every screen is a tree of UI elements: views on Android/iOS, widgets in Flutter.
Imperative UI: find views and change them by hand, which causes inconsistency bugs as screens grow.
Declarative UI: UI = f(state); change state and the framework rebuilds and updates only what changed.
Flutter, Jetpack Compose and SwiftUI are declarative; classic XML layouts and UIKit are imperative.
StatelessWidget depends only on its inputs; StatefulWidget keeps a State object and rebuilds when setState is called.
Flutter keeps widget, element and render trees; widgets are cheap immutable descriptions.
Keep build methods pure, fast and small: no network calls or heavy work inside build.
lessons.tip: When you write a screen, first write down its state on paper as a short list of variables. Then write build as if you only have those variables. If the screen needs something not on your list, your state is incomplete.
lessons.task: Pick one screen from an app you use, such as a ride app's booking screen. Draw its UI tree as boxes inside boxes, then write a list of the state variables that decide what it shows (for example: pickup, destination, fare, isLoading).

quiz.q: What does UI = f(state) mean in declarative UI?
options: The UI is stored in a database
The UI must be written in a functional language
Every view must be found by ID before changing
The screen is described as a function of the current state, and redrawn when state changes
quiz.explain: Declarative frameworks call your build function with the current state and update the screen from the result.

quiz.q: Which of these is an imperative UI approach?
options: Android XML layout with findViewById and setText
quiz.explain: XML layouts with findViewById require you to change each view by hand, which is the imperative style.

quiz.q: What does calling setState in a Flutter State object do?
options: Marks the widget as needing a rebuild so build runs again
Sends the state to the server
quiz.explain: setState marks the widget dirty; Flutter calls build again in the next frame with the new state.

quiz.q: When should you use a StatelessWidget?
options: When the widget must change its own data over time
When the widget only depends on the inputs given by its parent
Only for the app's main function
quiz.explain: StatelessWidgets have no changing internal data; they turn their constructor inputs into UI.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid starting network requests inside build?
options: build may run many times, so the request would repeat on every rebuild
Network requests are not allowed in Dart
build cannot use async code at all
It makes the app icon disappear
quiz.explain: build runs often, for example during animations, so side effects there repeat; put them in initState, handlers or state classes.

lessons.title: Building UI II: Layout, Screen Sizes and Input
lessons.content:
Think of arranging furniture in a rented flat in Mohammadpur. The landlord tells you the room size, you decide how much space the bed, table and almirah each need, and then you place them. If you buy a sofa that is too big, it simply does not fit, and something sticks out of the door. Laying out a mobile screen works almost the same way: the parent gives space, children decide their size within it, and if something is too big, you get an overflow. This lesson covers how layout works, how to handle many screen sizes and densities, and how to take input from the user through forms and gestures.

The Flutter layout rule: Flutter's layout fits in one sentence: constraints go down, sizes go up, and the parent sets the position. A parent widget tells each child the minimum and maximum width and height it may have; these are the constraints. The child picks a size within those limits and reports it back. Then the parent decides where to place the child. Every layout surprise in Flutter, such as a widget that refuses to be as big as you asked, can be explained with this rule.

A worked example of constraints: The screen is 360 by 800 logical pixels. The root passes tight constraints: exactly 360 by 800. A Center widget loosens them: its child may be anything from 0 up to 360 by 800. Inside is a Container with width 200 and height 100. It asks for 200 by 100, which fits, so it gets that size, and Center places it in the middle. If the Container asked for width 500, it would be clamped to 360, because a child cannot be bigger than its constraints allow. This is why a width you set sometimes seems ignored.

Row and Column: Most screens are built from Row (children side by side) and Column (children top to bottom). Each has a main axis, horizontal for Row and vertical for Column, and a cross axis. mainAxisAlignment controls spacing along the main axis: start, center, end, spaceBetween, spaceAround, spaceEvenly. crossAxisAlignment controls alignment across it, such as start or stretch. For example, a product row might be Row(mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.spaceBetween, children: [Text('Rice 5 kg'), Text('৳ 450')]), putting the name on the left and price on the right.

Expanded and flexible space: If Row children want more total width than available, Flutter shows an overflow error with yellow and black stripes in debug mode, and the message says a RenderFlex overflowed by some pixels. The fix is often to wrap a child in Expanded, which says: take the remaining space. Several Expanded children share space by their flex values: Expanded(flex: 2, ...) and Expanded(flex: 1, ...) split the leftover space two-to-one. Flexible is similar but lets the child be smaller than its share. Long text inside Expanded can then wrap or be cut with an ellipsis.

Other layout tools: Padding adds inner space around a child. SizedBox gives a fixed size or a fixed gap, such as SizedBox(height: 12) between two fields. Container combines padding, margin, colour, border and size. Stack puts children on top of each other, with Positioned to place one at a specific spot, useful for a badge on an icon or text on a banner image. Align places a child at a fraction of its parent. Wrap behaves like a Row that flows onto the next line, useful for tags or chips. ListView and SingleChildScrollView make content scroll when it is taller than the screen.

Why pixels lie, density: Phone screens differ not only in size but in density: how many physical pixels fit in an inch, measured in dots per inch (dpi). A button 100 physical pixels wide would look large on a low-density budget phone and tiny on a high-density flagship. So mobile platforms use a virtual unit. Android calls it the density-independent pixel, dp; iOS uses points; Flutter uses logical pixels, which behave the same way. One dp is defined as one physical pixel on a 160 dpi screen.

A worked density calculation: The formula is physical pixels = dp × (dpi / 160). A 48 dp button on a 160 dpi screen is 48 pixels. On a 320 dpi screen it is 48 × 2 = 96 pixels. On a 480 dpi screen it is 48 × 3 = 144 pixels. In all three cases it is roughly the same physical size, about the size of a fingertip. Android groups densities into buckets such as mdpi (160), hdpi (240), xhdpi (320), xxhdpi (480) and xxxhdpi (640), and you can supply images for each. For text, Android uses sp, which is like dp but also scales with the user's font size setting.

Screen sizes and orientation: Even in dp, screens differ: a small phone may be about 320 dp wide, a large phone around 400 dp, a tablet 600 dp or more. Rotation swaps width and height. In Flutter, MediaQuery gives the screen size, orientation, text scale and padding for notches, and LayoutBuilder tells you the constraints a particular widget received. Material Design suggests window size classes: compact for widths under 600 dp, medium from 600 to 840 dp, and expanded above that, as practical breakpoints for changing the layout.

Responsive layouts in practice: A responsive layout changes structure, not just scale. On a compact phone, a shop app might show a single column of products and a bottom navigation bar. On a tablet in landscape, it might show a grid of three columns and a side navigation rail, or a list on the left and details on the right. In code: LayoutBuilder(builder: (context, constraints) => constraints.maxWidth < 600 ? ProductList() : ProductGrid(columns: 3)). Avoid hard-coded pixel widths; prefer Expanded, fractions and constraints so the layout adapts.

Safe areas and system bars: Modern phones have notches, camera holes, rounded corners, a status bar at the top and gesture or navigation bars at the bottom. Content placed under them may be hidden or impossible to tap. Flutter's SafeArea widget adds padding to avoid these regions; Scaffold with an AppBar handles the top for you. Always check your screens on a phone with a notch and on one with on-screen navigation buttons.

Design systems, Material and Cupertino: Flutter ships two widget sets. Material widgets follow Google's Material Design and are the default on both platforms. Cupertino widgets imitate iOS controls, such as CupertinoButton and CupertinoNavigationBar. Some apps use Material everywhere for a consistent brand; others adapt certain controls, like switches and dialogs, to each platform. Why certain spacing, colours or control choices are better for users is a question for Human Computer Interaction; here we focus on how to build them.

Taking text input: The basic input widget is TextField, or TextFormField inside a form. A TextEditingController lets you read and set its text: final phoneCtrl = TextEditingController(); then TextField(controller: phoneCtrl). Create controllers in initState or as fields of a State object, and dispose them in dispose. Use decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: 'Mobile number', hintText: '01XXXXXXXXX') to label the field clearly, because placeholder text alone disappears as soon as the user types.

Choosing the right keyboard: Mobile keyboards change with the field. keyboardType: TextInputType.phone shows a dial pad, TextInputType.number shows digits, TextInputType.emailAddress adds the @ key, and TextInputType.multiline allows new lines. obscureText: true hides passwords. textInputAction: TextInputAction.next shows a Next key that moves focus to the following field, and TextInputAction.done closes the keyboard. These small details make forms much faster to fill on a phone, where typing is slow.

Forms and validation: Wrap fields in a Form with a GlobalKey<FormState>. Each TextFormField gets a validator function that returns null when the value is fine or an error message string when it is not. For a Bangladeshi mobile number: validator: (v) => RegExp(r'^01[3-9][0-9]{8}$').hasMatch(v ?? '') ? null : 'Enter a valid 11-digit number'. When the user taps Submit, call formKey.currentState!.validate(); it runs every validator and shows messages under the wrong fields. Validate on the device for quick feedback, but always validate again on the server, because client checks can be bypassed.

The keyboard covering fields: When the keyboard opens it covers roughly the bottom half of the screen. Scaffold resizes its body by default so content moves up, but if your form does not scroll, lower fields may still be hidden or cause overflow. Put long forms inside a SingleChildScrollView or ListView so the user can scroll to any field while the keyboard is open. Test every form with the keyboard open on a small phone.

Gestures: For taps and other touches, Flutter offers GestureDetector with callbacks such as onTap, onDoubleTap, onLongPress, onHorizontalDragEnd for swipes, and onScaleUpdate for pinch zoom. InkWell gives a tap with the Material ripple effect, which shows the user that the touch was registered. Dismissible lets the user swipe a list item away, for example to delete a notification. Keep touch targets at least about 48 by 48 dp so they are easy to hit; lesson 24 explains why this matters for accessibility.

Real-life example 1, a registration form for a coaching centre: The form has name, mobile number, email, class and a password. Name uses a normal keyboard with capitalisation, mobile uses the phone keyboard and the 11-digit validator, email uses the email keyboard, class is a dropdown, and the password field hides text with a show or hide icon. Next buttons move between fields, Done submits. The whole form sits in a scroll view, the Submit button is full width and at least 48 dp tall, and errors appear right under the field that is wrong.

Real-life example 2, a product grid on phones and tablets: An online grocery app in Dhaka shows products as cards with a picture, a name in Bangla and English, and a price. On a 360 dp phone, LayoutBuilder chooses a two-column grid; on a tablet, four columns. Card text uses Expanded and maxLines: 2 with an ellipsis so long names like a full brand name do not overflow. Images are supplied at several densities or loaded at the right size. The same code serves a cheap phone and a large tablet properly.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Using fixed pixel sizes everywhere so the layout breaks on other phones; ignoring overflow warnings; putting a ListView inside a Column without giving it bounded height, which causes an unbounded height error; forgetting SafeArea; using the wrong keyboard type; and validating only on the client. Exams ask: what is dp and how to convert dp to pixels at a given dpi; explain constraints in Flutter layout; how to design for multiple screen sizes; and how to validate form input.

Recap: In Flutter, constraints go down, sizes go up, and parents set positions. Row and Column arrange children along main and cross axes; Expanded and Flexible share leftover space; Stack, Padding, SizedBox and Wrap handle other layouts. Density-independent units (dp, points, logical pixels) keep sizes physically consistent: pixels = dp × dpi / 160. Use MediaQuery, LayoutBuilder and breakpoints for responsive layouts, and SafeArea for notches. Collect input with TextField, controllers, the right keyboard type and Form validators, keep forms scrollable, and use GestureDetector or InkWell for touches with large touch targets.
key_points: Flutter layout rule: constraints go down, sizes go up, and the parent sets the position.
Row and Column arrange children on main and cross axes; Expanded shares remaining space and fixes overflow.
Density-independent pixels keep sizes consistent: physical pixels = dp × (dpi / 160).
Responsive layouts change structure using MediaQuery, LayoutBuilder and breakpoints (around 600 dp for compact).
SafeArea keeps content away from notches, status bars and navigation bars.
TextField with a controller, the right keyboardType and Form validators gives fast, correct input; validate again on the server.
Use GestureDetector or InkWell for touches, and keep touch targets about 48 by 48 dp.
lessons.tip: Turn on Show layout bounds in Android Developer options and open your favourite apps. You will see the boxes and padding behind every screen, which teaches layout faster than any book.
lessons.task: Calculate on paper how many physical pixels a 48 dp button is on screens of 240, 320 and 480 dpi. Then sketch a login screen for a phone (360 dp wide) and for a tablet (800 dp wide), showing how the layout changes, not just the size.

quiz.q: In Flutter's layout system, what goes down from parent to child?
quiz.explain: Parents pass constraints (min and max sizes) down; children choose sizes and pass them up; parents set positions.

quiz.q: How many physical pixels is a 48 dp button on a 480 dpi screen?
A Row's children are wider than the screen and Flutter shows yellow and black stripes. What is a common fix?
options: Wrap a child in Expanded so it takes only the remaining space
quiz.explain: Expanded makes a child fill the leftover space instead of demanding more than is available.

quiz.q: What should a TextFormField validator return when the input is valid?
quiz.explain: Validators return null for valid input and an error message string for invalid input.

quiz.q: Why should form validation also happen on the server?
options: Client-side checks can be bypassed, so the server must check data too
quiz.explain: On-device validation is for quick feedback; the server is the trust boundary and must validate again.

lessons.title: Navigation Between Screens
lessons.content:
Imagine a stack of plates at a wedding buffet in a community centre. A waiter puts a clean plate on top, you take the top plate, and nobody pulls a plate from the middle. Mobile navigation works like that stack. You open the product list, then a product, then the cart: each new screen is placed on top. Press back and the top screen is removed, showing the one underneath. Understanding this stack, and the other patterns built around it, is the key to making apps that feel natural instead of confusing.

What navigation is: Navigation is how users move between the screens of an app and how the app remembers where they came from. It includes moving forward to a new screen, going back, switching between main sections, opening temporary panels like dialogs, passing data from one screen to another, and opening a specific screen directly from a link or notification. Good navigation means the user always knows where they are, how they got there, and how to go back.

The back stack idea: Both Android and iOS model drill-down navigation as a stack of screens. Opening a screen pushes it on the stack; going back pops it off. In lesson 6 you saw Android keep a stack of activities in a task. Inside one app, especially a Flutter app that runs in a single activity, the framework keeps its own stack of screens. In Flutter these screens are called routes, and the object that manages the stack is the Navigator.

Pushing a screen in Flutter: To open a detail screen you write Navigator.push(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (context) => ProductScreen(productId: 42)));. MaterialPageRoute builds the new screen and gives it the platform-style transition animation: on Android it slides or fades up, on iOS it slides in from the right. The new screen now covers the old one, but the old one is still alive on the stack underneath, keeping its state, such as the scroll position of the product list.

Popping and returning results: To go back you call Navigator.pop(context). You can also return a value: Navigator.pop(context, 'Mirpur 10'). The original push call returns a Future that completes with that value: final area = await Navigator.push<String>(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => AreaPicker()));. If the user pressed back without choosing, the result is null, so you must handle that case. This is a clean way to build picker screens: choose an address, choose a payment method, choose a date.

Passing data forward: The simplest and safest way to send data to a new screen is through its constructor, as in ProductScreen(productId: 42). Prefer passing an ID and letting the new screen load the details from the repository or cache, instead of passing a large object that may be out of date. This also makes deep links easy later, because a link can carry only an ID like 42, never a full object.

Replacing and clearing the stack: Sometimes the back button should not return to the previous screen. After a successful login, going back to the login form would be strange, so you replace it: Navigator.pushReplacement(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => HomeScreen()));. After logout, you want to remove every screen and show login: Navigator.pushAndRemoveUntil(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => LoginScreen()), (route) => false);. The false means remove all previous routes. After placing an order, apps often clear the cart and checkout screens and show an order status screen.

Named routes and router packages: For larger apps, writing MaterialPageRoute everywhere becomes messy. Flutter lets you register named routes in MaterialApp, such as '/cart' and '/profile', and open them with Navigator.pushNamed(context, '/cart'). For apps that need web-style URLs and deep links, Flutter also has a lower-level Router API, and most teams use a package such as go_router on top of it, where you define paths like '/product/:id' and navigate with context.go('/product/42'). The Flutter documentation now generally recommends a router package over plain named routes for apps with deep linking.

The Android back button and gesture: Android users go back with a system back button or a swipe from the screen edge. By default this pops the top route in Flutter, or finishes the activity if only one screen is left. Sometimes you must intercept it, for example to ask "Discard this unsent message?". Flutter provides the PopScope widget for this, where you can block the pop or handle it yourself. Use it sparingly; blocking back without a clear reason annoys users. iOS has no system back button, so every pushed screen needs a visible back button in its top bar, which Flutter's AppBar adds automatically.

Back versus up: Platform guidelines distinguish two ideas. Back goes to the previous screen in time, whatever it was. Up, the arrow in the top bar, goes to the logical parent screen in the app's hierarchy. Usually they are the same. They differ when the user arrived from outside, such as from a notification straight into a message: back may return to the previous app, while up should go to the inbox of your app. Thinking about this prevents users getting trapped or thrown out unexpectedly.

Native navigation briefly: In Jetpack Compose on Android, the Navigation library uses a NavHost that lists destinations with routes, and a NavController that you call to navigate, such as navController.navigate("product/42"), and to pop with popBackStack(). In classic Android, the Navigation component used a navigation graph file to describe screens and actions. On iOS, UIKit uses a UINavigationController that pushes and pops view controllers, and SwiftUI uses a NavigationStack. The stack concept is the same everywhere; only the API names differ.

Top-level navigation, bottom bar and tabs: Apps with a few main sections, usually three to five, use a bottom navigation bar, for example Home, Search, Orders and Profile. Tapping a tab switches sections instead of pushing onto a stack. In Flutter you can use a Scaffold with a NavigationBar or BottomNavigationBar and keep an index in state. A good app gives each tab its own history, so if you go deep into Orders, switch to Home, and come back, Orders is still where you left it. Tabs at the top of a screen, with TabBar and TabBarView, switch between related views within one section.

Drawers and modals: A navigation drawer slides in from the side with many destinations; it suits apps with many sections but hides options, so it is less used for the main few. Modal screens appear above the current flow for a short task and then disappear: dialogs for confirmations, bottom sheets for options like "Share, Edit, Delete", and full-screen dialogs for creating something new. In Flutter, showDialog and showModalBottomSheet open them; they are also routes on the stack, so Navigator.pop closes them.

Deep links: A deep link is a URL that opens a specific screen inside an app, not just its home page. For example, a link like https://shop.example.com/product/42 shared on Messenger could open product 42 in the shop's app if it is installed, or the website if not. Android App Links and iOS Universal Links make normal https links open apps; the developer proves ownership of the domain by placing a small verification file on the website. Custom schemes like myshop://product/42 also work but can be claimed by any app, so verified https links are preferred.

Notifications as navigation: Push notifications are a very common entry point. Tapping "Your order is out for delivery" should open that order's status screen, with a sensible back stack under it, such as the orders list. Your notification handler therefore needs the same routing logic as deep links: read an ID from the notification data and navigate to the route. Designing routes around IDs from the beginning, as in /order/:id, makes this easy. Lesson 21 covers notifications themselves.

Transitions and what they tell the user: The animation between screens is not decoration; it explains the navigation. A screen sliding in from the right says you went deeper and can come back. A sheet rising from the bottom says this is a temporary task above the current one. A cross-fade between tabs says you switched sections at the same level. MaterialPageRoute and CupertinoPageRoute pick the platform's normal transition for you; custom transitions with PageRouteBuilder are possible but should keep this meaning. If every screen animates differently, users lose their sense of where they are.

Using context safely after waiting: A common bug appears when a screen awaits something and then navigates. For example, the user taps Save, the app awaits a network call for two seconds, then calls Navigator.pop(context). If the user already pressed back during those two seconds, the screen is gone and its context is no longer valid. In a State object you check if (!mounted) return; after every await before using context. This small habit prevents confusing crashes reported only from users on slow networks, which in Bangladesh means many of your users.

Nested navigators: Bigger apps sometimes put a Navigator inside each tab, so that pushing a screen inside the Orders tab keeps the bottom bar visible and gives that tab its own stack. Router packages such as go_router support this with a shell route that wraps the tabs. The trade-off is more complex code: you must decide which navigator a push should go to, and how the system back button moves through nested stacks. Start simple with one navigator, and add nesting only when the design really needs persistent tabs.

Real-life example 1, a food delivery order flow: Home shows restaurants. Tap one: push RestaurantScreen. Add items and tap the cart: push CartScreen. Tap Checkout: push CheckoutScreen, where the user picks an address from a pushed picker screen that returns the selection with pop. After payment, pushAndRemoveUntil goes to OrderStatusScreen and removes cart and checkout from the stack, so back cannot accidentally reopen a finished checkout. The bottom bar keeps Home, Orders and Profile as separate tabs with their own history.

Real-life example 2, a shared link to a news article: A friend shares a link to an article from a national newspaper's website on WhatsApp. If the news app is installed and handles that domain with verified links, tapping opens the article screen directly. Pressing back should go to the app's home feed or back to WhatsApp, depending on the design, but never to a blank screen. The router reads the article ID from the URL path, loads the article, and shows a loading state while it arrives.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Pushing a new home screen every time the user taps Home, so the stack grows forever and back goes through dozens of copies. Passing full objects instead of IDs. Forgetting to handle a null result from a picker. Using context after an await when the screen may already be closed. Blocking back without reason. Exams ask: explain the back stack with push and pop; compare tabs, drawers and stack navigation; how to pass data between screens and return results; and what deep links are.

Recap: Navigation moves users between screens and remembers the path. Drill-down navigation is a stack: push to open, pop to go back. In Flutter, Navigator.push with MaterialPageRoute opens screens, Navigator.pop returns, and push returns a Future with the result. pushReplacement and pushAndRemoveUntil reshape the stack after login, logout or checkout. Router packages like go_router handle URL-style routes and deep links. Bottom bars and tabs handle top-level sections, drawers and modals handle the rest. Deep links and notifications should open specific screens using IDs in routes.
key_points: Drill-down navigation is a back stack: push opens a screen on top, pop removes it and shows the one below.
Flutter's Navigator manages routes: Navigator.push with MaterialPageRoute opens, Navigator.pop goes back.
push returns a Future that completes with the value given to pop, or null if the user just went back.
Pass small data like IDs through constructors; let the new screen load the details.
pushReplacement and pushAndRemoveUntil reshape the stack after login, logout or checkout.
Bottom navigation bars and tabs switch top-level sections; dialogs and bottom sheets are short modal routes.
Deep links (App Links, Universal Links) and notifications open specific screens, so design routes around IDs.
lessons.tip: Before coding an app, draw its navigation map: boxes for screens, arrows for push, and mark which screens are tabs and which arrows clear the stack. Ten minutes of drawing saves hours of confusing back-button bugs.
lessons.task: Open a shopping or food app and go five screens deep. Then press back five times and write down each screen you pass. Mark which screens were pushed, which were tabs, and whether any screen was skipped because the stack had been cleared.

quiz.q: In Flutter, what happens to the previous screen when you call Navigator.push?
options: It stays alive on the stack underneath, keeping its state
It is moved to a new app
quiz.explain: push places a new route on top; the old route remains in the stack and reappears when the new one is popped.

quiz.q: How does a picker screen send the chosen value back to the screen that opened it?
options: By saving it in a global variable only
By calling setState on the other screen directly
By calling Navigator.pop(context, value); the awaited push returns it
quiz.explain: The Future returned by push completes with the value passed to pop.

quiz.q: After a successful login, which call prevents the back button from returning to the login form?
quiz.explain: pushReplacement replaces the current route, so the login screen is no longer on the stack.

quiz.q: What is a deep link?
options: A link that only works offline
A URL that opens a specific screen inside an app
A link inside the app's source code
quiz.explain: Deep links take the user straight to particular content, such as a product page, inside the app.

quiz.q: Why are verified https links (App Links, Universal Links) preferred over custom schemes like myshop://?
options: The developer proves domain ownership, while any app can claim a custom scheme
quiz.explain: Verification files on the website prove ownership, so other apps cannot hijack the links.

lessons.title: State Management
lessons.content:
Imagine a family WhatsApp group planning Eid shopping. If everyone keeps their own private list, soon the lists disagree: Abbu thinks Ammu will buy the sugar, Ammu thinks you will, and nobody does. The family needs one shared list that everyone reads and that changes in a known way. Apps face the same problem. Many screens and widgets show pieces of the same data: the cart count, the logged-in user, the selected language. If each keeps its own copy, they drift apart. State management is the discipline of keeping that data in the right place and making every part of the UI agree with it.

What state is: State is any data that can change while the app runs and that affects what the user sees. A checkbox being ticked is state. The text typed in a search box is state. The list of products downloaded from the server, whether a request is loading, the logged-in user, the items in the cart, the chosen theme: all state. Remember from lesson 8 that UI = f(state). If the UI is a function of state, then deciding where state lives and how it changes is the central design question of any declarative app.

Ephemeral state versus app state: Flutter's documentation separates two kinds. Ephemeral state, also called local UI state, belongs to one widget and nobody else cares about it: the current page of a carousel, whether a password is shown, the progress of an animation. App state is shared across many parts of the app and often must survive between sessions: the user's login, the cart, notification settings, downloaded data. There is no strict rule; the same data can start ephemeral and become app state when another screen needs it.

setState for ephemeral state: For state that lives in one widget, a StatefulWidget with setState is perfect. For example, a show or hide password icon: bool _hidden = true; and onPressed: () => setState(() => _hidden = !_hidden), with TextField(obscureText: _hidden). No library is needed. Beginners sometimes think setState is bad practice; it is not. It is simply the right tool for local state and the wrong tool for state shared across the app.

Lifting state up: Suppose two sibling widgets need the same data: a product list where you tap plus, and a cart badge in the app bar showing the count. Neither sibling can own the count, because the other could not see it. The solution is to lift the state up to their closest common ancestor. The ancestor holds the count, passes it down to the badge as a value, and passes a callback such as onAdd down to the list. When the list calls onAdd, the ancestor updates the count with setState, and both children rebuild with the new value.

Unidirectional data flow: Lifting state creates a pattern that every modern UI framework follows: data flows down, events flow up. A parent passes state to children as plain values. Children never change that state directly; they report events, such as "plus tapped for product 7", through callbacks. The owner of the state decides how to update it, and the new state flows down again. Because there is exactly one place where each piece of state can change, bugs are easier to find: you look at the owner.

The problem with passing everything down: In a real app, the common ancestor of all screens that need the cart might be the root of the app, and the cart value would have to be passed through ten layers of widgets that do not care about it, just to reach the badge. This is called prop drilling, and it makes code noisy and fragile. We need a way for a widget deep in the tree to reach shared state directly, without every layer in between carrying it.

InheritedWidget, Flutter's built-in solution: Flutter has a special widget called InheritedWidget that makes data available to all its descendants. Any widget below can ask for it with a method on context, and Flutter remembers who asked so it can rebuild exactly those widgets when the data changes. You already use this: Theme.of(context) and MediaQuery.of(context) are built on InheritedWidget. Writing InheritedWidget by hand is verbose, so most apps use a package built on top of it.

Provider and ChangeNotifier: The provider package is a popular, simple wrapper. You write a model class that extends ChangeNotifier: class CartModel extends ChangeNotifier { final List<Item> _items = []; int get count => _items.length; void add(Item i) { _items.add(i); notifyListeners(); } }. You place ChangeNotifierProvider(create: (_) => CartModel(), child: MyApp()) near the top. Any widget can then call context.watch<CartModel>().count to display and rebuild on change, or context.read<CartModel>().add(item) inside a button handler to trigger a change without subscribing.

Other popular approaches: Riverpod, from the same author as Provider, removes the dependence on the widget tree and catches more mistakes at compile time. Bloc separates events and states explicitly: the UI sends events such as AddToCart, a Bloc processes them and emits new immutable states, often using Dart Streams. Others such as Redux, MobX and GetX exist too. The Flutter team does not force one choice. They differ in style and ceremony, but all solve the same problem: one source of truth, changed in controlled ways, with the UI rebuilding when it changes.

State in Jetpack Compose, hoisting: Compose names the lifting idea state hoisting. A composable that would hold state is rewritten to receive the value and an event callback instead: @Composable fun QuantityPicker(qty: Int, onQtyChange: (Int) -> Unit). The caller owns the state and passes it down. Such hoisted composables are reusable and easy to test, because they have no hidden state. The rule is to hoist state to the lowest common owner of everything that reads or writes it, no higher.

ViewModel with StateFlow on Android: In native Android, screen-level state usually lives in a ViewModel, which survives rotation as you saw in lesson 7. The ViewModel keeps a private mutable stream and exposes a read-only one: private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(CartUiState()); val ui: StateFlow<CartUiState> = _ui. Public functions like addItem update it with a new copy of the state. The UI collects the flow and redraws when it changes. This is unidirectional data flow again: the UI sends events to the ViewModel, the ViewModel sends state to the UI.

Immutable state objects: A strong habit in all these approaches is to treat each state as an immutable snapshot. Instead of changing fields inside the existing object, you create a new object with the change: state = state.copyWith(isLoading: false, items: newItems). Immutable state makes it easy to compare old and new, to debug by logging each state, and it prevents bugs where one part of the app changes data another part is still using. Dart's final fields and copyWith methods, and Kotlin's data classes with copy, make this easy.

Derived state, do not store what you can compute: If the cart has items with prices and quantities, the total price is derived from them. Storing total as a separate variable invites bugs: someone updates the items and forgets the total. Instead compute it: int get total => items.fold(0, (sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty);. Store the minimum facts; derive the rest. Only cache a derived value if computing it is truly expensive, and then recompute it in the same place that changes the inputs.

Modelling a screen's state: For screens that load data, a common pattern is a single state type with clear cases: loading, success with data, empty, and error with a message. In Dart you can use a sealed class or an enum plus fields. The build method then switches on the case: show a spinner, the list, a friendly "No orders yet" message, or an error with a Retry button. Thinking in explicit cases prevents impossible combinations like isLoading true and an error message both showing at once.

Choosing an approach without a war: Developers argue endlessly about which state library is best. A practical rule for students and small teams: start with setState for local state; when state must be shared across several screens, pick one well-documented solution such as Provider or Riverpod, and use it consistently everywhere. Choose Bloc if your team likes strict structure and explicit events, for example in a larger banking or fintech codebase. What really matters is not the library but the principles: one owner per piece of state, clear events, and UI that only reads state.

State is easy to test when it is separate: When state lives in a plain Dart class like CartModel instead of inside widgets, you can test it without any screen at all: create the model, call add twice, and check that count is 2 and total is correct. A ViewModel can be tested the same way by calling its functions and checking the emitted states. This is a big hidden benefit of good state management, and lesson 23 builds on it. If you find you cannot test some logic without tapping buttons on a phone, that logic probably lives in the wrong place.

Real-life example 1, a shopping cart across screens: In a Daraz-like shop app, the cart badge on the home screen, the plus buttons on product pages, and the cart screen all need the cart. A CartModel provided at the top of the app is the single source of truth. Product pages call add; the badge watches count; the cart screen watches items and derives the total. When the user logs out, the app clears the cart model, and every screen updates at once. Saving the cart to local storage, so it survives restarts, is a job for lessons 16 and 17.

Real-life example 2, language switching for Bangla and English: A government services app lets the user choose Bangla or English in settings. The chosen locale is app state: it affects every screen and must be saved. A settings model holds locale and exposes setLocale. MaterialApp watches it and passes locale to the localisation system, so the whole app rebuilds in the new language immediately, without restarting. The settings screen only sends the event; it does not know which screens depend on the language.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Putting everything into global state, even a single text field's focus, which makes the app hard to follow. The opposite mistake, copying shared data into several widgets so they drift apart. Calling notifyListeners or setState after the widget is disposed. Mixing several state libraries in one app. Exams ask: define state and give examples; ephemeral versus app state; explain lifting state up and unidirectional data flow; compare setState with a state management solution; or describe how a ViewModel exposes state.

Recap: State is changing data that affects the UI. Ephemeral state belongs to one widget and is handled with setState; app state is shared and needs a shared owner. Lift state to the common ancestor, pass data down and events up. To avoid passing state through many layers, use InheritedWidget-based solutions like Provider, or Riverpod or Bloc in Flutter, state hoisting in Compose, and ViewModels with StateFlow in Android. Keep one source of truth, prefer immutable state with copyWith, derive values instead of storing them, and model screen states as explicit cases.
key_points: State is any data that changes while the app runs and affects what the user sees.
Ephemeral state belongs to one widget (use setState); app state is shared across screens and needs a shared owner.
Lifting state up: the closest common ancestor owns the state, passes values down and callbacks for events.
Unidirectional data flow: data flows down, events flow up, and only the owner changes the state.
InheritedWidget, Provider (ChangeNotifier), Riverpod and Bloc let deep widgets reach shared state without prop drilling.
On Android, ViewModels expose immutable state with StateFlow; Compose hoists state to the caller.
Keep one source of truth, use immutable state with copyWith, and derive values like totals instead of storing them.
lessons.tip: For every piece of state in your app, ask two questions: who reads it, and who changes it? Put the state in the lowest place that can see all of them. This single question settles most state management debates.
lessons.task: Choose an app you use daily, such as a food delivery app. List ten pieces of state you can see (cart items, address, search text, filters, etc.) and mark each as ephemeral or app state, and which screen should own it.

quiz.q: Which of these is best described as ephemeral (local UI) state?
options: Whether a password field is currently shown or hidden
quiz.explain: Show or hide password matters only to that one widget, so setState inside it is enough.

quiz.q: Two sibling widgets need the same counter. What is the basic solution?
options: Lift the state up to their closest common ancestor and pass it down
Give each sibling its own copy of the counter
Store it in a file and reread it every second
quiz.explain: The common ancestor owns the state and passes values and callbacks down, so both stay in sync.

quiz.q: In unidirectional data flow, how do children change shared state?
options: They edit the state object directly
They create a new copy for themselves
They send events through callbacks, and the owner updates the state
quiz.explain: Data flows down and events flow up; only the owner of the state changes it.

quiz.q: In a ChangeNotifier model, what must you call after changing data so listening widgets rebuild?
quiz.explain: notifyListeners tells all listeners, such as widgets using context.watch, that the model changed.

quiz.q: Why should a cart's total price usually be computed instead of stored separately?
options: Stored numbers use too much memory
A separate total can become out of sync when items change
quiz.explain: Derived values computed from the items can never disagree with them; a stored copy can be forgotten.

lessons.title: App Architecture: MVC, MVP, MVVM and Layers
lessons.content:
Walk into a well-run restaurant kitchen in Old Dhaka during iftar rush. The waiter takes orders and talks to customers. The cooks only cook. A storekeeper manages rice, oil and spices and knows which supplier to call when stock is low. Nobody does everyone's job. If the waiter also cooked and also ran to the market, orders would be wrong and the place would collapse at the first rush. App architecture is the same idea for code: split the app into parts with clear jobs, so it can grow, be tested and be changed without collapsing.

What architecture means here: App architecture is the overall structure of your code: which parts exist, what each one is responsible for, and how they talk to each other. It is not a library you install. It is a set of decisions, such as "screens never call the network directly" or "all data access goes through repositories". Good architecture makes the common changes easy: adding a screen, changing an API, replacing a database, or writing a test.

The problem it solves, the giant screen: Beginners often put everything inside one screen class: the layout, the button handlers, the HTTP calls, the JSON parsing, the database writes and the business rules. On Android this was nicknamed the God Activity; on iOS, the Massive View Controller. It works for a week. Then the same API call is copied into three screens, a change to the server format breaks five places, rotation loses data, and nothing can be tested without running the whole app on a phone. Architecture patterns exist to stop this.

Separation of concerns: The core principle is separation of concerns: each part of the code should handle one kind of job. Showing things and capturing taps is one concern. Deciding what should happen, like applying a discount, is another. Fetching and storing data is a third. When concerns are separated, a change in one rarely ripples into the others. You met this idea in Software Engineering as high cohesion and low coupling; architecture applies it to apps.

MVC, Model-View-Controller: MVC is the oldest of the classic patterns. The Model holds data and business rules. The View displays the model. The Controller receives user input, updates the model, and chooses what the view shows. Apple's UIKit was designed around MVC, with view controllers playing the controller. In practice on mobile, the view controller or activity is so tied to the view that it becomes both view and controller, and everything drifts into it, which is how the massive view controller problem appeared.

MVP, Model-View-Presenter: MVP pulls the logic out of the screen into a Presenter. The View is made passive: it is described by an interface with methods like showLoading(), showProducts(list) and showError(message), and the activity simply implements those. The Presenter holds the logic: on load, it calls the model, then tells the view what to show. Because the Presenter talks to an interface, you can test it with a fake view and check which methods it called. The downside is lots of interface code, and the presenter holds a reference to the view, which must be managed across the lifecycle.

MVVM, Model-View-ViewModel: MVVM changes the direction of the connection. The ViewModel exposes observable state, such as a StateFlow or a ChangeNotifier, and functions for events. The View observes that state and redraws itself; the ViewModel never holds a reference to the view. This fits declarative UI perfectly: the view is just UI = f(state), and the ViewModel produces the state. It also fits the lifecycle, because an Android ViewModel survives rotation. MVVM is the pattern Google's Android guidance is built around and is widely used in Flutter as well, sometimes under other names.

Comparing the three in one sentence each: In MVC, the controller handles input and updates both model and view, and on mobile it tends to merge with the view. In MVP, the presenter commands a passive view through an interface. In MVVM, the view model exposes state and the view observes it, with no reference back. Exams often ask for exactly this comparison, plus a small diagram of the arrows between the three parts.

Layers, the bigger picture: Patterns like MVVM describe the UI side. The whole app is usually organised into layers. Android's official architecture guidance recommends a UI layer, made of UI elements and state holders such as ViewModels; a data layer, made of repositories and data sources; and an optional domain layer in between for reusable business logic. Dependencies point one way: the UI layer depends on the domain or data layer, never the reverse. Flutter teams commonly use the same layering.

The data layer and repositories: A repository is the single entry point for one type of data, such as products or orders. The rest of the app asks the repository, "give me the orders", and does not know or care whether they come from the network, a local database or a memory cache. Inside, the repository coordinates data sources: a remote data source that calls the REST API, and a local data source that reads and writes the SQLite database. This is where caching rules and offline behaviour live, as lessons 15 to 18 show.

The domain layer and use cases: When the same business rule is needed in several places, it can move into a use case, a small class that does one action, like PlaceOrderUseCase or CalculateDeliveryFeeUseCase. A use case may combine several repositories: check stock, compute the fee, create the order. Use cases keep ViewModels thin and make rules reusable and testable. For small apps this layer is often skipped; the ViewModel calls repositories directly. That is fine.

Clean architecture in brief: Clean architecture, a name popularised by Robert C. Martin, draws the layers as circles: entities and business rules in the centre, use cases around them, then interface adapters, and frameworks such as the UI, database and network on the outside. The key rule is the dependency rule: inner circles must not know anything about outer ones. Your business rules should not import Flutter or know about JSON. Many mobile teams apply this idea loosely through the UI, domain and data layers.

Errors across layers: Each layer should translate errors into the language of the layer above. The remote data source sees low-level problems such as a socket timeout or an HTTP 500. The repository turns them into meaningful results, such as a NetworkError or a ServerError, perhaps falling back to cached data. The ViewModel turns that into UI state, such as an error message in Bangla with a Retry button. The screen never sees raw exceptions or status codes. This keeps error handling consistent and stops technical messages from leaking to users.

Models at each layer: The JSON the server sends may not match what the UI needs. A common practice is to have a data transfer object, or DTO, that mirrors the API, such as OrderDto with fields exactly as in the JSON, and a domain model, Order, that the rest of the app uses. The repository maps one to the other. If the backend renames a field, only the DTO and the mapping change, not every screen. In small apps one model class is often enough; add the split when the API and the UI start to disagree.

Dependency injection: A class should receive the things it depends on rather than create them itself. Instead of class OrderRepository { final api = OrderApi(); }, write class OrderRepository { final OrderApi api; OrderRepository(this.api); }. This is called dependency injection, and in its simplest form it is just passing objects into constructors. The benefit: in a test you can pass a fake OrderApi that returns fixed data without the internet. Tools such as Hilt on Android, or get_it and Riverpod in Flutter, automate creating and wiring these objects in big apps.
