A worked feature, order history: The screen OrderHistoryScreen observes OrderHistoryViewModel. When opened, the screen calls viewModel.load(). The ViewModel sets state to loading and calls orderRepository.getOrders(). The repository first returns cached orders from OrderDao, the local data source, so the screen shows something immediately, then calls OrderApi, the remote source, saves fresh results into the database, and returns them. The ViewModel maps them into a success state with a list; the screen redraws. Each class has one job, and each can be tested alone.

Folder structure: Two common ways exist. Layer-first puts all screens in one folder, all ViewModels in another, all repositories in another. Feature-first puts everything for one feature together: lib/features/orders/ with orders_screen.dart, orders_view_model.dart and orders_repository.dart, and shared code in lib/core/. Feature-first scales better in big apps because a developer working on orders finds everything in one place. For a student project, either is fine if it is consistent.

Do not over-architect: Architecture has a cost: more files, more classes and more indirection. A two-screen app built for a class assignment does not need use cases, DTO mappers and a dependency injection framework. A good rule is to start with a screen, a ViewModel or state class, and a repository, and to add layers when you actually feel the pain they solve: duplicated rules, an API that keeps changing, or tests that are hard to write. Architecture should make the next change easier, not prove how many patterns you know.

Real-life example 1, a large fintech app: A mobile financial service app in Bangladesh may have dozens of developers working on send money, cash out, bill payment, mobile recharge and savings. Feature-first folders let each team own its part. Shared repositories handle the account and transaction history. Use cases enforce rules like daily limits in one place. Strong layering means the security team can review data access in the data layer without reading every screen.

Real-life example 2, a final year project: A student team builds a blood donor finder app for their university. They use MVVM: each screen has a ViewModel; a DonorRepository wraps a REST API and a small local cache. No domain layer, because rules are simple. When the supervisor asks for offline search before the defence, they change only the repository, and the screens do not change at all. That moment is when architecture pays off.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Letting screens call the HTTP client directly; ViewModels that hold a reference to a BuildContext or an Activity, causing leaks; repositories that return raw JSON maps; copying the same logic into several ViewModels; and adding every pattern to a tiny app. Exams ask: explain separation of concerns; compare MVC, MVP and MVVM with diagrams; what is a repository; what is dependency injection and why does it help testing; and describe the layers of a recommended app architecture.

Recap: Architecture splits an app into parts with clear jobs so it can grow and be tested. MVC, MVP and MVVM differ in how the screen and its logic connect; MVVM, where the view observes state exposed by a view model, fits declarative UI and is widely recommended. Apps are organised into a UI layer, an optional domain layer of use cases, and a data layer of repositories that hide remote and local data sources. Inject dependencies through constructors to make testing easy, organise folders consistently, and add layers only when they solve a real problem.
key_points: Architecture is the structure of the code: which parts exist, their responsibilities, and how they communicate.
Separation of concerns avoids the God Activity or Massive View Controller where one screen does everything.
MVC: controller handles input; MVP: presenter commands a passive view interface; MVVM: view observes state from a view model.
Recommended layers: UI layer (UI + ViewModels), optional domain layer (use cases), data layer (repositories + data sources).
A repository is the single entry point for a type of data and hides whether it comes from network, database or cache.
Dependency injection passes dependencies in through constructors so tests can use fakes.
Start simple and add layers only when they solve a real pain; over-architecting small apps adds cost without benefit.
lessons.tip: For any architecture question, draw boxes for View, ViewModel, Repository, Remote and Local data sources, and draw arrows only in the direction of dependencies. If you can explain why no arrow points upward, you understand the topic.
lessons.task: Take an app idea, such as a mess (hostel) meal tracker. On paper, list its screens, then for one screen write the names of its ViewModel, repository and data sources, and one sentence describing each class's job.

quiz.q: In MVVM, how does the View get updated?
options: The ViewModel calls methods on the View directly
The View observes state exposed by the ViewModel
quiz.explain: The ViewModel exposes observable state and holds no reference to the view; the view observes and redraws.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a repository?
options: Being the single entry point for a type of data, hiding network and local sources
quiz.explain: The rest of the app asks the repository for data without knowing whether it came from the API, database or cache.

quiz.q: What does dependency injection mean in its simplest form?
options: Passing the objects a class needs into its constructor instead of creating them inside
quiz.explain: Receiving dependencies from outside lets you swap them, for example with fakes in tests.

quiz.q: In MVP, how is the View usually defined so the Presenter can be tested?
options: As an interface with methods like showLoading and showError
quiz.explain: The presenter talks to a view interface, so a fake view can record which methods were called in tests.

quiz.q: When is adding a separate domain layer of use cases usually NOT worth it?
options: In a large app with rules shared by many screens
In a tiny two-screen app with simple rules
When several repositories must be combined for one action
When business rules must be tested independently
quiz.explain: Extra layers add files and indirection; small apps can let ViewModels call repositories directly.

lessons.title: Lists, Images and Smooth UI
lessons.content:
Think of a flip-book cartoon you made in school by drawing a slightly different picture on each page corner. Flip fast and the drawing moves smoothly. Skip a few pages, or flip unevenly, and the motion jerks. A phone screen is a very fast flip-book. It shows a new picture many times every second, and if your app is late with even a few of those pictures, the user sees stutter. Scrolling through a long list, like a Facebook feed or a Daraz product list, is where this is most visible. This lesson explains the frame budget, how lazy lists keep scrolling smooth, and how to handle images without eating all the memory.

Frames and the frame budget: Most phone screens refresh 60 times per second, and many newer ones 90 or 120 times. To look smooth, the app must produce a new frame for each refresh. At 60 Hz, that leaves 1000 / 60, about 16.7 milliseconds, per frame. At 120 Hz it is about 8.3 ms. In that time the app must handle input, run your build and layout code, and paint. If a frame takes 40 ms, the screen shows the old frame two or three times in a row, and the user sees a stutter, called jank.

Where the time goes in Flutter: Flutter does its work in two main stages. On the UI thread, Dart code runs: your build methods, layout calculations and animations, producing a description of what to draw. On the raster thread, the engine turns that description into pixels with the GPU. Both stages must finish within the frame budget. Flutter's performance overlay shows two graphs, one per thread; bars that go above the line mean slow frames. Flutter DevTools shows exactly which build or paint took too long.

The naive list and why it fails: Suppose your app shows 10,000 transactions. The naive approach is ListView(children: transactions.map((t) => TransactionTile(t)).toList()). This creates 10,000 widgets up front, even though the screen can show only about 10 at a time. Startup becomes slow, memory use jumps, and every rebuild touches thousands of objects. The same mistake in native code, adding 10,000 views to a scrolling layout, would be even worse.

Lazy lists, building only what is visible: The fix is a lazy list that creates items only when they are about to appear. In Flutter: ListView.builder(itemCount: transactions.length, itemBuilder: (context, index) => TransactionTile(transactions[index])). Flutter calls itemBuilder only for the visible items plus a small buffer above and below. As you scroll, items that leave the screen are discarded and new ones are built. With 10 visible items, you build roughly 15 or 20 at any time instead of 10,000. ListView.separated adds dividers, and GridView.builder does the same for grids.

Recycling in native lists: Native Android's RecyclerView goes one step further: it recycles. When a row scrolls off the top, its view object is not thrown away; it is put in a pool and reused for the row coming in at the bottom, with new data bound into it. You write an Adapter that creates ViewHolders and binds data to them. Jetpack Compose has LazyColumn and LazyRow, which compose only visible items. iOS UITableView and UICollectionView reuse cells through a dequeue method in the same spirit. Creating views is expensive, so reusing them saves time and memory.

Updating lists efficiently: When the data changes, refreshing the whole list wastes work and loses scroll position or animations. RecyclerView's ListAdapter uses DiffUtil to compute the difference between the old and new lists and updates only the changed rows, with animations. In Flutter, a lazy list rebuilds only visible items, but you should give each item a stable key so Flutter can match items correctly when they move.

Keys and why they matter: Imagine a to-do list where each row has a checkbox with its own state. You delete the first item. Without keys, Flutter matches rows by position, so the State of the old first row is reused for what is now the first row, and checkmarks appear on the wrong items. Giving each row key: ValueKey(task.id) tells Flutter which item is which, so state moves with the item. Use keys based on stable IDs from your data, not on the list index.

Fixed heights help: If every row has the same height, telling the list so with itemExtent: 72 or a prototypeItem lets Flutter compute scroll positions without measuring every row. Jumping to item 5,000 then becomes instant. Native lists have similar hints. If rows vary in height, that is fine, but very complex rows with deep nested layouts will cost more per frame, so keep rows simple.

Pagination, loading in pages: Even with lazy building, you should not download 10,000 transactions at once; that wastes data and time. Servers return data in pages: page 1 with 20 items, page 2 with the next 20, and so on. The API may use offset and limit, like ?offset=40&limit=20, or a cursor, like ?after=txn_9812, which is more reliable when new items are being added. The app loads the first page, shows it, and loads more as needed.

Infinite scroll, a worked example: Attach a ScrollController to the list and listen: if (controller.position.pixels > controller.position.maxScrollExtent - 300 && !isLoadingMore && hasMore) loadNextPage();. When the user is within 300 pixels of the end, the next page is requested. The isLoadingMore flag prevents ten duplicate requests while one is in flight, and hasMore stops requests when the server says there are no more pages. A small spinner at the bottom shows that more is coming, and a Retry row appears if the request fails.

Images are heavy: Images are often the biggest cost in a list. A photo from a phone camera might be 4000 by 3000 pixels. Compressed as JPEG, the file may be only 2 or 3 MB, but to draw it, the image must be decoded into raw pixels, typically 4 bytes per pixel. That is 4000 × 3000 × 4 = 48,000,000 bytes, about 48 MB of memory for one image. A list of thumbnails showing ten such photos at full resolution could use hundreds of megabytes and crash a 2 GB phone.

Decode images at display size: The thumbnail on screen might be 100 by 100 logical pixels, which at 3x density is 300 by 300 physical pixels: 300 × 300 × 4 = 360,000 bytes, about 0.36 MB. So decode images at the size you display. In Flutter, Image.network(url, cacheWidth: 300) tells the engine to decode at that width. Better still, ask the server for a thumbnail sized for mobile; many image services accept a width parameter. Native libraries such as Glide and Coil on Android resize automatically to the view size.

Caching images: Downloading the same picture every time the user scrolls past it wastes data and time. Image caching keeps decoded images in memory for quick reuse and downloaded files on disk for later sessions. In Flutter, the framework has an in-memory image cache, and a package such as cached_network_image adds a disk cache with placeholders and error widgets. Glide and Coil do both on Android. For users on prepaid data packs in Bangladesh, a good image cache is not an optimisation; it is respect for their money.

Placeholders and perceived speed: Show a grey box or a blurred tiny preview while an image loads, sized exactly like the final image, so the layout does not jump when it arrives. Content that shifts while the user is about to tap causes wrong taps. Fade the image in when ready. Skeleton screens, grey shapes in the layout of the real content, make loading feel faster than a spinner in the middle of a blank page.

Avoiding unnecessary rebuilds: Even with lazy lists, a careless rebuild can redo too much. If a cart badge in the app bar changes, the whole product list should not rebuild. Use const widgets where possible, split big widgets so state changes affect small subtrees, and in Provider use context.select or Selector to listen to only the field you need. Never do heavy work like sorting 5,000 items or parsing JSON inside build; do it once when data arrives, and for really heavy work move it off the UI thread, as lesson 14 explains.

Animations without jank: Animations are frames too, so they must fit the same budget. Prefer the built-in animated widgets, such as AnimatedContainer, AnimatedOpacity or FadeTransition, which are designed to change only what is needed each frame. Avoid rebuilding a large screen sixty times a second just to move one small icon; put the animated part in its own small widget. Always measure on a real, ideally low-end, phone in profile mode, because an emulator on a fast laptop and debug mode both give a false picture of how smooth the app really is.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet transaction history: A user with three years of transactions opens the statement screen. The app loads the 30 most recent from the local database instantly, shows them in a ListView.builder with fixed-height rows, and fetches newer ones from the server. As the user scrolls, older pages load 30 at a time from the server using a cursor. Each row is simple: icon, name, date, amount. Scrolling stays smooth even on a budget phone, and memory stays low because only about 20 rows exist at a time.

Real-life example 2, an online marketplace product grid: A marketplace shows a grid of products with photos. Product images are requested from the server as 400-pixel-wide thumbnails, not full photos. A disk cache keeps them for the next visit. Each card has a fixed aspect ratio placeholder, so nothing jumps. Infinite scroll loads 40 products per page. When a user taps a product, the detail screen loads the larger image only then. The app feels fast on slow 3G in a district town and uses far less data.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Using ListView with a children list for long or unknown-length data; loading full-resolution images into thumbnails; not using keys in lists with stateful items; triggering page loads repeatedly; doing heavy work in build; and judging performance in debug mode. Exams ask: what is the frame budget at 60 Hz; explain jank; how RecyclerView or ListView.builder improve performance; what view recycling is; how pagination works; and calculate the memory needed for a decoded image.

Recap: At 60 Hz each frame has about 16.7 ms; missing it causes jank. Lazy lists such as ListView.builder, RecyclerView, LazyColumn and UITableView build or reuse only visible items, so lists of any length scroll smoothly. Give list items stable keys, use fixed heights when possible, and load data in pages with infinite scroll guarded against duplicate requests. Images cost width × height × 4 bytes when decoded, so decode at display size, request thumbnails, cache in memory and on disk, and use placeholders. Keep build cheap and rebuild only what changed.
key_points: At 60 Hz each frame has about 16.7 ms (8.3 ms at 120 Hz); missing the budget causes visible stutter called jank.
Lazy lists (ListView.builder, LazyColumn) build only visible items; RecyclerView and UITableView also recycle views.
Give list items stable keys like ValueKey(id) so state stays with the right item when the list changes.
Load long data in pages (offset/limit or cursor) and guard infinite scroll against duplicate requests.
A decoded image uses about width × height × 4 bytes: a 4000×3000 photo needs about 48 MB.
Decode images at display size, request thumbnails, cache in memory and on disk, and show same-size placeholders.
Keep build methods cheap and rebuild small subtrees; never sort or parse large data inside build.
lessons.tip: Turn on the Profile GPU rendering or performance overlay option on a budget phone and scroll your app. Learning to read those bars once will make you notice jank everywhere, which is the first step to fixing it.
lessons.task: Calculate the decoded memory for these images: 1080×1920, 4000×3000 and a 300×300 thumbnail, at 4 bytes per pixel. Then estimate how many full-size 4000×3000 photos would fit in 512 MB, and explain why lists must use thumbnails.

quiz.q: About how much time does an app have to produce each frame on a 60 Hz screen?
quiz.explain: 1000 ms / 60 frames is about 16.7 ms per frame.

quiz.q: Why is ListView.builder better than ListView with a children list for 10,000 items?
options: It builds only the items near the visible area instead of all 10,000
quiz.explain: The builder is called lazily for visible items plus a small buffer, saving time and memory.

quiz.q: Approximately how much memory does a decoded 4000×3000 image need at 4 bytes per pixel?
Why should each item in a list of stateful rows have a key like ValueKey(task.id)?
options: Keys make the list scroll faster
Keys are needed to download images
So Flutter can match state to the right item when items are removed or reordered
quiz.explain: Without keys, Flutter matches by position, so state can attach to the wrong item after changes.

quiz.q: In infinite scroll, what is the purpose of an isLoadingMore flag?
options: To prevent sending many duplicate page requests while one is already in progress
quiz.explain: Scroll events fire often; the flag ensures only one next-page request runs at a time.

lessons.title: Asynchronous Programming on Mobile
lessons.content:
Picture a tea stall near a bus stand in Gabtoli. One man runs it. A customer orders tea; he puts the kettle on and, instead of staring at it for three minutes, he takes the next order, hands out biscuits, and collects money. When the kettle whistles, he pours the tea. One worker serves many people because he never stands frozen waiting. A mobile app's main thread is that tea seller. If it stops to wait for the network, nobody else gets served: the screen freezes and taps are ignored. Asynchronous programming is how apps keep serving while slow things finish.

The main thread: Every mobile app has one special thread, usually called the main thread or UI thread. It handles touch events, runs your UI code, and prepares frames for the screen. As you saw in lesson 13, it must produce a frame every 16.7 ms at 60 Hz. Anything that blocks this thread for longer, such as waiting for a server, reading a large file, or decoding a big image, makes the app stutter or freeze.

What happens when you block it: If an Android app's main thread is blocked so the app cannot respond to user input for roughly five seconds, the system shows the Application Not Responding dialog, known as ANR, offering to close the app. Android goes further for networking: by default, making a network call on the main thread throws an exception called NetworkOnMainThreadException. iOS has a watchdog that can terminate apps that hang during launch or other key moments. Users experience all of this as "the app is hanging".

Slow operations on a phone: Network requests can take from 100 milliseconds on good Wi-Fi to many seconds on weak mobile data. Reading and writing files and databases takes milliseconds to seconds depending on size. Decoding images, parsing large JSON, encrypting data and compressing photos use real processor time. Location fixes, camera capture and Bluetooth scans wait on hardware. All of these must happen without blocking the main thread.

Two kinds of slow, waiting and working: It is important to separate two kinds of slow work. I/O-bound work spends most of its time waiting for something outside the processor: the network, the disk, a sensor. CPU-bound work keeps the processor busy calculating: parsing, sorting, image processing. Async code with Futures handles I/O-bound work well on a single thread, because during the waiting the thread is free to do other things. CPU-bound work truly needs another thread or isolate, because calculation cannot be paused by waiting. Mixing these up is the most common async mistake.

Threads, the classic answer: The traditional solution, from your Operating Systems course, is to run slow work on a background thread and post the result back to the main thread. Threads share memory, which is powerful but dangerous: two threads changing the same list can corrupt it, which is a race condition, and you need locks to prevent it. Threads are also relatively heavy to create. Modern mobile platforms give higher-level tools so you rarely manage threads directly.

Dart's model, the event loop: Dart runs your code on a single thread inside an isolate, with an event loop. Think of the event loop as the tea seller's queue of tasks: a tap event, a timer firing, a network response arriving, a frame to build. The loop takes one task at a time and runs it to completion. When your code starts a network request, Dart hands the actual waiting to the operating system and moves on. When the response arrives, a new task is added to the queue to continue your code.

Futures: A Future represents a value that will be available later, or an error. It starts uncompleted, and later completes with a value or with an error. http.get(uri) returns a Future<Response> immediately, before any data arrives. You can attach callbacks with then and catchError, but most Dart code uses async and await, which reads like normal step-by-step code.

async and await, a worked timeline: Consider Future<void> loadProfile() async { setState(() => loading = true); final res = await http.get(uri); setState(() { profile = parse(res.body); loading = false; }); }. At time 0, the user taps; loading becomes true and a spinner appears. The await line starts the request and pauses only this function, returning control to the event loop. For the next two seconds, the event loop keeps building frames, so the spinner animates and the user can still scroll or press back. At time 2 seconds the response arrives, the function resumes after await, and the profile appears. The main thread was never frozen.

Handling errors and timeouts: Network calls fail often on mobile. With await, you use normal try, catch and finally: try { final res = await http.get(uri).timeout(const Duration(seconds: 15)); ... } on TimeoutException { showError('Network is slow, please try again'); } catch (e) { showError('Something went wrong'); } finally { setState(() => loading = false); }. The finally block guarantees the spinner stops whether the call succeeded or failed. Without a timeout, a request on a dead connection can hang for a very long time.

Running things in parallel: If a screen needs the user's profile and their recent orders, and the two requests do not depend on each other, start both and wait for both: final results = await Future.wait([api.profile(), api.orders()]);. On a slow network, two parallel 2-second requests take about 2 seconds total instead of 4. If one depends on the other, such as needing the user ID before fetching orders, await them one after another.

The async trap, CPU work still blocks: Marking a function async does not move it to another thread. If you write an async function that loops over 200,000 items to compute statistics, every iteration runs on the main thread, and the UI freezes just as badly. await only helps while waiting on something external. This surprises many beginners, who wonder why their async code still causes jank.

Isolates for heavy work: For CPU-heavy work, Dart offers isolates. An isolate is like a separate worker with its own memory and its own event loop; isolates do not share memory, so there are no race conditions, and they communicate by sending messages. Recent Dart versions provide Isolate.run, and Flutter provides compute, to run a function in a new isolate and get the result back as a Future: final products = await Isolate.run(() => parseHugeJson(body));. Use this for parsing very large JSON, image filters or encryption of big files, not for tiny tasks, since starting an isolate has its own cost.

Streams, many values over time: A Future gives one value. A Stream gives a sequence of values over time: location updates, a chat's new messages, download progress, the state of a Bluetooth connection. You listen to a stream: final sub = locationStream.listen((pos) => updateMap(pos));, and you must cancel the subscription when you no longer need it: sub.cancel(); usually in dispose. Functions marked async* can produce streams with yield. Flutter's StreamBuilder and FutureBuilder widgets rebuild when new data or a result arrives.

A FutureBuilder pitfall: FutureBuilder(future: api.getOrders(), builder: ...) looks neat, but because build can run many times, every rebuild creates a brand new request, and the screen flickers between loading and data. The fix is to create the Future once, for example in initState, store it in a field such as late final Future<List<Order>> _ordersFuture = api.getOrders();, and pass that field to FutureBuilder. The same rule from lesson 8 applies: build describes the UI; it must not start work.

Kotlin coroutines on Android: Native Android uses coroutines. A suspend function can pause without blocking a thread, similar to await. You launch coroutines in a scope, and choose where code runs with dispatchers: Dispatchers.Main for UI, Dispatchers.IO for network and disk, Dispatchers.Default for CPU-heavy work. A typical ViewModel does viewModelScope.launch { val orders = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { api.getOrders() }; _ui.value = UiState.Success(orders) }. Kotlin Flow plays the role of Dart streams. Swift on iOS has its own async and await with tasks, following the same ideas.

Structured concurrency and cancellation: When the user leaves a screen, its pending work should usually stop. Kotlin's viewModelScope cancels all its coroutines automatically when the ViewModel is cleared, and lifecycleScope does the same for a screen; this tying of work to a scope is called structured concurrency. Dart Futures cannot be cancelled directly, so in Flutter you cancel stream subscriptions and timers in dispose, and after each await you check mounted before touching the UI, so a late result is simply ignored.

Race conditions in the UI: Even on one thread, async code can produce races. Imagine search-as-you-type. The user types "dh", then "dha", then "dhaka"; three requests go out. If the response for "dha" arrives after the one for "dhaka", a naive app shows results for "dha" under the word "dhaka". Fixes: debounce typing so a request is sent only after the user pauses, say 300 ms; and keep the latest query or a request counter, ignoring responses that do not match the latest one.

Real-life example 1, a news app's home screen: When the app opens, it starts three requests in parallel with Future.wait: top stories, local news for the user's district, and the weather. Each has a 15-second timeout. While waiting, it shows cached stories from the last session. If the weather call fails, only that card shows a retry button; the others still appear. A large JSON of archived stories is parsed in an isolate. The user can scroll from the first second, and the app never shows an ANR, even on a congested evening network.

Real-life example 2, a photo upload for an e-commerce seller: A small seller in Narayanganj uploads ten product photos. Each photo is resized and compressed in a background isolate, then uploaded one or two at a time. A stream of progress events drives a progress bar per photo. If the seller leaves the screen, the uploads continue only if they were handed to a background work system (lesson 21); otherwise the subscriptions are cancelled in dispose. The UI stays responsive throughout, even while megabytes of image data are being processed.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Doing network or database work on the main thread; thinking async makes CPU work non-blocking; forgetting try and catch, so one failed request crashes the screen; no timeout; never cancelling stream subscriptions; using context after await without checking mounted; and showing stale search results. Exams ask: why must the main thread not be blocked; what is an ANR; what is a Future and how do async and await work; difference between Future and Stream; what are isolates or coroutines; and how to run requests in parallel.

Recap: The main thread handles input and draws frames, so it must never be blocked; blocking causes jank, ANRs and frozen apps. I/O-bound work is handled with Futures, async and await on Dart's single-threaded event loop, or with coroutines and suspend functions in Kotlin. CPU-bound work needs a separate isolate or a background dispatcher. Use try, catch, finally and timeouts for errors, Future.wait for independent parallel requests, Streams or Flows for values over time, and cancel work when screens close. Watch for race conditions like out-of-order search results.
key_points: The main (UI) thread handles input and draws frames; blocking it causes jank, frozen screens and ANR dialogs.
I/O-bound work waits on network or disk; CPU-bound work keeps the processor busy; they need different tools.
Dart runs code on one thread with an event loop; await pauses the function, not the thread.
A Future is a single value later; handle errors with try/catch/finally and add timeouts to network calls.
async does not move CPU work off the main thread; use isolates (Isolate.run or compute) for heavy calculation.
Streams deliver many values over time; cancel subscriptions in dispose. Kotlin uses coroutines, dispatchers and Flow.
Run independent requests with Future.wait, cancel work when screens close, and guard against out-of-order results.
lessons.tip: Whenever you write await, ask yourself: what is the user seeing during this wait, and what happens if they leave the screen before it finishes? Answering both questions prevents most async bugs.
lessons.task: On paper, draw a timeline for a screen that loads profile and orders with Future.wait, each taking 2 seconds, then parses the result for 0.1 seconds. Mark what the main thread is doing at each moment, and compare the total time with doing the two requests one after another.

quiz.q: What does Android show if the main thread is blocked so the app cannot respond to input for several seconds?
quiz.explain: A blocked main thread leads to an ANR dialog offering to close the app.

quiz.q: In Dart, what does await do inside an async function?
options: Blocks the whole app until the Future completes
Creates a new thread for the function
Pauses only this function and lets the event loop continue other work
quiz.explain: await suspends the function; the single thread keeps handling frames and events while waiting.

quiz.q: You put a loop that processes 200,000 items inside an async function. What happens?
options: It runs on a background thread automatically
It still runs on the main thread and can freeze the UI
quiz.explain: async does not move CPU work to another thread; use an isolate for heavy calculation.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a Future and a Stream?
options: A Future gives one value later; a Stream gives a sequence of values over time
A Future only works on iOS
quiz.explain: Futures complete once; Streams deliver many events, such as location updates or messages.

quiz.q: Two independent requests each take 2 seconds. Using Future.wait, about how long does the screen wait?
quiz.explain: Future.wait runs them at the same time, so the total is about the longer of the two.

lessons.title: Networking and Consuming REST APIs
lessons.content:
Imagine ordering a parcel through a courier service in Dhaka. You fill in a form with exactly the right fields: sender, receiver, address, phone. The courier office replies with a receipt containing a tracking number and status. If you write the address wrong, they send it back with a note saying what was wrong. If their office is closed, you try again later. A mobile app talking to a server works the same way: it sends a carefully formatted request, the server replies with a status and data, and the app must handle success, mistakes and outages gracefully. Almost every real app does this all day.

Why apps need servers: Most useful apps show data that lives somewhere else: product catalogues, bank balances, chat messages, ride locations, news. The phone cannot hold all of it, and many users share the same data. So apps talk to backend servers through an API, an application programming interface, which is a set of URLs the server understands. The most common style for mobile APIs is REST over HTTPS, with JSON as the data format. Some apps also use GraphQL, gRPC or WebSockets for special needs, but REST and JSON are what you will meet first.

HTTP recap, kept short: Web Engineering covers HTTP and REST in depth; here is the minimum. A request has a method, a URL, headers and an optional body. GET reads data, POST creates something, PUT replaces, PATCH partly updates, and DELETE removes. The response has a status code, headers and usually a body. Status codes in the 200s mean success, 400s mean the client made a mistake, and 500s mean the server failed. Resources are named by URLs such as https://api.example.com/products/42.

JSON in one paragraph: JSON, JavaScript Object Notation, is text that represents data with objects in curly braces, arrays in square brackets, strings in double quotes, numbers, true, false and null. A product might arrive as {"id": 42, "name": "Miniket rice 5 kg", "price": 450, "inStock": true, "tags": ["rice", "staple"]}. It is easy for humans to read and for every language to parse, which is why it became the default for mobile APIs.

Permissions and HTTPS rules: On Android, an app needs the INTERNET permission declared in its manifest to open network connections. It is a normal permission, granted at install without a dialog. Flutter's generated project includes it for debug builds, so make sure the main manifest has it too, or your release build will mysteriously fail to connect. Both platforms push you towards encryption: newer Android versions block plain http traffic by default, and iOS's App Transport Security requires HTTPS unless you add exceptions. Use HTTPS for everything.

Making a GET request in Flutter: With the http package: final res = await http.get(Uri.parse('https://api.example.com/products?page=1'), headers: {'Accept': 'application/json'});. Then check the status: if (res.statusCode == 200) { final List data = jsonDecode(res.body); } else { throw ApiException(res.statusCode); }. jsonDecode comes from dart:convert and turns JSON text into Dart maps and lists. Never assume success; always look at the status code before parsing.

Sending data with POST: To create an order, you send JSON in the body: final res = await http.post(Uri.parse('$base/orders'), headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Authorization': 'Bearer $token'}, body: jsonEncode({'productId': 42, 'qty': 2, 'address': 'House 12, Road 5, Dhanmondi'}));. The Content-Type header tells the server the body is JSON. The Authorization header carries the user's access token, which lesson 22 discusses. A successful creation often returns status 201 with the created object.

From JSON maps to model classes: Passing raw maps around the app is fragile: a typo in a key like json['prise'] gives null at runtime. Convert JSON into typed classes once, at the edge. class Product { final int id; final String name; final double price; Product({required this.id, required this.name, required this.price}); factory Product.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> j) => Product(id: j['id'] as int, name: j['name'] as String, price: (j['price'] as num).toDouble()); }. Then the rest of the app works with Product objects, and the compiler checks every use.

Dealing with messy JSON: Real APIs send surprises: a missing field, a null, a number sent as a string, an empty array instead of an object. Decide in fromJson what is required and what is optional: j['discount'] as num? for an optional value, with a sensible default. Note that (j['price'] as num).toDouble() accepts both 450 and 450.5. For large apps, code generators such as json_serializable in Dart, and kotlinx.serialization or Moshi in Kotlin, write this mapping for you from annotated classes.

Other HTTP clients: The http package is simple and fine for small apps. The dio package adds interceptors, which are hooks that run on every request or response, useful for adding tokens, logging, or refreshing an expired token in one place; it also adds timeouts, cancellation and upload progress. On native Android, Retrofit is the classic choice: you describe the API as a Kotlin interface with annotations like @GET("products"), and Retrofit generates the code, using OkHttp underneath. iOS has URLSession built in. The ideas are identical across all of them.

Where networking code lives: Do not scatter http calls across screens. Create one small API client class that knows the base URL, adds common headers such as the token and language, applies timeouts, and turns error responses into your own exception types. Repositories from lesson 12 call this client and return model objects. When the backend moves to a new domain or adds a required header, you change one file. This also lets tests replace the client with a fake that returns prepared JSON.

Seeing what goes over the wire: When something fails, look at the actual request and response. Flutter DevTools has a Network view that lists each call with its headers, body, status and timing, and Android Studio has a Network Inspector for native apps. A logging interceptor in dio or OkHttp can print requests during development; switch it off in release builds so tokens and personal data never end up in logs. Most networking bugs, such as a wrong field name or a missing header, become obvious once you see the raw exchange.

Status codes your app must handle: 200 OK and 201 Created: show the data. 204 No Content: success with nothing to show. 400 Bad Request or 422: the input was wrong; show the server's message next to the form. 401 Unauthorized: the token is missing or expired; try refreshing it, otherwise log the user out. 403 Forbidden: logged in but not allowed. 404 Not Found: the item does not exist, maybe deleted. 429 Too Many Requests: slow down. 500 and 503: server trouble; show a friendly message and allow retry. Map these to clear UI states rather than showing raw numbers.

Timeouts: A request on a dead or extremely slow connection might never finish. Set timeouts: a connect timeout for establishing the connection and a receive timeout for waiting on data, for example 10 to 30 seconds depending on the call. With the http package you can use .timeout(Duration(seconds: 20)) on the Future; dio and OkHttp have timeout settings. When a timeout happens, tell the user the network is slow and offer a retry button.

Retries and backoff: Some failures are temporary: a dropped connection, a 503. Retrying automatically can help, but carefully. Use exponential backoff: wait 1 second, then 2, then 4, adding a little randomness, called jitter, so thousands of phones do not retry at exactly the same moment. Retry only safe, idempotent requests such as GET, PUT and DELETE. A POST that creates an order or sends money might have reached the server even though the response was lost; retrying could create a duplicate. Payment APIs solve this with an idempotency key, a unique ID per attempt, so the server can ignore duplicates.

The four UI states: Every screen that loads data should handle four states: loading, success, empty and error. Loading shows a skeleton or spinner. Success shows the data. Empty shows a friendly message like "No orders yet" with a suggestion, not a blank screen. Error shows what went wrong in plain language with a Retry button. Add pull-to-refresh with Flutter's RefreshIndicator so users can reload. Lesson 11's sealed state class fits this perfectly.

Using less data: Mobile data costs money, and in Bangladesh many users count every megabyte. Ask the backend for exactly what a screen needs, in pages, not entire tables. Request thumbnails rather than full images. Responses are usually compressed with gzip automatically by the HTTP stack, which shrinks JSON a lot. Use HTTP caching headers such as ETag and Cache-Control so unchanged data is not downloaded again; Web Engineering explains how they work. And keep a local copy, as lesson 18 shows.

Is the user online: Plugins can tell you whether the phone has Wi-Fi or mobile data, but being connected to Wi-Fi does not guarantee the internet works; a router may have no upstream connection, or a hotel network may need a login page. Treat connectivity information as a hint, for example to show an offline banner or to retry when the network comes back, but always handle the real result of each request.

Real-life example 1, a weather app for Bangladesh districts: The app calls GET /weather?district=Rajshahi. It sets a 15-second timeout, parses the JSON into a Weather object with temperature, humidity and a list of hourly forecasts, and shows a skeleton while loading. If the call fails, it shows the last saved forecast with a note "Updated 3 hours ago" and a Retry button. During cyclone season the server might be overloaded and return 503; the app backs off and retries automatically twice, then asks the user.

Real-life example 2, placing an order with payment: A grocery app sends POST /orders with the cart, address and an idempotency key generated on the phone. The network drops right after sending, and no response arrives. The app shows "Checking your order" and asks the server for the order status using the same key, instead of blindly posting again. The server says the order exists, so the app shows the confirmation. Without the key, the customer might have been charged twice, which is exactly the kind of bug that destroys trust in an app.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Parsing the body without checking the status code; forgetting the INTERNET permission in release builds; using http instead of https; passing raw maps instead of models; no timeouts; retrying POST requests blindly; showing a blank screen for empty or error states; and using context after await. Exams ask: steps to consume a REST API in a mobile app; how to parse JSON into objects; how to handle different status codes; what idempotency means; and how to design loading, empty and error states.

Recap: Apps talk to servers through REST APIs over HTTPS using JSON. Android needs the INTERNET permission, and both platforms expect HTTPS. Use an HTTP client such as http, dio, Retrofit or URLSession to send GET and POST requests with proper headers, check status codes, and convert JSON into typed model classes with fromJson. Handle 4xx and 5xx codes meaningfully, set timeouts, retry only idempotent requests with exponential backoff, and protect payments with idempotency keys. Every screen needs loading, success, empty and error states, and should use as little data as possible.
key_points: Mobile apps usually talk to servers through REST APIs over HTTPS with JSON; see Web Engineering for HTTP details.
Android needs the INTERNET permission; both platforms block or discourage plain http, so always use HTTPS.
Check the status code before parsing; convert JSON into typed model classes with fromJson once, at the edge.
Handle status codes meaningfully: 2xx success, 400/422 input errors, 401 re-login or refresh, 404 missing, 5xx server trouble.
Set connect and receive timeouts; retry only idempotent requests, with exponential backoff and jitter.
Use idempotency keys for payments and orders so a lost response never causes duplicate charges.
Every data screen needs loading, success, empty and error states, plus pull-to-refresh, and should save mobile data.
lessons.tip: Use a free public test API (for example one that returns fake posts or users) with a REST client on your laptop or phone before writing app code. Seeing the raw JSON and status codes first makes the Dart code obvious.
lessons.task: Write on paper the JSON a server might return for a list of three bus tickets (id, route, departure time, seat, price). Then write the Dart fromJson factory for a Ticket class, and list what your app should show for status codes 200, 401, 404 and 503.

quiz.q: Your Flutter app connects to the API in debug mode but fails in the release APK on Android. What is a likely cause?
options: The INTERNET permission is missing from the main AndroidManifest.xml
quiz.explain: The generated project adds INTERNET for debug builds; release builds need it in the main manifest.

quiz.q: What should you do before calling jsonDecode on a response body?
options: Check the status code to see if the request succeeded
Convert the body to an image
quiz.explain: Error responses may contain HTML or error JSON; check the status code first to decide how to handle it.

quiz.q: Which request is generally safe to retry automatically after a timeout?
options: A GET request that reads the product list
A POST that sends money without an idempotency key
A POST that creates a new order without any key
Any request, retries are always safe
quiz.explain: GET is idempotent; retrying non-idempotent POSTs can create duplicates unless an idempotency key is used.

quiz.q: What does a 401 Unauthorized status usually mean for a mobile app?
options: The user's token is missing or expired, so refresh it or ask them to log in
quiz.explain: 401 means authentication failed; the app should refresh the token or send the user to login.

quiz.q: Why is exponential backoff with jitter used for retries?
options: To make each retry faster than the last
To spread retries out over time so servers are not flooded by many phones at once
quiz.explain: Growing delays plus randomness avoid synchronized retry storms when a server is struggling.

lessons.title: Local Storage I: Key-Value Settings and Files
lessons.content:
Every home has different places to keep things. A small key hook near the door holds the keys you grab every day. A drawer holds documents, neatly filed. An almirah holds big things like blankets. A locked box holds jewellery and important papers. You would not hang a blanket on the key hook or keep gold on the open shelf. Phones offer apps similar choices for storing data locally: small key-value settings, files, databases and secure storage. Picking the right one for each kind of data is a basic skill of mobile development. This lesson covers the first two; lesson 17 covers databases and lesson 22 covers secure storage.

Why store data on the phone at all: The server holds the truth for most data, so why keep anything locally? First, speed: reading from local storage takes milliseconds, while the network can take seconds. Second, offline use: the app should show something useful in a lift, on a launch or in a village with weak signal. Third, saving data costs: what is already stored does not need downloading again. Fourth, some data belongs only on the device: user preferences, drafts, onboarding status, the last opened tab.

The main options: Key-value storage holds small pieces of data under names, like darkMode = true or language = 'bn'. File storage holds documents, images, downloaded media and JSON files. A database, usually SQLite, holds structured records you need to query, sort and update, such as thousands of messages or orders. Secure storage, backed by the Android Keystore and iOS Keychain, holds secrets such as tokens. And some data can be synced to the cloud so it survives a new phone.

Key-value storage, the idea: A key-value store is like a tiny dictionary saved on disk. You put a value under a key and get it back later by the same key. It suits a small number of simple values: settings, flags, counters, the last selected district, whether the user has seen the welcome screens. It does not suit large lists, relationships or anything you need to search.

On Android, SharedPreferences and DataStore: Android's classic key-value store is SharedPreferences, which saves an XML file in the app's private folder. Writing with apply() saves in the background, while commit() writes immediately and blocks, which should be avoided on the main thread. Jetpack DataStore is the newer, recommended replacement: it uses Kotlin coroutines and Flow, never blocks the main thread, and handles errors and consistency better. Preferences DataStore stores key-value pairs; Proto DataStore stores typed objects.

On iOS, UserDefaults: iOS provides UserDefaults for the same purpose. You write UserDefaults.standard.set(true, forKey: "darkMode") and read it back with bool(forKey:). Like SharedPreferences, it is for small, non-sensitive values. Neither SharedPreferences nor UserDefaults encrypts data, so passwords, tokens and personal secrets do not belong there.

In Flutter, the shared_preferences plugin: Flutter's shared_preferences plugin wraps both: SharedPreferences or DataStore-backed storage on Android and UserDefaults on iOS. A typical use: final prefs = await SharedPreferences.getInstance(); await prefs.setString('language', 'bn'); and later final lang = prefs.getString('language') ?? 'en';. Supported types include bool, int, double, String and List<String>. Always provide a default with ??, because on first launch nothing is stored yet. Newer versions of the plugin also offer an asynchronous API that avoids caching everything in memory.

A worked example, remembering onboarding: Many apps show three welcome screens on first launch. In main, before runApp, you read final seen = prefs.getBool('seenOnboarding') ?? false;. If false, the app starts at the onboarding screen; when the user taps Get started, you call prefs.setBool('seenOnboarding', true) and navigate home with pushReplacement. Next launch, seen is true and the app goes straight home. One key, one boolean, and a much nicer experience.

Startup cost of stored settings: Whatever you read before the first screen appears adds to startup time. Reading a few preferences is fast, but loading a 5 MB JSON file in main before runApp can delay the first frame noticeably on a budget phone. Read only what the first screen truly needs, such as the language, theme and login state, before showing the UI. Load everything else after the first frame, showing a skeleton while it loads. Users judge an app in its first two seconds.

What key-value storage is bad at: Imagine storing a list of 500 saved addresses as a single JSON string under one key. Every small change rewrites the whole string, reading one address loads all 500, and you cannot search without decoding everything. If two parts of the app write at once, one change can overwrite the other. When data grows beyond a handful of values or needs queries, move to files or a database.

File storage, app-private directories: Each app has private directories inside its sandbox that no other app can read and that need no permission. They are deleted when the app is uninstalled. On Android, the main ones are the files directory for permanent app data and the cache directory for temporary data. On iOS, the Documents directory holds user-created content and is included in device backups by default, Library/Caches holds re-downloadable data that is not backed up and may be cleared by the system, and tmp holds very short-lived files.

Finding these paths in Flutter: The path_provider plugin gives the right directory on each platform: getApplicationDocumentsDirectory() for important app files, getApplicationSupportDirectory() for internal files the user does not see, and getTemporaryDirectory() for caches. Then you use dart:io: final dir = await getApplicationDocumentsDirectory(); final file = File('${dir.path}/cart.json'); await file.writeAsString(jsonEncode(cart.map((i) => i.toJson()).toList()));. Reading is await file.readAsString() followed by jsonDecode.

Cache versus permanent data: Put data you can download again into cache directories, and data you cannot recreate, such as a user's unsent drafts or downloaded offline content they paid for, into permanent directories. The operating system may delete cache files when storage runs low, and users can tap Clear cache in Android settings. Clear storage, also called Clear data, removes everything, permanent files included, as if the app were freshly installed. Design your app so clearing the cache is always safe.

Shared storage and user files: Sometimes data must be visible outside the app: a photo the user wants in their gallery, or a PDF receipt they want to open in another app. Newer Android versions use scoped storage, which limits broad access to shared storage; apps add media to shared collections through the MediaStore API, and let users pick or save other documents through the system file picker, called the Storage Access Framework. iOS uses the photo library APIs and document pickers. Plugins exist for all of these in Flutter.

Writing files safely: If the app is killed while writing a file, the file can be left half-written and corrupt, and next launch the JSON fails to parse. A safe pattern is to write to a temporary file in the same folder first, then rename it over the old file; renaming within the same file system is usually atomic, so the file is either fully old or fully new. Also wrap reads in try and catch and fall back to defaults if the file is damaged, instead of crashing.

Size and space: Many budget phones in Bangladesh have small storage that is almost full of photos and videos. An app that silently grows to several gigabytes of cache will be the first one users delete. Put limits on caches, for example keep at most 100 MB of images and remove the oldest first. Show users how much space downloaded content uses and let them remove it. Handle the error when the disk is full instead of crashing.

Backups and new phones: On Android, Auto Backup can back up a limited amount of an app's private data to the user's Google account, and restore it on a new phone; on iOS, device backups include the Documents directory. This is helpful for settings and drafts, but you should exclude caches, which are large and re-downloadable, and anything sensitive or tied to the old device, such as device-specific tokens. Both platforms let you configure which files are excluded.

Connecting storage to app state: Storage should not be sprinkled through widgets. A settings repository reads saved values once at startup and exposes them to a settings model, the app state from lesson 11. When the user changes the language, the model updates its state, the UI rebuilds, and the repository writes the new value to storage in the background. The UI never touches SharedPreferences directly. This keeps one source of truth in memory and storage as its saved copy, and it makes the settings logic easy to test with a fake repository.

A quick decision table: Ask what the data is and pick accordingly. A flag or setting: key-value storage. A user draft that must survive restarts: a permanent file or a database row. A list of hundreds of records that must be searched or sorted: a database. Re-downloadable images or API responses: the cache directory with a size limit. A token, PIN or private key: secure storage. A photo the user wants in their gallery: shared storage through MediaStore or the photo library. Writing this table into your project notes saves many later arguments.

Real-life example 1, an offline dictionary app: A Bangla-English dictionary app lets users download the word database for offline use. The downloaded data goes into the app support directory, not the cache, because re-downloading 40 MB on a slow connection is painful. Settings such as font size and the last searched words are stored in key-value storage. Recently viewed definitions are kept as a small JSON file in the cache directory, which can be safely cleared. The settings screen shows how much space the offline pack uses, with a Delete button.

Real-life example 2, a ride app's saved places: A ride app stores the user's chosen language and whether they enabled dark mode in key-value storage. It saves Home and Office addresses, plus the last five destinations, as a small JSON file in app-private storage, so the destination screen opens instantly even before the network responds. The login token is not stored here at all; it goes into secure storage. When the user logs out, the app deletes the personal files and resets preferences.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Storing tokens or passwords in SharedPreferences or UserDefaults; using key-value storage as a database; using commit() on the main thread; putting important data in cache directories; never limiting cache size; writing files non-atomically; and forgetting defaults on first launch. Exams ask: list local storage options in mobile apps and when to use each; difference between SharedPreferences and a database; internal versus external storage; what scoped storage is; and difference between cache and permanent storage.

Recap: Local storage makes apps fast, usable offline and lighter on data. Key-value stores, SharedPreferences or DataStore on Android, UserDefaults on iOS and shared_preferences in Flutter, hold small, non-sensitive settings and flags, always read with defaults. Files hold documents, media and JSON, placed in app-private directories found with path_provider: permanent data in documents or support directories, re-downloadable data in cache. Shared storage uses MediaStore and system pickers under scoped storage. Write files atomically, limit cache size, configure backups sensibly, and keep secrets out of both, in secure storage.
key_points: Local storage gives speed, offline use and lower data costs; the server still holds the truth for most data.
Options: key-value for small settings, files for documents and media, databases for structured data, secure storage for secrets.
SharedPreferences/DataStore (Android), UserDefaults (iOS) and Flutter's shared_preferences store small, unencrypted values; always use defaults.
App-private directories need no permission and are deleted on uninstall; path_provider finds them in Flutter.
Cache directories can be cleared by the system or user; keep only re-downloadable data there.
Newer Android uses scoped storage: MediaStore and the system file picker for shared files.
Write files atomically (temp file then rename), limit cache sizes, and never store tokens or passwords in plain storage.
lessons.tip: Before storing anything, ask three questions: how big is it, can it be downloaded again, and would it hurt if someone read it? The answers point straight to key-value, cache, permanent files, a database or secure storage.
lessons.task: On an Android phone, open Settings, Apps, and look at three apps' storage pages. Write down app size, user data and cache for each. Then guess what kinds of data each app keeps in its data and its cache, and which one would be safest to clear.

quiz.q: Which of these is the best fit for key-value storage like shared_preferences?
options: The user's chosen language and a dark mode flag
quiz.explain: Key-value storage is for small, non-sensitive settings; large or sensitive data belongs elsewhere.

quiz.q: Why should you not store passwords or tokens in SharedPreferences or UserDefaults?
options: They do not encrypt data, so secrets should go to secure storage
quiz.explain: These stores are plain files; use Keystore or Keychain-backed secure storage for secrets.

quiz.q: Where should you put image files that can easily be downloaded again?
options: The Documents directory, backed up forever
A cache directory, which the system may clear when space is low
quiz.explain: Re-downloadable data belongs in the cache, which is safe to clear and not backed up.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to avoid a half-written, corrupt file if the app is killed during a write?
options: Write directly over the old file
Write to a temporary file first, then rename it over the old one
Store the file in RAM only
quiz.explain: Renaming within the same file system is usually atomic, so the file is either fully old or fully new.

quiz.q: On first launch, prefs.getBool('seenOnboarding') returns null. What should your code do?
options: Provide a default, for example ?? false, and show onboarding
Crash, because the data is missing
Ask the server for the value
quiz.explain: Nothing is stored on first launch, so always read key-value data with a sensible default.

lessons.title: Local Storage II: SQLite and On-Device Databases
lessons.content:
Picture the khata, the account book, of a grocery shop in Mirpur. Every customer who buys on credit gets a line: name, date, items, amount, paid or not. At the end of the month the shopkeeper needs answers: who owes more than 2,000 taka, what did Karim buy last week, how much credit is outstanding in total. If he had written everything as one long paragraph, answering would take hours. Because the book has columns and rows, he can find answers quickly. When an app has hundreds or thousands of records to search, sort and update, it needs the same thing on the phone: a database. On mobile, that database is almost always SQLite.

When you need a database: Lesson 16 showed key-value storage for small settings and files for documents. Choose a database when you have many records of the same shape, such as notes, messages, transactions, products or survey responses; when you need to query them, for example by date, by category or by text; when you update individual records often; or when records relate to each other, like orders and their items. A chat app with 50,000 messages, an offline catalogue, or a field survey app with hundreds of forms all need a real database.

What SQLite is: SQLite is a small, fast, embedded relational database engine. Embedded means there is no separate server process: the database is a library inside your app, and the whole database lives in a single file in the app's private storage. It supports standard SQL, tables, indexes and ACID transactions, the same ideas you learned in DBMS. It is included in both Android and iOS, it is public domain, and it is one of the most widely deployed pieces of software in the world. Your phone already contains many SQLite databases used by system apps.

SQL recap with a notes table: To create a table: CREATE TABLE notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, title TEXT NOT NULL, body TEXT, pinned INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL). To add a note: INSERT INTO notes (title, body, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?). To read pinned notes newest first: SELECT * FROM notes WHERE pinned = 1 ORDER BY updated_at DESC. To edit: UPDATE notes SET body = ?, updated_at = ? WHERE id = ?. To remove: DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = ?. SQLite has no separate boolean or date types, so booleans are stored as 0 and 1, and dates usually as integer timestamps in milliseconds or ISO text.

Always use parameters: Notice the question marks. Never build SQL by joining user input into the string, as in "... WHERE title = '" + search + "'". If the user types a quote character, the query breaks, and a malicious input could change the meaning of the query; this is SQL injection, which Web Engineering discusses in detail. Passing values separately, as parameters, lets SQLite treat them strictly as data. Every mobile database library supports this, so there is no excuse not to use it.

SQLite in Flutter with sqflite: The sqflite plugin gives direct access to SQLite. You open a database with a version number and a creation callback: final db = await openDatabase(join(await getDatabasesPath(), 'notes.db'), version: 1, onCreate: (db, version) => db.execute('CREATE TABLE notes (...)'));. Then helper methods do common operations: await db.insert('notes', note.toMap()); final rows = await db.query('notes', where: 'pinned = ?', whereArgs: [1], orderBy: 'updated_at DESC'); await db.update('notes', note.toMap(), where: 'id = ?', whereArgs: [note.id]); and db.delete in the same style. Rows come back as maps that you turn into model objects with fromMap.

Type-safe wrappers: Writing SQL as strings means typos are only found at runtime. Libraries add safety on top of SQLite. In Flutter, drift lets you describe tables in Dart, generates type-safe query code, and can return a Stream that emits new results whenever the table changes. Other local databases exist for Flutter, some of them NoSQL object stores, but SQLite-based solutions remain the most common and portable choice.

Room on Android: Jetpack Room is Google's recommended layer over SQLite. You define an entity: @Entity data class Note(@PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Long = 0, val title: String, val body: String?, val pinned: Boolean = false, val updatedAt: Long). You define a DAO, a data access object: @Dao interface NoteDao { @Query("SELECT * FROM Note ORDER BY updatedAt DESC") fun observeAll(): Flow<List<Note>>; @Insert suspend fun insert(note: Note); @Delete suspend fun delete(note: Note) }. Room checks your SQL queries at compile time against the schema, and by default refuses to run queries on the main thread, which protects you from jank.

On iOS, Core Data and SwiftData: Apple's Core Data framework manages a graph of model objects and can store them in SQLite underneath. The newer SwiftData framework offers a simpler, Swift-first way to define and store models. Many iOS developers also use SQLite directly or through wrapper libraries. In a Flutter app, sqflite or drift work on both platforms, so you write the database code once.

The DAO idea: Whatever the library, keep database code in one place behind a small interface, the DAO. For example, NoteDao with insert, update, delete, getById, watchAll and search. Screens and ViewModels never write SQL; they call the repository, which calls the DAO. This matches the architecture of lesson 12: the DAO is the local data source. When you change a query or add an index, only the DAO changes.

Transactions: A transaction groups several operations so they all succeed or all fail. Suppose an offline shop app records a sale: insert the sale, insert three sale items, and reduce stock for each product. If the app crashes after inserting the sale but before reducing stock, the data becomes inconsistent. Wrapping the steps in a transaction, await db.transaction((txn) async { ... }); in sqflite or @Transaction in Room, guarantees all-or-nothing. Transactions also make bulk inserts much faster, because SQLite commits to disk once for the whole batch instead of once per row.

Schema versions and migrations: Apps change. Version 2 of your notes app adds a colour for each note. Users who already have version 1 have a database with the old table and their precious notes inside. You cannot simply delete and recreate it. Instead, you increase the database version to 2 and provide a migration: in sqflite, onUpgrade: (db, oldVersion, newVersion) async { if (oldVersion < 2) { await db.execute('ALTER TABLE notes ADD COLUMN color INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0'); } }. Room has migration objects for the same purpose and can generate simple ones automatically.

Migration rules that save you: Never change a migration after it has shipped; add a new one instead. Write migrations step by step, from 1 to 2, 2 to 3, so a user jumping from version 1 to 5 runs every step in order. Test upgrading from every old version you shipped, with real data in it. Avoid the shortcut of destroying and recreating the database on upgrade unless the data is only a cache, because users lose everything. A broken migration crashes the app at launch for every updating user, which is one of the worst bugs you can ship.

Indexes: Without an index, SELECT * FROM messages WHERE chat_id = 42 must scan every row. With 50,000 messages that can take noticeable time on a budget phone. CREATE INDEX idx_messages_chat ON messages(chat_id, sent_at) lets SQLite jump directly to the matching rows, already in time order. Indexes make reads faster but writes a bit slower and take extra space, so index the columns you actually filter and sort by, not everything. SQLite also offers full-text search tables for searching words inside long text, useful for note or message search.

Reactive queries: Modern libraries can turn a query into a stream. Room returns a Flow, and drift returns a Stream, that emits the new result every time the underlying table changes. The UI simply listens: when a background sync inserts new messages, the chat screen updates by itself, without anyone calling refresh. This fits declarative UI and makes the local database the natural single source of truth, which is the foundation of offline-first apps in lesson 18.

Keep the database off the main thread: Database operations read and write the disk, which can take milliseconds or more. sqflite runs its work off the main thread and returns Futures; Room requires suspend functions or Flows by default. Still, avoid huge queries on screen open, such as loading 50,000 rows when you show 20; use LIMIT and OFFSET or cursor-style paging with WHERE sent_at < ?. Open the database once and reuse the connection rather than opening it for every query.

Worked example, a notes app end to end: The NotesScreen observes a NotesViewModel. The ViewModel subscribes to noteRepository.watchAll(), which returns the DAO's stream of notes ordered by pinned first, then updated_at descending. Tapping Save calls repository.save(note), which inserts or updates with a new timestamp. The stream emits, and the list redraws with the note on top. Search calls a DAO method that uses a full-text search or a LIKE query with a parameter. Version 2 adds a colour column through a migration, tested by installing version 1, adding notes, and upgrading.

Real-life example 1, a field survey app for an NGO: Field workers in Kurigram fill in household surveys offline all day. Each survey is a row in a surveys table, with child rows in an answers table, all written inside a transaction so a survey is never half-saved. A status column marks each survey as draft, ready or uploaded. An index on status lets the sync code quickly find ready surveys. When version 3 of the app adds a GPS location column, a migration adds it with a default, and no worker loses a single saved survey.

Real-life example 2, a chat app's message history: A messaging app stores messages locally in SQLite so chats open instantly and are readable offline. The messages table has an index on chat ID and timestamp. Opening a chat loads the latest 50 messages; scrolling up loads older pages with WHERE sent_at < ? LIMIT 50. New messages arriving from the server are inserted in a transaction, and the reactive query updates the open chat. Searching old messages uses a full-text table. Without these database basics, a long chat would freeze on budget phones.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Building SQL with string concatenation; running big queries on the main thread; forgetting migrations, so updated apps crash; destroying user data on upgrade; no indexes on columns used in WHERE; doing many separate inserts without a transaction; and opening a new connection for every query. Exams ask: why use SQLite on mobile; write SQL to create and query a table; what is a DAO; explain transactions with an example; what is a database migration and why is it needed; and what indexes do.

Recap: Use a database when you have many structured records to query and update. SQLite is an embedded, serverless, single-file relational database built into Android and iOS. Use parameterised SQL to avoid injection. In Flutter use sqflite or drift; on Android, Room with entities and DAOs; on iOS, Core Data or SwiftData. Keep queries in a DAO behind a repository, wrap related writes in transactions, version your schema with careful step-by-step migrations, add indexes for frequent filters and sorts, use reactive queries so the UI follows the database, and keep all of it off the main thread.
key_points: Use a database when you have many structured records to query, sort, update or relate.
SQLite is an embedded, serverless relational database stored in one file, built into Android and iOS, with SQL and ACID transactions.
Always use parameterised queries (?) instead of joining user input into SQL, to prevent SQL injection.
Flutter uses sqflite or drift; Android uses Room with entities and DAOs; iOS uses Core Data or SwiftData.
Transactions make related writes all-or-nothing and speed up bulk inserts.
Schema changes need versioned, step-by-step migrations tested from every shipped version; never wipe user data.
Indexes speed up filters and sorts at some write cost; reactive queries let the UI follow the database automatically.
lessons.tip: Install a free SQLite browser on your laptop and copy an app's database file from an emulator to look inside. Seeing the real tables and running your own SELECT queries makes mobile databases feel familiar fast.
lessons.task: Design on paper the tables for an offline expense tracker: expenses (amount, category, date, note) and categories. Write the CREATE TABLE statements, one INSERT, a SELECT for this month's total by category, and the ALTER TABLE migration needed if version 2 adds a payment method column.

quiz.q: What does it mean that SQLite is embedded?
options: It only runs on embedded chips in cars
It runs as a library inside the app with the database in a single file, no separate server
It must be installed separately by the user
It stores data only in RAM
quiz.explain: SQLite is a library linked into the app; the whole database is one file in app storage.

quiz.q: Why should you write WHERE title = ? with parameters instead of joining the search text into the SQL string?
options: It makes the database file smaller
It is required for indexes to exist
It prevents broken queries and SQL injection by treating input strictly as data
quiz.explain: Parameters keep user input separate from the SQL code, so special characters cannot change the query.

quiz.q: Version 2 of your app adds a column to an existing table. What must you provide?
options: A migration that alters the table and keeps existing data
A new app with a different package name
A command to delete the old database
quiz.explain: Increase the schema version and add a migration such as ALTER TABLE so existing users keep their data.

quiz.q: Why wrap 'insert sale, insert items, reduce stock' in a transaction?
options: To send it to the server
So all steps succeed or none do, keeping the data consistent if something fails midway
quiz.explain: Transactions are all-or-nothing, preventing half-finished updates.

quiz.q: What is the main trade-off of adding an index on a column?
options: Filters and sorts on it get faster, but writes get slightly slower and use more space
The column can no longer be updated
quiz.explain: Indexes speed up lookups but must be maintained on every insert and update.

lessons.title: Offline-First Apps and Data Sync
lessons.content:
Think about a village shopkeeper who keeps sales in a notebook all day, then once a week travels to the upazila town to update the wholesaler's records. The shop never stops selling just because the wholesaler is far away. He writes locally, and synchronises later. If he and the wholesaler both changed the same entry, they sit together and decide which is right. That is exactly the idea behind offline-first apps: the app keeps working with local data, and synchronises with the server when it can, handling disagreements carefully. In a country where signal drops on trains, in lifts, during load-shedding and across much of rural Bangladesh, this is not a luxury.

Online-only apps and their problem: The simplest app design asks the server for everything and shows nothing until the server answers. When the network is fine, it works. When the network is slow, the user stares at spinners. When it is absent, the app shows an error screen and becomes useless, even for data the user saw five minutes ago. Every action, such as saving a note, fails without a connection. Users experience this as a broken app, even though the code has no bugs.

What offline-first means: In an offline-first app, the local database on the phone is the single source of truth for the UI. Screens always read from local storage, so they show data instantly, online or not. The network is used to keep that local data fresh and to send local changes to the server, but the UI never waits on it directly. In practice this combines everything from lessons 15 to 17: a REST API, a local SQLite database, reactive queries and a repository that coordinates them.

The read path, step by step: The user opens the orders screen. One: the ViewModel subscribes to a reactive query on the local orders table, which emits immediately with whatever is stored, even if it is a day old. Two: the repository starts a network request in the background. Three: when the response arrives, the repository writes the new orders into the database inside a transaction. Four: the reactive query emits again and the screen updates by itself. If the request fails, nothing breaks; the user still sees the stored orders, maybe with a small note saying when they were last updated.

Caching strategies: Different data needs different rules. Cache-first: use local data if present, and only go to the network if nothing is stored, good for rarely changing data like a list of districts. Network-first: try the network, fall back to cache on failure, good when freshness matters most, like a balance. Cache-then-network, also called stale-while-revalidate: show cached data at once, then refresh in the background and update the screen, good for feeds and lists. Many apps also use a time-to-live: data older than, say, 10 minutes is refreshed automatically, newer data is trusted.
