The write path, local first: When the user creates or edits something offline, such as a note, a survey or an expense, the app writes it to the local database immediately and marks it with a sync status such as pending. The UI updates at once, because it reads from the database. This is called an optimistic update: the app assumes the server will accept the change and shows it right away. A small icon, like a clock or a cloud with a slash, can tell the user that the item is not yet synced.

The outbox or sync queue: To make sure local changes reach the server, the app keeps an outbox: a table of pending operations, each with the action (create, update, delete), the record ID, the data and a retry count. When the network is available, a sync worker reads the outbox in order, sends each operation to the API, and on success marks the record as synced and removes the outbox entry. On failure it retries later with exponential backoff. The outbox survives app restarts because it is in the database, not in memory.

IDs created on the phone: If records are created offline, they need IDs before the server ever sees them, so other records can refer to them; a sale item must point to its sale. If the server assigns IDs, the app must later swap temporary IDs for real ones everywhere, which is error-prone. A simpler approach is to generate a universally unique identifier, a UUID, on the phone. UUIDs are long random values with a negligible chance of collision, so the phone and server can both use the same ID from the start. The same UUID also works as an idempotency key, so a retried upload does not create duplicates.

Syncing only what changed: Downloading the full list of orders on every sync wastes data. Instead, the app remembers when it last synced, or a cursor the server gave it, and asks only for changes: GET /orders?updated_since=2025-03-01T10:00:00Z. The server returns records created or modified after that point. This is called delta or incremental sync. It is much lighter for users on limited data packs and much faster on slow networks.

Syncing deletions: Deletes are tricky. If a record is simply removed from the server database, a phone asking for changes since yesterday will never hear about it and will keep showing the deleted record forever. The usual fix is a tombstone: instead of erasing the row, the server marks it deleted with a flag and an updated timestamp, so delta sync can report the deletion. Locally too, the app may soft-delete a record by marking it, hiding it from the UI, until the delete is confirmed by the server.

Conflicts, the hard part: A conflict happens when the same record is changed in two places before they sync. A shop's stock count is edited by the owner on his phone and by the manager on a tablet, both offline. When both sync, which value wins? There is no single right answer; you choose a strategy based on what the data means. It is important to decide this deliberately during design, rather than letting it happen by accident.

Conflict strategy 1, last write wins: The simplest rule: the change with the latest timestamp wins, and the other is overwritten. It is easy to implement but can silently lose data. It also depends on clocks, and phone clocks can be wrong; a phone set to the wrong date could win every conflict. Using the server's time when changes arrive, or version numbers, is safer than trusting device clocks. Last write wins is acceptable for data where losing an occasional edit is harmless, like a profile picture.

Conflict strategy 2, versions and rejection: Each record carries a version number. When the phone sends an update, it includes the version it started from: "update stock of item 7, based on version 12". If the server's version is still 12, it accepts and makes it 13. If it is already 13 because someone else changed it, the server rejects the update, for example with status 409 Conflict. The app then fetches the latest version and either merges automatically or asks the user. This is called optimistic concurrency control, and you may recognise the idea from DBMS.

Conflict strategy 3, merge or ask: Sometimes changes can be merged: if one person changed the phone number and another changed the address of the same customer, both changes can be kept field by field. For lists, such as items in a shared shopping list, additions from both sides can be combined. When a true clash happens on the same field, some apps show both versions and let the user choose. Advanced systems use special data structures called CRDTs that merge automatically, but they are beyond this course; knowing they exist is enough.

When to sync: Sync can be triggered when the app opens, when the user pulls to refresh, when connectivity returns, and periodically in the background. On Android, WorkManager can run a sync job with a constraint that the network must be connected, and it retries with backoff if the job fails; lesson 21 explains background work in detail. Push notifications can also tell the app that new data is waiting, so it syncs only when there is something to fetch, saving battery.

What must stay online: Not everything can be offline-first. Sending money, buying a ticket for a specific seat, or booking a doctor's appointment needs immediate confirmation from the server, because the result depends on what other people are doing at the same moment. For these actions, the app should clearly say an internet connection is needed, and never pretend the action succeeded. A good offline-first app is honest about which actions are pending, which are complete and which require a connection.

The UI of an offline-first app: Users should never be confused about what is happening. Show an unobtrusive offline banner when there is no connection. Mark pending items with an icon and complete items normally. Show "Last updated 10:30 AM" on data screens. If a sync fails permanently, for example the server rejected the change, show the item with an error and a way to fix or discard it. Avoid modal error dialogs for every failed background sync; they make an offline-first app feel more broken than an online-only one.

Real-life example 1, a health worker's app: Community health workers in a haor region visit homes by boat and record pregnant mothers' check-ups. The app saves every visit locally with a UUID and a pending status, adds it to the outbox, and shows it in the visit list immediately. When the worker returns to an area with signal, WorkManager runs the sync: pending visits are uploaded in order, each with its UUID as an idempotency key, then the app downloads updated schedules with delta sync. If a supervisor edited the same mother's record meanwhile, the version check detects it and the app shows both versions for the worker to review.

Real-life example 2, a small shop's sales app during load-shedding: A shop in a market uses a tablet for sales. During load-shedding the Wi-Fi router goes off, but the app keeps working: products and prices come from the local database, each sale is saved locally and queued. Stock counts are updated locally as sales happen. When power returns, the queue syncs to the server. Stock conflicts between two tablets are handled by sending sale events, such as "sold 2 of item 7", instead of overwriting the final stock number, so both tablets' sales add up correctly.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Showing an error screen instead of cached data; keeping pending changes only in memory so they vanish when the app is killed; using server-generated IDs for offline creation; re-downloading everything every sync; forgetting deletions; trusting phone clocks for conflicts; and pretending online-only actions succeeded. Exams ask: what is offline-first and why is it important; explain caching strategies; how a sync queue works; what conflicts are and strategies to resolve them; and design the sync for a given app scenario.

Recap: Offline-first apps treat the local database as the single source of truth; the UI reads locally and the network updates the database in the background. Choose cache-first, network-first or stale-while-revalidate per type of data. Write changes locally first with a pending status, record them in a persistent outbox, and sync with retries and idempotency. Use UUIDs for records created offline, delta sync for efficiency and tombstones for deletions. Decide conflict rules deliberately: last write wins, version checks, merging or asking the user. Keep truly online actions clearly online, and show users honest sync status.
key_points: Offline-first means the local database is the single source of truth; the UI reads locally and never waits directly on the network.
Caching strategies: cache-first, network-first, and cache-then-network (stale-while-revalidate), often with a time-to-live.
Writes go to the local database first with a pending status (optimistic update) and into a persistent outbox for syncing.
Phone-generated UUIDs let records be created offline and double as idempotency keys for safe retries.
Delta sync downloads only changes since the last sync; tombstones make deletions visible to other devices.
Conflicts need a deliberate strategy: last write wins, version checks with rejection, field merge, or asking the user.
Some actions, like payments and seat bookings, must stay online and should say so clearly.
lessons.tip: For any app you design, make a two-column list: actions that can work offline and queue, and actions that must be online. Doing this before coding shapes your database, your sync code and your UI messages correctly.
lessons.task: Design on paper the sync for a hostel meal-tracker app used by several boarders on their own phones. Decide which table needs an outbox, how IDs are created, how deletions are synced, and what happens if two boarders edit the same day's meal count offline.

quiz.q: In an offline-first app, where does the UI read its data from?
options: The local database, which acts as the single source of truth
Directly from the server on every screen
quiz.explain: The UI reads local data instantly; the network updates the local database in the background.

quiz.q: What does stale-while-revalidate (cache-then-network) do?
options: Refuses to show data until the network answers
Only uses the network, never the cache
Shows cached data immediately, then refreshes from the network and updates the screen
quiz.explain: Users see something at once, and fresh data replaces it when it arrives.

quiz.q: Why are UUIDs generated on the phone useful for offline creation?
options: Records get stable IDs before reaching the server, and the ID can act as an idempotency key
They replace the need for a database
quiz.explain: Client-generated unique IDs avoid temporary-ID swapping and prevent duplicates on retry.

quiz.q: Why do sync systems often use tombstones instead of physically deleting rows on the server?
options: So delta sync can tell other devices that the record was deleted
quiz.explain: A deleted flag with an updated timestamp lets 'changes since' queries report deletions.

quiz.q: What is a weakness of last-write-wins conflict resolution based on device timestamps?
options: It is very hard to implement
It always asks the user to choose
It can silently lose edits, and wrong phone clocks can decide the winner
quiz.explain: Overwriting loses one change, and device clocks can be wrong; server time or version numbers are safer.

lessons.title: Permissions and Privacy
lessons.content:
When a guest visits your home in Bangladesh, they are welcomed into the drawing room. They do not walk into the bedrooms, open the almirah or read the family's letters without asking, and if they ask, you can say no. A good guest also explains why: "Can I use your bathroom? I need to wash my hands." A mobile app on someone's phone is a guest in the most personal space they have. Permissions are the house rules that decide which rooms an app may enter, and privacy is the good manners that decide what it does once inside. Getting both right is now required by the platforms, the stores and, increasingly, the law.

Why permissions exist: Recall the sandbox from lessons 1 and 2. By default an app can only touch its own files and memory. But useful features need more: a QR payment needs the camera, a ride app needs location, a voice note needs the microphone, a contact picker needs contacts. These are sensitive because they reveal where you are, who you know, what you look like and what you say. Permissions are the controlled doors in the sandbox wall, and the user holds the keys.

Android permission types: Android groups permissions by risk. Normal permissions cover low-risk actions, such as INTERNET or setting an alarm; they are declared in the manifest and granted automatically at install. Dangerous permissions, also called runtime permissions, cover private data and hardware, such as CAMERA, RECORD_AUDIO, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION and READ_CONTACTS; since Android 6.0 they must be declared in the manifest and also granted by the user at runtime through a system dialog. A few special permissions, such as drawing over other apps, can only be granted from a settings page. On newer Android versions, posting notifications is also a runtime permission.

The runtime permission flow: The correct sequence has four steps. First, check whether the permission is already granted; if so, go ahead. Second, if not, decide whether to show a short explanation first; Android provides a method that tells you when the user has denied before and an explanation would help. Third, request the permission, which shows the system dialog. Fourth, handle the answer: if granted, continue; if denied, keep the app working without that feature. The system dialog itself cannot be customised; your explanation goes on your own screen before it.

Denial and "don't ask again": Users may deny a permission. On newer Android versions, if the user denies the same permission twice, the system stops showing the dialog, and further requests are silently refused. iOS shows the dialog only once per permission. After that, the only way to grant the permission is through the system Settings app. So the app must detect a permanent denial and, if the feature is truly needed, show a polite message with a button that opens the app's settings page, instead of asking again and again.

Permissions in Flutter: The popular permission_handler plugin wraps both platforms. final status = await Permission.camera.request(); if (status.isGranted) { openScanner(); } else if (status.isPermanentlyDenied) { showDialogWithButton(openAppSettings); } else { showSnack('Camera is needed to scan QR codes'); }. You still must declare the permission in AndroidManifest.xml and add the usage description to the iOS Info.plist; the plugin cannot do that for you.

iOS permissions and usage descriptions: On iOS, before accessing protected resources such as the camera, microphone, photo library, contacts or location, the app must include a usage description string in its Info.plist, for example NSCameraUsageDescription with the text "We use the camera to scan payment QR codes." This text appears in the system dialog. If the description is missing, the app is terminated when it tries to access the resource, and App Review checks that these explanations are clear and honest. Writing them in plain language, and in Bangla for Bangla users if your app is localised, builds trust.

Location permissions in detail: Location is especially sensitive, so both platforms split it. Users can grant access only while the app is in use, or, separately, in the background. Newer Android and iOS versions also let users grant only approximate location, accurate to roughly a neighbourhood, instead of precise GPS location. Some versions offer "Only this time" grants that expire. Background location requires a separate request after foreground access, and Google Play restricts which apps may use it, requiring a clear justification. Ask for the least precise, least persistent access your feature truly needs.

Avoid permissions entirely when you can: The best permission is the one you never need. To let users pick a profile photo, use the system photo picker: on newer Android versions and on iOS, the picker lets the user choose specific photos and gives your app only those, with no broad photo library permission. To make a phone call, use an implicit intent to open the dialer with the number filled in, which needs no permission, instead of placing the call directly. To share content, use the share sheet. Fewer permissions mean fewer scary dialogs, simpler store review and less risk.

Asking at the right time: Many apps ask for every permission on the first screen. Users, who do not yet trust the app, tap Deny. Ask in context instead: request the camera when the user taps "Scan QR", not at launch. If a permission is central to the app, such as location in a ride app, show a short screen before the system dialog explaining the benefit: "Allow location so drivers can find you without calling." Both Android and Apple guidelines recommend this, because a user who understands why a permission is needed, at the moment it is needed, is far more likely to accept it and to trust the app afterwards.

Graceful degradation: The app must keep working when a permission is denied. If location is denied, let the user type their area or pick on a map. If the camera is denied, offer manual entry of the merchant number. If notifications are denied, show important updates inside the app. Never lock the whole app behind an optional permission. Platform guidelines and store reviewers expect this, and users who change their mind later will find the feature waiting for them.

What privacy means for a developer: Permission controls access; privacy is about what you do with data. Core principles, found in most privacy laws and platform policies: collect only what you need (data minimisation), use it only for the purpose you stated (purpose limitation), tell users clearly what you collect and why (transparency), get consent where required, keep data only as long as needed (retention), protect it in storage and transit (security), and let users see, export or delete their data. A practical test: would the user be surprised to learn what your app does with their data? If yes, change it.

Third-party SDKs are your responsibility: Apps often include analytics, crash reporting, ads and social login SDKs. These libraries may collect device identifiers, location or usage data on their own. In the eyes of users, the stores and regulators, whatever runs inside your app is your app's behaviour. Before adding an SDK, read what data it collects, configure it to collect less where possible, and include it in your privacy disclosures. Many privacy problems in real apps come from SDKs the developer never examined.

Store privacy disclosures: Google Play requires a Data safety section in the store listing, where you declare what data the app collects and shares, why, and whether it is encrypted and deletable. Apple requires App Privacy details, often called privacy nutrition labels, with similar information. Both require a privacy policy link. These declarations must match the app's real behaviour, including SDKs; mismatches can lead to rejection or removal. If your app lets users create accounts, both stores now expect a way to delete the account and its data.

Tracking and advertising identifiers: Advertising often relies on identifiers that follow a user across apps. On iOS, App Tracking Transparency requires apps to ask the user's permission before tracking them across apps and websites owned by other companies, and many users say no. On Android, users can reset or delete their advertising ID in settings. If your app uses ads or attribution, these rules affect how much data you get. Never try to work around them with fingerprinting; both stores forbid it.

Visible privacy signals: Newer versions of Android and iOS show an indicator, such as a small coloured dot, when an app is using the camera or microphone, and keep a dashboard of which apps accessed location, camera and microphone recently. Some versions also automatically reset permissions for apps that have not been used for months. This means users can see and judge what your app does. An app that uses the microphone when the user did not expect it will be noticed, reviewed badly and possibly reported.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet's QR payment: The wallet app does not ask for the camera at launch. When the user taps Scan QR, a short screen says "Camera is used only to read the shop's QR code. We do not save photos." Then the system dialog appears. If the user denies, the scanner screen offers "Enter merchant number instead". If they denied permanently, a button opens settings. The Info.plist string on iOS uses the same honest sentence. No photo is stored, and the Data safety form states this.

Real-life example 2, a ride app's location: The ride app asks for location only while in use, and supports approximate location for browsing fares. When the user books, it explains that precise location helps the driver find the exact gate of their building in a crowded area like Gulshan or Old Dhaka, and asks for precise access. It never requests background location; the driver's app, not the passenger's, tracks the ride. Location history is deleted after a set period and explained in the privacy policy.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Asking for all permissions at startup; requesting permissions the app does not need; forgetting the iOS usage strings or Android manifest entries; asking repeatedly after permanent denial; blocking the app when a permission is denied; using background location without strong need; and adding SDKs without checking their data collection. Exams ask: difference between normal and dangerous permissions; explain the runtime permission flow; why apps should ask in context; what data minimisation means; and what privacy disclosures stores require.

Recap: Permissions are the doors in the sandbox, controlled by the user. Android has normal permissions granted at install and dangerous ones granted at runtime; iOS requires usage descriptions and asks once. Check, explain, request and handle the answer, including permanent denial with a link to settings. Ask in context, request the least access needed, prefer pickers and intents that need no permission, and keep the app usable when access is denied. Privacy means collecting the minimum, using it only as promised, securing it, disclosing it honestly in store forms, respecting tracking rules, and owning what your SDKs do.
key_points: Permissions are user-controlled doors in the app sandbox for sensitive data and hardware like camera, location and contacts.
Android: normal permissions are granted at install; dangerous (runtime) permissions need a user dialog; iOS needs usage description strings.
Runtime flow: check, explain if helpful, request, then handle grant, denial and permanent denial (link to settings).
Ask in context at the moment of need, request the least access (approximate, while-in-use), and keep the app working if denied.
Prefer system pickers, intents and the share sheet, which often need no permission at all.
Privacy principles: data minimisation, purpose limitation, transparency, consent, retention limits, security and user control.
Stores require honest disclosures (Play Data safety, Apple App Privacy) covering SDKs too; respect tracking consent rules.
lessons.tip: Open Settings, then Privacy or Permission manager, on your phone and review which apps can access your location, camera and microphone. Seeing it as a user makes you a more careful developer.
lessons.task: Choose three features of an app idea, such as scanning a QR code, finding nearby pharmacies and attaching a prescription photo. For each, write which permission (if any) is needed, when you would ask, the one-sentence explanation you would show, and what the app does if the user says no.

quiz.q: Which Android permission is a normal permission granted automatically at install?
quiz.explain: INTERNET is low-risk and normal; camera, location and contacts are dangerous runtime permissions.

quiz.q: When is the best time to request the camera permission in a payment app?
options: On the very first launch screen
When the user taps the Scan QR button
quiz.explain: Asking in context, when the user understands why, leads to more acceptance and better trust.

quiz.q: On iOS, what happens if your app accesses the camera without an NSCameraUsageDescription in Info.plist?
options: The App Store adds it automatically
The app is terminated when it tries to access the camera
quiz.explain: iOS requires a usage description for protected resources; without it the app is killed on access.

quiz.q: A user has permanently denied location. What should the app do if the feature is needed?
options: Explain politely and offer a button that opens the app's settings page, while keeping alternatives available
Ask again in a loop until they accept
quiz.explain: After permanent denial only Settings can grant it; the app should guide the user there and still offer alternatives.

quiz.q: What does data minimisation mean?
options: Collecting only the data you actually need for the stated purpose
quiz.explain: Data minimisation is a core privacy principle: do not collect what you do not need.

lessons.title: Sensors, Location and Camera
lessons.content:
Close your eyes and tilt your head. You still know which way is down, whether you are moving, and roughly where you are in the room. Your inner ear, muscles and memory act as sensors. A smartphone has its own set of senses: it can feel motion and tilt, sense which way north is, measure light, know when it is near your ear, find its position on Earth, and see through its cameras. These senses let apps count steps, rotate maps, scan QR codes and guide a rider to your door. This lesson explains how the main sensors work, how apps read them, and how to use them without draining the battery.

The sensor family: Android groups sensors into three broad kinds. Motion sensors measure acceleration and rotation: the accelerometer and the gyroscope. Position sensors measure the phone's orientation and nearness: the magnetometer, which senses the Earth's magnetic field like a compass, and the proximity sensor, which turns the screen off during calls. Environmental sensors measure surroundings: light, and on some phones air pressure through a barometer. Not every phone has every sensor, especially budget models, so apps must check before using one.

Hardware and software sensors: Some sensors are physical chips. Others are software sensors that combine several hardware sensors to give a cleaner answer. For example, a rotation vector sensor fuses the accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer to give the phone's orientation in space; a linear acceleration sensor removes gravity from the accelerometer reading; a step counter detects walking steps, often using a low-power dedicated chip. Prefer these composite sensors when they fit your need, because the platform has already done the hard maths.

The accelerometer, a worked example: The accelerometer reports acceleration along three axes, in metres per second squared. On Android, with the phone held upright in portrait, x points to the right, y points up the screen, and z points out of the screen towards you. Lying flat on a table, the phone reads about x = 0, y = 0, z = 9.8, because the sensor feels gravity pushing up against it. Hold it upright and y becomes about 9.8. So the accelerometer can tell which way is down, which is how screens auto-rotate. The total magnitude, the square root of x² + y² + z², stays near 9.8 when the phone is still.

Detecting a shake: To detect a shake, compute the magnitude of each reading and compare it with gravity. If the magnitude jumps well above 9.8, for example above 25, a few times within half a second, the user is probably shaking the phone. A real implementation adds a short cooldown so one shake does not trigger ten actions. Some apps use shake to report a bug or undo. Thresholds need tuning on real devices, because sensor chips differ between phone models.

Noise and filtering: Raw sensor readings are noisy; even a phone on a table shows tiny random changes. A simple low-pass filter smooths them by mixing each new reading with the previous smoothed value: smoothed = 0.8 × previous + 0.2 × new. A higher weight on the previous value gives smoother but slower response. The opposite, a high-pass filter, keeps only quick changes and removes slow ones like gravity. Filtering is a small idea from Signals and Systems that appears constantly in sensor code.

Reading sensors in code: On Android, you get a SensorManager, choose a sensor, and register a listener with a sampling rate, from normal, suitable for screen orientation, up to fastest, suitable for games. Readings arrive in onSensorChanged. On iOS, the Core Motion framework provides similar data. In Flutter, a sensors plugin exposes accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer readings as Streams, so you listen and cancel the subscription in dispose, exactly as in lesson 14.

Sensors and battery: Sensors cost power, and faster sampling costs more. A game might need 50 or more readings per second; a step counter needs very few. Always ask for the slowest rate that works, unregister listeners when the screen is not visible, in onPause or when the Flutter app goes to the paused state, and never leave sensors running in the background without a clear reason. Forgetting to unregister a sensor listener is a classic cause of the "this app drains my battery" review.

Where location comes from: Phones combine several sources. Satellite positioning, often called GPS though modern phones also use other satellite systems, can be accurate to a few metres outdoors, but it needs a clear sky, takes time for the first fix and uses significant power; it works poorly indoors and between tall buildings. Wi-Fi positioning uses nearby access points and works well in cities and indoors. Cell tower positioning is cheap but coarse, sometimes off by hundreds of metres or more. Each location result includes an accuracy radius, which apps should use.

Fused location: Rather than choosing sources yourself, you normally ask the platform for location with a priority. On Android, the Fused Location Provider from Google Play services combines GPS, Wi-Fi, cell and sensors, and you choose high accuracy, balanced power or low power. iOS's Core Location does similar fusion with a desired accuracy setting. In Flutter, plugins such as geolocator wrap both. A navigation screen needs high accuracy and frequent updates; showing the user's city for weather needs only low power, coarse location once.

Controlling update frequency: Continuous location updates can be limited in two ways: by time, such as an update every 10 seconds, and by distance, such as only when the user has moved 20 metres. A delivery rider's app might use high accuracy with a 10-metre distance filter while on a delivery, and stop updates completely when the rider goes off duty. Most apps only need one location: get the current position, show nearby results, and stop listening.

Coordinates and simple distance maths: A location is a latitude and longitude in degrees. One degree of latitude is about 111 kilometres everywhere, so moving 0.001 degrees north is roughly 111 metres. A degree of longitude shrinks as you move away from the equator; at Dhaka's latitude, around 23.8 degrees north, it is about 111 × cos(23.8°), roughly 102 kilometres. For real distances between two points, apps use the haversine formula or a library function, which accounts for the Earth's curvature. Converting coordinates to an address is called reverse geocoding, and the opposite is geocoding.

Geofencing: A geofence is a virtual circle around a place, defined by a centre and radius. The system can notify the app when the user enters or leaves it, even in the background, using low-power methods rather than constant GPS. A coaching centre app could mark attendance when a student enters the campus circle, or a shop app could remind a customer about their saved cart near the branch. Geofencing needs background location permission, which, as lesson 19 explained, must be strongly justified.

Maps: Showing a map usually means using a map SDK, such as Google Maps for Android and iOS, Apple's MapKit, or open alternatives based on OpenStreetMap data. In Flutter, plugins exist for these. Commercial map services usually require an API key and may charge after a free quota, so restrict your key to your app's package and signing certificate so others cannot misuse it. Map tiles use data, so caching and avoiding needless reloads matter for users on limited data.

The camera, two approaches: The simplest way to take a photo is to launch the system camera or gallery through an image picker, which returns the chosen file. This needs little code and often fewer permissions, because the system app does the capturing. For a custom experience, such as a live preview with an overlay frame for scanning documents, you embed a camera preview using a camera library: CameraX on Android, AVFoundation on iOS, and the camera plugin in Flutter. Custom capture needs the camera permission and more care with lifecycle, because the camera must be released when the app is paused.

Handling photos responsibly: Phone photos are large, often several megabytes. Before uploading, resize to the size the server actually needs and compress, for example to about 1280 pixels on the long side with moderate JPEG quality; this can shrink a 4 MB photo to a few hundred kilobytes. Respect the orientation information stored in the image, or photos appear sideways. Photos may also contain metadata, including GPS coordinates of where they were taken; strip it before sharing images publicly to protect users' privacy.

Scanning QR codes and barcodes: QR payments are common in Bangladesh. Scanning works by analysing camera frames to find and decode the code. On-device libraries, such as Google's ML Kit barcode scanning on Android, Apple's Vision framework on iOS, and Flutter plugins built on them, decode codes quickly without sending images anywhere. Good scanners show a clear target frame, work in poor light with a torch button, and offer manual entry when the code is damaged.

Real-life example 1, a delivery rider app: While a rider is on an active delivery, the app requests high-accuracy location with a distance filter, shows the route on a map, and sends position updates to the server every few seconds so the customer can see the rider approaching. When the rider marks the order delivered, location updates stop. The app uses a foreground service with a visible notification during the delivery, as lesson 21 explains, and the rider sees exactly when they are being tracked.

Real-life example 2, a farmer's crop doctor app: A farmer in Rangpur photographs a diseased rice leaf. The app opens the camera with an overlay frame, resizes the photo on the device, removes GPS metadata, and attaches only the district the farmer selected. If offline, the photo is queued for upload. The light sensor is not needed; the camera's own exposure handles it. The app works on budget phones because it captures with the system camera and compresses before upload.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Assuming every phone has every sensor; sampling sensors too fast; not unregistering listeners; requesting high-accuracy GPS continuously when one coarse fix is enough; ignoring the accuracy radius; uploading full-size photos; leaking location through photo metadata; and leaving the camera open when the app is paused. Exams ask: classify mobile sensors; explain what an accelerometer measures and what a flat phone reads; compare GPS, Wi-Fi and cell location; explain a low-pass filter; describe how to use location in a battery-friendly way; and compare the image picker with a custom camera.

Recap: Phones have motion, position and environmental sensors, some hardware and some fused in software. The accelerometer reads about 9.8 m/s² from gravity when still, which reveals orientation, and spikes reveal shakes; filters smooth noisy data. Read sensors as streams at the slowest useful rate and stop when not visible. Location fuses satellites, Wi-Fi and cell towers; choose accuracy and update intervals to match the feature, use distance filters, and remember one degree of latitude is about 111 km. Geofences watch regions efficiently. Use image pickers for simple photos, camera libraries for custom capture, compress and strip metadata before upload, and decode QR codes on the device.
key_points: Sensors are motion (accelerometer, gyroscope), position (magnetometer, proximity) or environmental (light, pressure); not every phone has all.
A still phone's accelerometer reads about 9.8 m/s² due to gravity; flat on a table, z ≈ 9.8 and x, y ≈ 0.
Raw readings are noisy; a low-pass filter (smoothed = 0.8 × previous + 0.2 × new) smooths them.
Use the slowest sampling rate that works and unregister sensors when the screen is not visible to save battery.
Location fuses GPS (accurate outdoors, costly), Wi-Fi and cell towers (cheaper, coarser); always respect the accuracy radius.
Choose accuracy, time and distance filters per feature; one degree of latitude is about 111 km.
Use the image picker for simple photos and a camera library for custom capture; compress, fix orientation and strip GPS metadata before upload.
lessons.tip: Install a free sensor viewer app on your phone and watch the accelerometer while you lay the phone flat, stand it up and shake it. Ten minutes of watching real numbers makes the theory stick.
lessons.task: With a sensor viewer app, record accelerometer x, y, z for three positions: flat on a table, upright in portrait, and on its side in landscape. Compute the magnitude for each and check it is close to 9.8. Then calculate roughly how many metres 0.0005 degrees of latitude is.

quiz.q: A phone lies flat on a table, screen up. Roughly what does the accelerometer read?
quiz.explain: Flat on a table, gravity acts along the z axis (out of the screen), so z is about 9.8 m/s².

quiz.q: Which location source is usually most accurate outdoors but uses the most power and works poorly indoors?
quiz.explain: GPS can reach a few metres outdoors but needs open sky and significant power.

quiz.q: What does a low-pass filter do to sensor data?
options: Smooths out quick random noise by blending with previous values
quiz.explain: Blending each new value with the previous smoothed value reduces jitter; a high-pass filter does the opposite.

quiz.q: An app only needs to show the user's city for a weather card. What is the best location request?
options: Precise location with a 1-metre distance filter
quiz.explain: Match accuracy and frequency to the feature: a city needs one coarse, cheap fix.

quiz.q: Why should you strip metadata from photos before sharing them publicly?
options: Metadata can include the GPS location where the photo was taken
Metadata contains the app's API key
quiz.explain: Photo metadata may reveal precise location, which is a privacy risk.

lessons.title: Notifications and Background Work
lessons.content:
Think of the guard at the gate of a Dhaka apartment building. He does not run up to every flat each time something happens. When a parcel arrives, he calls the intercom of exactly one flat. When the lift is under repair, he puts one notice on the board. At night, he sleeps lightly and wakes only for real visitors. A phone works the same way. Apps cannot run freely all the time, because battery and memory are limited, so the system acts like that guard: it delivers messages to apps through a shared channel, wakes them only when needed, and keeps the noise down. This lesson covers notifications, which tell users that something happened, and background work, which lets apps do tasks when the user is not looking.

What a notification is: A notification is a message shown outside the app's UI: in the status bar, the notification shade, on the lock screen, and sometimes as a pop-up banner. It usually has an icon, a title, text, and a tap action that opens a specific screen. It may include action buttons, such as Reply or Mark as paid, a large image, or a progress bar. Notifications are powerful because they reach the user when the app is closed, and dangerous for the same reason: too many, and the user mutes or uninstalls the app.

Local versus push notifications: There are two sources. A local notification is created by the app itself on the phone, for example a medicine reminder at 8 PM or a timer finishing; it needs no server. A push notification is sent from a server through the internet, for example "Your parcel is out for delivery" or a new chat message. The phone receives it even if the app is not running, then shows it or wakes the app. Choosing correctly matters: a daily prayer-time reminder can be local and works offline; a payment confirmation must come from the server.

How push works, the big picture: Apps do not keep their own permanent connection to their server; that would drain the battery with dozens of apps each holding a connection. Instead, each platform has one shared push service with one efficient connection from the phone. On Android this is Firebase Cloud Messaging, FCM; on iOS it is the Apple Push Notification service, APNs. FCM can also deliver to iOS by passing messages through APNs, which is why many cross-platform apps use it.

The push flow step by step: One: when the app starts, it asks the push service for a device token, a long string identifying this app on this phone. Two: the app sends the token to its own backend, along with the user ID. Three: when something happens, such as an order shipping, the backend sends a request to FCM or APNs saying: send this message to this token. Four: the push service delivers it over its shared connection. Five: the phone shows the notification or passes the data to the app. Tokens can change, for example after reinstalling or restoring the phone, so the app must send the new token to the server whenever it changes.

Notification messages and data messages: FCM supports two kinds of payload. A notification message contains a title and body that the system displays automatically when the app is in the background. A data message contains key-value data that the app's code handles, for example to update a local database and then decide whether to show a notification. Data messages give more control but depend on the app being allowed to run its handler. Never put secrets or sensitive data, such as full account balances or OTP codes for other services, in push payloads; send a hint and let the app fetch details securely.

Notification permission: Showing notifications now needs user permission on both platforms. iOS has always asked; newer Android versions also require the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission. As lesson 19 explained, ask in context: after the user places an order, ask "Do you want delivery updates?", not on the first launch. If denied, the app must still work, perhaps with an in-app updates screen.

Android notification channels: Since Android 8.0, every notification belongs to a channel, such as Order updates, Chat messages, or Offers. The app defines channels with a name and importance level, and users can turn each channel off or change its sound separately in settings. This is a gift to well-behaved apps: a user annoyed by offers can silence that channel while keeping order updates. Design channels by type of message, and never put marketing messages into an important channel.

Notification etiquette: Send notifications that are timely, personal and actionable. "Your mobile wallet payment of 500 taka to Rahim Store was successful" is useful. "We miss you! Open the app" is spam. Group related notifications, such as five messages from one chat, into one. Respect quiet hours: a sale announcement at 2 AM is rude. Each notification should open exactly the screen it talks about, which is deep linking from lesson 10. Measure opt-out rates; if users keep turning notifications off, you are sending too many.

Why background work is restricted: In early smartphones, apps could run in the background freely, and many did, polling servers and holding the CPU awake, and phones died by afternoon. Over the years both platforms tightened the rules sharply. Android added Doze, which, when the phone is idle and unplugged for a while, defers apps' network access and jobs into occasional maintenance windows; App Standby buckets, which limit apps the user rarely opens; and limits on starting background services. iOS has always been stricter: an app moved to the background is usually suspended within seconds.

The main tools on Android: For deferrable work that must eventually happen, even if the app is closed or the phone restarts, use WorkManager. You describe a work request, add constraints such as network connected or device charging, and the system runs it at a good time, retrying with backoff on failure. It can be one-time, such as upload this survey, or periodic, with a minimum interval of 15 minutes, such as sync every few hours. For work the user is actively aware of and that must continue now, such as navigation, music playback or an ongoing delivery tracking, use a foreground service, which must show a persistent notification so the user knows something is running.

WorkManager in practice: In Kotlin you write a Worker class whose doWork function performs the task and returns success, retry or failure. You then enqueue it: a OneTimeWorkRequest with a Constraints object requiring a connected network. To avoid duplicates, use unique work names: enqueueUniqueWork("sync-surveys", KEEP, request) means if a sync is already queued, do not add another. In Flutter, plugins such as workmanager wrap this on Android and use iOS background mechanisms where possible.

Background work on iOS: iOS gives apps a few controlled options rather than free running. Background modes, declared in the project, allow specific long-running activities, such as audio playback, navigation-style location updates and VoIP calls. The BackgroundTasks framework lets an app request short refresh tasks and longer processing tasks, which the system schedules when it decides, often when the phone is charging and on Wi-Fi. A background URL session can complete large downloads or uploads even after the app is suspended. Silent push notifications can wake the app briefly to fetch data, but the system limits how often. You cannot count on exact timing.

Exact timing and alarms: Sometimes timing matters, such as a medicine reminder at exactly 8 PM. For user-visible reminders, schedule a local notification for that time; the system delivers it without your code running. Android has exact alarms for alarm clock and calendar style apps, but recent versions restrict them with special permissions, and you should not use them to run general background code. For most apps, approximate timing within a window is fine and kinder to battery.

Manufacturer battery savers: In Bangladesh many people use phones from brands that add their own aggressive battery management on top of Android. These may kill background apps, block WorkManager jobs or delay notifications beyond what standard Android does. Developers often see complaints like "notifications only arrive when I open the app". There is no perfect fix: use high-priority push only for truly urgent messages, rely on WorkManager rather than custom services, test on popular local phone models, and, when necessary, show users a short guide to exclude your app from battery optimisation.

Battery-friendly habits: Batch network work instead of making many small requests. Prefer push over polling: polling every minute wakes the radio again and again, while one push says exactly when there is something new. Use constraints, such as unmetered network for big uploads, so users on mobile data are not charged. Stop location, sensors and wake locks as soon as they are not needed. Android Studio's profilers and Battery Historian style tools can show what your app keeps awake.

Real-life example 1, an e-commerce app's order updates: The app requests notification permission after the first order. It registers its FCM token with the server. When the seller ships, the backend sends a push through FCM to the user's tokens on the Order updates channel: "Your order #4521 has been shipped". Tapping it deep-links to the order screen, which fetches fresh details. Offers go to a separate, low-importance channel that users can mute. The app refreshes its token on change and removes it on logout so the next user of a shared phone does not get the previous user's messages.

Real-life example 2, an NGO's survey uploads: The field survey app from earlier lessons saves surveys offline. Each time a survey is marked ready, it enqueues a unique WorkManager job with a network-connected constraint. When the worker reaches signal, even if the app is closed, the job uploads pending surveys from the outbox and retries with backoff on failures. A daily local notification at 6 PM reminds workers if any surveys are still pending. No foreground service is needed, because uploads can wait until a good moment.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Asking for notification permission at first launch; sending too many or irrelevant notifications; putting sensitive data in push payloads; forgetting to update tokens on the server; polling servers instead of using push; trying to keep a background service running forever; using exact alarms for ordinary sync; ignoring manufacturer battery savers; and doing large uploads on mobile data without asking. Exams ask: difference between local and push notifications; explain the push flow with tokens; what notification channels are; why background execution is restricted; compare WorkManager and foreground services; and list battery-friendly practices.

Recap: Notifications reach users outside the app; local ones are scheduled on the phone, push ones come from a server through FCM or APNs using device tokens kept up to date on the backend. Ask for notification permission in context, use Android channels by message type, keep payloads free of secrets, and send only timely, useful messages that deep-link correctly. Background work is limited to protect battery: on Android use WorkManager with constraints for deferrable tasks and foreground services with a visible notification for ongoing user-visible work; on iOS use background modes, BackgroundTasks and background transfers. Prefer push to polling, batch work, and test on real local phones.
key_points: Local notifications are scheduled on the phone; push notifications come from a server via FCM (Android) or APNs (iOS).
Push flow: app gets a device token, sends it to the backend, backend asks FCM/APNs to deliver to that token; tokens must be refreshed on change.
Notification permission is required on iOS and newer Android; ask in context and keep the app useful if denied.
Android notification channels let users control each type of message; separate important updates from offers.
Background execution is restricted (Doze, App Standby, iOS suspension) to protect battery.
Use WorkManager with constraints for deferrable, guaranteed work, and a foreground service with a visible notification for ongoing user-aware work.
Prefer push over polling, batch network work, avoid secrets in payloads, and test on popular local phones with aggressive battery savers.
lessons.tip: Look at your phone's notification settings for a few apps you use. Notice which ones use separate channels and which lump everything together. Copy the good ones when you design your own app's notifications.
lessons.task: For a coaching centre app, list five notifications it might send. For each, decide: local or push, which channel, what the tap opens, and whether it is worth sending at all. Then describe one background task the app needs and whether WorkManager or a foreground service fits.

quiz.q: Which notification is best implemented as a local notification?
options: A new chat message from a friend
A daily medicine reminder at 8 PM set by the user
quiz.explain: A user-set reminder can be scheduled on the phone without any server; the others depend on server events.

quiz.q: What is a device token in push notifications?
options: An identifier for this app on this device that the backend uses to target pushes
quiz.explain: The app gets the token from FCM or APNs and sends it to its backend, which uses it to address messages.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of Android notification channels?
options: To let users control each type of notification separately, such as muting offers but keeping order updates
quiz.explain: Channels group notifications by type, and users can change or disable each channel in settings.

quiz.q: An app must upload a survey eventually, even if the app is closed, but only when the network is connected. What should it use on Android?
options: A foreground service that runs forever
A thread started from the Activity
quiz.explain: WorkManager handles deferrable, guaranteed work with constraints and retries, surviving app closure and restarts.

quiz.q: Why is push generally better than polling the server every minute?
options: Polling is not allowed by HTTP
Push avoids waking the radio repeatedly; the server notifies only when something new exists, saving battery and data
quiz.explain: Frequent polling keeps waking the network; one shared push connection delivers updates only when needed.

lessons.title: Mobile App Security
lessons.content:
Imagine a shop owner in a busy market who keeps the day's cash in a drawer under the counter. The drawer is convenient, but anyone who reaches over can grab it. A sensible owner keeps only small change in the drawer, puts the rest in a locked safe, sends large amounts to the bank with a trusted person, and never writes the safe's combination on a sticker. Mobile security works the same way: the phone is a convenient but exposed place. Anything shipped inside the app can be inspected, the network can be watched, and the phone itself can be lost, stolen or rooted. Good mobile security means deciding what to keep where, and protecting each layer.

Thinking like an attacker, the threat model: Before choosing defences, list who might attack and how. A thief who steals an unlocked phone. Malware on the same phone trying to read your app's data. A person on public Wi-Fi at a café or a university watching network traffic. Someone who downloads your app's package and takes it apart to find secrets or bypass checks. A fraudster who calls your API directly with a script, pretending to be your app. Each threat needs different defences. This exercise, called threat modelling, keeps you from spending effort on unlikely risks while ignoring obvious ones.

Rule one, the client cannot be trusted: Everything inside an app, the code, strings, images and configuration, is delivered to the user's phone and can be extracted. Android packages can be decompiled into readable code with free tools, and iOS apps can be analysed too, especially on jailbroken devices. Even Flutter's compiled code can be examined with effort. So never rely on the app for security decisions that matter. Price checks, discount rules, permission checks and balance limits must be enforced on the server; the app's checks are only for a good user experience.

Rule two, no secrets in the app: A secret key placed in the app, such as a payment gateway's secret key, an admin password, or a cloud storage master key, is not secret; anyone can extract it. Real examples of leaked keys from apps leading to stolen data are common. Keep secret keys on your server. If the app needs to call a third-party service that requires a secret, route the call through your backend, which adds the key. Keys that are designed to be public, such as a maps key restricted to your app's package and signing certificate, are acceptable, but restrict them as tightly as the service allows.

Protecting data at rest: Data stored on the phone lives inside the app's sandbox, which other apps cannot normally read. Modern phones with a screen lock also encrypt storage. That is a good base, but a rooted phone, a backup or a debugging connection can expose files. So store only what you need, never store passwords, and put the most sensitive small items, such as tokens and encryption keys, in the platform's secure storage. Lesson 16 already warned that SharedPreferences and UserDefaults are plain files, not vaults.

The Keystore and the Keychain: Android Keystore lets an app create cryptographic keys that are stored in a protected area, on many devices backed by secure hardware, and that cannot be exported; the app asks the Keystore to encrypt or decrypt, and the key itself never leaves. The iOS Keychain stores small secrets, such as passwords and tokens, encrypted by the system, with options controlling whether they are available only when the device is unlocked. In Flutter, the flutter_secure_storage plugin uses the Keychain on iOS and Keystore-based encryption on Android. Use it for access tokens and refresh tokens.

Protecting data in transit: Every network call must use HTTPS, which uses TLS to encrypt traffic and verify the server's identity with a certificate. Without it, anyone on the same Wi-Fi can read or change the data. Both platforms now block plain HTTP by default: Android through its network security configuration and iOS through App Transport Security. Do not switch these protections off to fix a development problem; fix the server's certificate instead. Web Engineering covers how TLS and certificates work in depth.

Certificate pinning, the idea: Normally the phone trusts any certificate signed by any of many trusted certificate authorities. Pinning makes your app accept only a specific certificate or public key for your server, so even a fake certificate from a compromised or user-installed authority is rejected. Banking and wallet apps often use it. But pinning has a real cost: if the server's certificate changes and the app has not been updated with the new pin, the app stops working for everyone. If you pin, include a backup pin and plan certificate rotation carefully.

Authentication on mobile: Most apps log users in once and then stay logged in. The common pattern uses tokens: after login, the server returns a short-lived access token, for example valid for 15 minutes, and a longer-lived refresh token. The app sends the access token with each request in an Authorization header. When it expires, the app uses the refresh token to get a new one, without asking the user to log in again. Store both tokens in secure storage, never in plain preferences or logs. On logout, delete them locally and ask the server to revoke the refresh token.

OTP, biometrics and login with other accounts: Bangladeshi apps often log in with a phone number and an SMS one-time password. Android offers ways to read the OTP automatically without the broad SMS permission, such as the SMS Retriever and SMS User Consent APIs, which keep the app from needing access to all messages. Biometric login with fingerprint or face, through BiometricPrompt on Android and Local Authentication on iOS, is convenient for unlocking the app or confirming a payment; the biometric data itself never reaches your app, only a yes or no from the system, often tied to a Keystore or Keychain key. Social logins should use the official SDKs and verify tokens on the server.

Protecting the API from fake clients: Because attackers can call your API without your app, the server must treat every request as potentially hostile: validate all input, check that the user is allowed to do the action on that specific record, rate-limit login and OTP attempts, and log suspicious behaviour. Platform services can help the server judge whether a request comes from a genuine copy of your app on a real device: Google's Play Integrity API and Apple's App Attest. These raise the bar for fraud but are not perfect; never let them replace proper server checks.

Obfuscation and code hardening: Release builds should shrink and obfuscate code. On Android, R8 renames classes and methods to short meaningless names and removes unused code, which also makes the app smaller. Flutter release builds compile Dart to native machine code, and the flutter build command supports an obfuscate option with a split debug info directory, so you keep symbols to decode crash reports. Obfuscation slows attackers down; it does not stop a determined one, so it is a layer, not a wall.

Rooted and jailbroken devices: Rooting an Android phone or jailbreaking an iPhone removes the system's normal restrictions, which also weakens the sandbox. Some high-risk apps, such as banking apps, detect rooted devices and limit features or warn the user. Detection can be bypassed by skilled attackers, so treat it as one signal among many. For most apps, a warning is enough; blocking millions of legitimate users with modified phones has a cost too.

Leaks developers create themselves: Many real leaks are accidental. Logging tokens or personal data, then shipping those logs in release builds. Showing sensitive data in the app switcher's screenshot; banking apps often hide content when the app goes to the background, and on Android a secure window flag can also block screenshots on sensitive screens. Copying OTPs or account numbers to the clipboard, where other apps may read them. Exporting Android components that should be private, letting other apps open internal screens. Accepting data from deep links without validation. Each is easy to avoid once you know to look.

OWASP Mobile Top 10: The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, OWASP, publishes a list of the most common mobile security risks, updated over the years. It includes issues such as improper credential usage, insecure authentication and authorisation, insufficient input and output validation, insecure communication, inadequate privacy controls, insecure data storage, insufficient cryptography and supply chain risks from third-party libraries. It is a good checklist for reviews and a frequent exam topic. OWASP also maintains a detailed mobile testing guide for security testers.

The supply chain: Your app includes many packages from pub.dev, Maven or other sources. A malicious or vulnerable package becomes part of your app. Choose well-maintained, widely used packages, keep them updated, review what permissions and data a new package uses, and pin versions in lock files so builds are reproducible. Lesson 19 already noted that SDKs are your responsibility for privacy; the same is true for security.

Real-life example 1, a mobile wallet: The wallet app logs in with phone number, OTP and a PIN. Tokens live in secure storage. All traffic uses HTTPS with certificate pinning and a backup pin. The app hides balances in the app switcher, blocks screenshots on payment screens, and asks for the PIN or biometrics before every transfer. The server, not the app, checks balance, limits and fraud rules, and uses integrity signals as an extra input. If the device is rooted, the app warns and limits high-value transfers.

Real-life example 2, a student project done right: A university team builds a hall-management app with Firebase. Their first version had an admin password inside the app and database rules that let any logged-in user edit any record. A senior reviewed it, removed the password, moved admin actions to server-side functions, and wrote database security rules so students can only edit their own records. The team learned that the real security lived on the server side, not in hiding buttons in the app.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Hard-coding secret keys; trusting client-side checks; storing tokens in plain preferences; allowing plain HTTP; disabling certificate checks during development and forgetting to re-enable them; logging sensitive data; exporting components accidentally; pinning without a backup plan; and ignoring third-party libraries. Exams ask: why the client cannot be trusted; how to store sensitive data on Android and iOS; explain HTTPS and certificate pinning; describe token-based authentication with refresh tokens; list OWASP Mobile Top 10 categories; and discuss root detection and obfuscation.

Recap: Think in threat models: thieves, malware, network watchers, reverse engineers and fake clients. Assume everything in the app can be read, so keep secrets and real decisions on the server. Store little on the phone, and keep tokens and keys in the Keystore or Keychain, via secure storage. Use HTTPS everywhere, consider pinning carefully, and use short access tokens with refresh tokens. Harden the API with validation, authorisation and rate limits, add integrity checks as extra signals, obfuscate release builds, avoid self-made leaks, use OWASP as a checklist, and treat dependencies as part of your attack surface.
key_points: Threat modelling lists who might attack (thieves, malware, network watchers, reverse engineers, fake clients) and how.
The client cannot be trusted: app code can be decompiled, so real checks belong on the server.
Never ship secret keys in the app; route secret-key calls through your backend and restrict public keys.
Store tokens and keys in Android Keystore or iOS Keychain (e.g. flutter_secure_storage), not plain preferences.
Use HTTPS everywhere; certificate pinning adds protection but needs backup pins and rotation planning.
Token auth: short-lived access token plus refresh token, stored securely and revoked on logout.
Add layers: server validation and rate limits, integrity APIs, obfuscation, root detection, avoiding log and clipboard leaks, and OWASP Mobile Top 10 reviews.
lessons.tip: Download a release APK of a small app you built, rename it to .zip and look inside, or open it with a free APK analysis tool. Seeing your own strings and resources in plain view will convince you never to hide secrets in an app.
lessons.task: Write a one-page threat model for a hostel fee payment app: list four attackers, what each wants, and one defence for each. Then list exactly which data the app stores on the phone, where (secure storage, database, preferences), and why.

quiz.q: Why should a payment gateway's secret key never be placed inside the mobile app?
options: Anyone can extract it from the app package, so it is not secret
It makes the app too large
Keys only work on servers running Linux
quiz.explain: App contents can be decompiled; secret keys must stay on the server.

quiz.q: Where should an app store its refresh token?
options: In secure storage backed by Android Keystore or iOS Keychain
In a public file in Downloads
quiz.explain: Secure storage encrypts small secrets with system-protected keys.

quiz.q: What is a risk of certificate pinning?
options: If the server's certificate changes without a matching pin in the app, the app can stop connecting
quiz.explain: Pinning rejects unexpected certificates, so rotation must be planned with backup pins.

quiz.q: An app hides the Delete button for non-admin users. Is that enough security?
options: Yes, users cannot see the button
Yes, if the code is obfuscated
No, the server must also check that the user is allowed to delete, because attackers can call the API directly
No, the button must also be red
quiz.explain: Client-side checks are for UX; authorisation must be enforced on the server.

quiz.q: What does R8 or Flutter's obfuscate option mainly do for security?
options: Makes reverse engineering harder by renaming code symbols, without making it impossible
quiz.explain: Obfuscation slows attackers down but is only one layer, not a complete defence.

lessons.title: Testing, Debugging and Profiling
lessons.content:
A garment factory in Gazipur does not wait until a full shipment reaches Europe to check the stitching. Workers check each piece at the machine, supervisors check finished batches on the floor, and a quality team checks random cartons before they leave. Problems found early are cheap; a rejected container is a disaster. Mobile apps are the same. A bug caught by a test on your laptop costs a minute. The same bug found by thousands of users after release costs ratings, money and an urgent update that takes time to reach everyone. This lesson covers how to test mobile apps, how to debug them when something goes wrong, and how to profile them so they run smoothly on real phones.

Why mobile testing is harder: Mobile apps run on thousands of device models, screen sizes, OS versions and manufacturer customisations. They face slow and broken networks, permissions that may be denied, low memory, interruptions from calls, and process death. And unlike a website, a buggy release cannot be fixed instantly for everyone; users must download the update, and some never do. So mobile teams invest in automated tests, careful release processes and monitoring after release.

The test pyramid: A healthy test suite looks like a pyramid. At the base are many unit tests: fast, small tests of single functions and classes, such as a price calculator or a ViewModel. In the middle are fewer widget or component tests, which check one screen or widget in isolation. At the top are a small number of integration or end-to-end tests that run the real app on a device or emulator and walk through a full flow like login and checkout. Lower layers run in seconds and pinpoint failures; higher layers are slow and fragile but prove the whole system works together.

Unit tests in Flutter: A Dart unit test uses the test package. Example: test('discount is capped at 200 taka', () { final cart = Cart(items: [Item(price: 3000)]); expect(cart.discount(percent: 10), 200); });. Good unit tests follow arrange, act, assert: set up the data, call the code, check the result. Test edge cases: empty cart, zero price, maximum discount, Bangla digits in input. Because the architecture from lesson 12 keeps logic out of widgets, ViewModels and repositories can be unit-tested with fake dependencies instead of a real server or database.

Fakes and mocks: A unit test should not call the real network. Instead you pass a fake repository that returns fixed data, or use a mocking library such as mockito or mocktail to create objects whose responses you define and whose calls you can verify. Example: when the fake repository throws a network error, does the ViewModel show the error state with a retry button? Testing failure paths this way is easy in unit tests and almost impossible to do reliably by hand.

Widget tests in Flutter: Flutter's widget tests run a widget in a test environment without a real device, quickly. testWidgets('shows error and retry', (tester) async { await tester.pumpWidget(MaterialApp(home: OrdersScreen(viewModel: failingViewModel))); await tester.pump(); expect(find.text('Retry'), findsOneWidget); await tester.tap(find.text('Retry')); await tester.pump(); verify(...); });. pumpWidget builds the UI, pump advances frames, find locates widgets, and tap simulates touches. Widget tests are a Flutter strength: they give near-UI confidence at close to unit-test speed.

Integration tests: Flutter's integration_test package runs the full app on an emulator or real device and drives it like a user: launch, enter phone number, enter OTP from a test backend, place an order, check the confirmation screen. Native Android uses Espresso for UI tests and JUnit for unit tests; iOS uses XCTest and XCUITest. Integration tests catch problems that only appear when real parts meet, such as navigation, plugins and platform permissions, but they are slower and more fragile, so keep only the most important flows here.

Golden tests and other checks: Flutter supports golden tests, which render a widget to an image and compare it with a stored reference image to catch unintended visual changes. Static analysis, through flutter analyze and lint rules, catches many mistakes without running anything, such as unused variables or missing awaits. Together with tests, these run automatically in continuous integration, CI, on every pull request, so problems are caught before code is merged.

Writing tests that last: Good tests are readable and stable. Give each test a name that states the behaviour, such as 'shows Retry when orders fail to load', so a failure explains itself. Test one behaviour per test. Avoid depending on the current time, random values or the order tests run in; inject a fake clock instead. When you fix a bug, first write a test that fails because of the bug, then fix the code until it passes. That test stays in the suite and makes sure the same bug never returns silently in a later release.

Testing on real devices: Emulators are fast and convenient but differ from real phones in performance, sensors, cameras and manufacturer quirks. Test on a few real devices, including at least one low-end Android phone of the kind many users in Bangladesh carry, with limited RAM and storage. Cloud device farms, such as Firebase Test Lab, let you run tests on many physical and virtual devices without buying them. Also test on slow networks: Android emulators and developer tools can simulate poor connections, and you can test airplane mode by hand.

Debugging basics: When something goes wrong, first reproduce it reliably, then narrow it down. Read the logs: Android's Logcat in Android Studio shows system and app logs, including crash stack traces; Xcode's console does the same for iOS; flutter run prints Dart logs and errors. A stack trace reads from the error at the top down through the calls that led to it; find the first line from your own code. Use debugPrint or a logging package, and remove noisy or sensitive logs from release builds, as lesson 22 warned.

Breakpoints and stepping: A debugger pauses the app at a line you choose, a breakpoint, and lets you inspect variables, step over or into functions, and continue. Android Studio and VS Code support breakpoints for Flutter and Kotlin, and Xcode for Swift. Conditional breakpoints pause only when an expression is true, such as when orderId equals 4521. Debugging this way is far faster than adding print statements and rebuilding, especially for bugs that depend on state.

Flutter DevTools: DevTools is a suite of debugging and profiling tools for Flutter. The widget inspector shows the widget tree and lets you select a widget on screen to see its properties and layout, which helps fix overflow and alignment problems. The performance view shows frame timings, separating UI thread and raster thread work, so you can see which frames missed their deadline. The CPU profiler shows which functions take time. The memory view tracks objects over time. The network view shows HTTP requests from the app.

Profiling performance: Remember from lesson 13 that a 60 Hz screen gives about 16 ms per frame. Profile in profile mode, never debug mode, because debug builds are much slower and can mislead you. Look for frames that take too long and find the cause: building huge widget trees, heavy work on the main isolate, decoding large images, or rebuilding too much on every change. Android Studio's profilers do the same for native code, showing CPU, memory, network and energy. Measure first, then optimise the actual bottleneck, not what you guess is slow.

Memory leaks: A memory leak happens when objects are no longer needed but are still referenced, so they cannot be freed. Common mobile leaks are listeners, stream subscriptions, controllers, timers and sensor callbacks that are not disposed when a screen closes, or a long-lived object holding a reference to a screen. Each time the user opens and closes the screen, memory grows, until the app slows or is killed. Dispose what you create, a habit from lessons 7 and 14. On Android, tools such as LeakCanary detect leaked activities automatically in debug builds.

App startup and size: Users judge an app in its first seconds. Measure cold start time, from tap to first useful frame. Avoid heavy work before the first frame: load only what the first screen needs, initialise other SDKs later, and show cached content quickly. App size matters in Bangladesh, where many users have limited storage and data: remove unused packages and assets, compress images, and use app bundles so stores deliver only the code and resources each device needs. Flutter can produce a size analysis to show what makes the app large.

After release, crash reporting and monitoring: Some bugs appear only in the wild. Crash reporting services, such as Firebase Crashlytics or Sentry, collect crash stack traces, device models and OS versions from users' phones and group them so you can fix the most common first. Upload obfuscation mapping or symbol files so traces are readable. Track the crash-free users rate, and watch the Android vitals in Play Console, which reports crash rate and ANR rate, application not responding, the dialog shown when the main thread is blocked for too long.

Real-life example 1, fixing a mystery crash: Crashlytics shows a crash on an order screen, mostly on one manufacturer's budget phones. The stack trace points to a null value in an order's delivery date. The developer writes a failing unit test with a null date, reproducing it in seconds, fixes the parsing to handle missing dates, and confirms the test passes. A widget test checks that the screen shows 'Date pending'. The fix ships in a staged rollout, and the crash-free rate returns to normal.

Real-life example 2, a janky list: A news app's feed stutters on low-end phones. In profile mode, DevTools shows frames over 30 ms whenever new items appear. The CPU profiler reveals that each item decodes a full-size image on the main isolate. The team switches to cached, resized thumbnails with cacheWidth, moves date formatting out of build, and uses ListView.builder correctly. Frames drop under 16 ms and scrolling feels smooth even on a two-year-old budget phone.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Testing only by hand; writing only slow end-to-end tests; tests that call the real network; testing only the happy path; profiling in debug mode; never testing on low-end devices; not disposing listeners; ignoring crash reports; and shipping without symbol files so traces are unreadable. Exams ask: explain the test pyramid; difference between unit, widget and integration tests; what mocks are; how to read a stack trace; tools for profiling and what jank is; what memory leaks are and how to avoid them; and how crash reporting helps.

Recap: Mobile testing is harder because of device variety, networks and slow updates, so automate. Build a pyramid: many fast unit tests with fakes and mocks, a good number of widget tests, and a few integration tests for key flows, plus static analysis and CI. Test on real and low-end devices and slow networks. Debug by reproducing, reading logs and stack traces, and using breakpoints. Profile in profile mode with DevTools and Android Studio, fix measured bottlenecks, dispose resources to avoid leaks, watch startup time and app size, and monitor crashes and ANRs after release.
key_points: Mobile testing is harder due to device variety, networks and slow update adoption; automated tests catch bugs early and cheaply.
Test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer widget/component tests, a few slow integration (end-to-end) tests.
Use fakes and mocks so unit tests never hit the real network, and test failure paths, not just the happy path.
