Flutter widget tests (pumpWidget, pump, find, tap) give near-UI confidence quickly; integration_test, Espresso and XCUITest drive the real app.
Debug with logs (Logcat, Xcode console), stack traces and breakpoints; reproduce reliably first.
Profile in profile mode with DevTools or Android Studio; look for frames over about 16 ms and fix the measured bottleneck.
Dispose resources to avoid memory leaks, watch startup time and app size, and monitor crashes, crash-free rate and ANRs after release.
lessons.tip: Pick the most important function in your current project, such as a fee calculation, and write five unit tests for it, including at least two edge cases. Run them on every change. You will find a bug sooner than you expect.
lessons.task: For a simple login screen with phone number and OTP, write down: three unit tests for the validation logic, two widget tests for the screen (what you pump, find and tap), and one integration test flow. Then list two things you would check in DevTools if the screen felt slow.

quiz.q: In the test pyramid, which kind of test should you have the most of?
options: Manual tests by the QA team
quiz.explain: Unit tests are fast and precise, so they form the wide base of the pyramid.

quiz.q: Why do unit tests use fakes or mocks instead of the real server?
options: Real servers are illegal in tests
Mocks replace the need for any other tests
To make tests fast, reliable and able to simulate errors like network failures
quiz.explain: Fakes give controlled responses, including failures that are hard to produce with real systems.

quiz.q: Why should you profile performance in profile mode rather than debug mode?
options: Debug builds are much slower and give misleading performance numbers
quiz.explain: Debug mode includes extra checks and no full optimisation, so timings do not match release behaviour.

quiz.q: Each time a user opens and closes a chat screen, the app's memory grows. What is the most likely cause?
options: A memory leak, such as a stream subscription or controller not disposed when the screen closes
The screen uses too many colours
The app has too many unit tests
The device has an old screen
quiz.explain: Undisposed listeners keep screens referenced, so memory cannot be freed.

quiz.q: What does ANR mean on Android?
options: Application Not Responding, shown when the main thread is blocked too long
quiz.explain: ANRs happen when the main thread cannot respond to input in time; Play Console tracks the ANR rate.

lessons.title: Accessibility and Localization
lessons.content:
Think of a public building in Dhaka with only stairs at the entrance. A wheelchair user cannot enter, an elderly person with bad knees struggles, and a parent with a pram gives up. Add a ramp, and everyone benefits, including the delivery person with a heavy trolley. Now think of a government notice printed only in English: a large part of the people it is meant for cannot read it. Accessibility and localization are the ramp and the Bangla translation of mobile apps. They decide whether your app works for everyone, or only for young, sharp-eyed, English-reading users with the latest phone. This lesson shows the practical techniques; the deeper design theory belongs to Human-Computer Interaction.

Who needs accessibility: Accessibility, often written a11y, means designing so that people with disabilities can use the app. That includes people who are blind or have low vision, colour blindness, hearing loss, motor difficulties such as tremors, and cognitive or learning differences. It also includes temporary and situational limits: a broken arm, bright sunlight on the screen, a noisy bus, holding a child in one arm. The World Health Organization estimates that a large share of the world's population lives with some form of disability, and everyone's eyesight and dexterity decline with age. Accessible apps simply work better for more people.

Screen readers: Blind and low-vision users often use a screen reader: TalkBack on Android and VoiceOver on iOS. The screen reader speaks what is under the user's finger, and users move between elements with swipes and activate them with a double tap. For this to work, every important element needs a meaningful label. A button that shows only a trash icon must be announced as "Delete note", not "Button" or nothing. Images that carry meaning need descriptions; decorative images should be hidden from the screen reader so they do not add noise.

Semantics in Flutter: Flutter builds an accessibility tree from widget semantics. Standard widgets such as ElevatedButton, TextField, Checkbox and Switch provide semantics automatically. Icons need labels: IconButton(icon: Icon(Icons.delete), tooltip: 'Delete note', onPressed: ...) gives the screen reader a label through the tooltip. Images can use the semanticLabel property. For custom widgets, wrap them in Semantics(label: 'Balance: 1,250 taka', child: ...). Use ExcludeSemantics for decorative parts and MergeSemantics to read a group, such as an icon and a text in a list tile, as one item. On Android native views the equivalent is contentDescription; on iOS, accessibilityLabel.

Touch target size: Small targets are hard for everyone and impossible for some. Material Design recommends touch targets of at least 48 by 48 dp, and Apple recommends at least 44 by 44 points. The visible icon can be smaller, as long as the tappable area is large enough; Flutter's IconButton already provides a large enough area by default. Leave space between targets so users do not tap the wrong one. A tiny close button in the corner of a pop-up is a classic failure.

Colour and contrast: Text must stand out from its background. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, WCAG, which are widely used for apps too, recommend a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. Light grey text on white fails this, and so does it in bright sunlight for everyone. Never use colour alone to carry meaning: a red border on a wrong field should also have an error message and maybe an icon, because colour-blind users may not see the red. Support dark mode properly, with contrast checked in both themes.

Text scaling: Many users, especially older ones, increase the system font size. Your app must respect it. Flutter applies the user's text scale automatically to Text widgets, unless you override it. Test with the largest font settings: does the text wrap instead of being cut off? Do buttons grow instead of overflowing? Avoid fixed heights on containers with text, prefer flexible layouts from lesson 9, and never disable text scaling to protect your design. If a layout breaks at large sizes, the layout must change, not the user's setting.

Other accessibility habits: Provide captions or transcripts for videos and audio. Do not rely on gestures alone, such as a swipe to delete, without a visible alternative. Avoid time limits, or allow users to extend them; an OTP screen that expires too fast punishes slow typists. Keep a logical focus order so screen reader and keyboard users move through the screen top to bottom. Announce important changes, such as "Payment successful", so screen reader users know something happened. Respect the system setting to reduce motion.

Testing accessibility: Turn on TalkBack or VoiceOver and try to complete your main task with your eyes closed; it is humbling and very effective. Use the Accessibility Scanner app on Android, which suggests fixes for small targets, low contrast and missing labels. Xcode's Accessibility Inspector does similar checks for iOS. Flutter provides guideline checks you can use in widget tests, such as meetsGuideline(androidTapTargetGuideline) and textContrastGuideline, so regressions are caught automatically.

Internationalization and localization: Internationalization, i18n, is engineering the app so it can support many languages and regions: no hard-coded strings, flexible layouts, locale-aware formatting. Localization, l10n, is the work of adapting it for a specific locale: translating text into Bangla, using Bangla date and number formats, and choosing suitable images and examples. Do i18n from the first day; retrofitting it into a large app full of hard-coded English strings is painful.

How string resources work: On Android, strings live in res/values/strings.xml, with translations in res/values-bn/strings.xml; the system picks the right file for the device language. iOS uses string catalogs or Localizable.strings files per language. In Flutter, the official approach uses ARB files, such as app_en.arb and app_bn.arb, containing keys and translations; code generation creates a class, so you write AppLocalizations.of(context)!.welcomeTitle instead of a literal string. Set supportedLocales to include English and Bangla, and add the localization delegates so built-in widgets, such as date pickers, are translated too.

Placeholders and plurals: Never build sentences by joining pieces, such as 'You have ' + count + ' new messages', because word order differs between languages. Use placeholders: 'You have {count} new messages' in English and the natural Bangla sentence with the same placeholder. Plurals also differ: English needs "1 message" and "2 messages", while Bangla usually does not change the noun the same way, and some languages have several plural forms. ARB files support ICU message syntax with plural rules, so each language can express it correctly.

Numbers, dates and currency: Formatting must follow the locale. The intl package in Dart formats numbers, dates and currency per locale. In the Bangla locale, digits can be displayed as Bangla numerals, such as ১২৩, and month and day names appear in Bangla. South Asian grouping writes large numbers as 1,00,000 for one lakh instead of 100,000; check what your formatter produces and what your users expect. Show taka with the ৳ symbol or the word টাকা consistently. When parsing user input, accept both Bangla and English digits, because users type both.

Bangla text rendering: Bangla script uses conjuncts, called juktakkhor, and vowel signs that attach to consonants, which require proper text shaping. Modern Android and iOS handle this well with system fonts, and Flutter uses the platform's text shaping too. Still, test on real devices, especially older or budget phones, choose a well-designed Bangla font if you bundle one, and allow extra line height, because Bangla letters have marks above and below the line. Bangla words can be longer than English ones, so leave room in buttons and tabs.

Right-to-left and layout direction: Languages like Arabic and Urdu are written right to left, and apps must mirror their layouts: back arrows point right, lists align right. Flutter handles this with Directionality and by using start and end instead of left and right, such as EdgeInsetsDirectional. Even if your app supports only English and Bangla today, using start and end costs nothing and keeps the door open for more languages later.

Good translation is more than word swapping: Machine translation is a useful first draft, but a native speaker must review every string in context. A literal Bangla translation of a technical English label can be stiff or confusing; users understand short, everyday words better. Keep a small glossary so the same idea, such as order, payment or delivery, is always translated the same way across screens. Give translators screenshots or notes for short strings, because a single English word like Save or Book can mean different things in different places.

Letting users choose: By default, apps follow the device language. But many Bangladeshi users keep their phone in English while preferring Bangla in a particular app, or the reverse. Offer an in-app language switch, store the choice locally, and apply it at startup. Newer Android versions also support per-app language settings in the system. Do not guess the language from location; a Bangladeshi user abroad or a foreigner in Dhaka would be annoyed.

Real-life example 1, a government service app: A citizen service app is used by people of all ages across the country. Every icon button has a Bangla label for TalkBack. Text scales up to the largest system size without cutting off, because forms use flexible layouts. Error messages appear as text, not just red borders. The OTP screen allows a generous time limit and a clear resend option. Before each release, the team tries the main flows with TalkBack and runs automated guideline checks in widget tests.

Real-life example 2, an e-commerce app in two languages: An online shop supports English and Bangla with ARB files. Prices are formatted by the intl package, product counts use plural-aware messages, and dates show Bangla month names in the Bangla locale. The search box accepts Bangla and English digits. A language switch in settings changes the app instantly. Product names come from the server in both languages, chosen by the app's current locale sent in a request header, so the server and the app stay consistent.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Icon buttons without labels; tiny touch targets; low-contrast grey text; using colour alone for meaning; disabling text scaling; hard-coded strings; building sentences by concatenation; formatting numbers and dates by hand; assuming left-to-right; and guessing language from location. Exams ask: define accessibility and list user groups; how screen readers work and how to label elements; minimum touch target size; contrast ratios; difference between i18n and l10n; how string resources and ARB files work; and handling of plurals, numbers and dates.

Recap: Accessibility makes apps usable by people with permanent, temporary and situational limits. Give every meaningful element a label for TalkBack and VoiceOver, keep touch targets at least 48 dp or 44 pt, ensure contrast, never rely on colour alone, respect text scaling, and test with screen readers and automated checks. Internationalize from day one with string resources or ARB files, placeholders and plural rules, format numbers, dates and currency by locale, test Bangla rendering, use start and end for direction, and let users choose their language. For design principles behind all of this, see Human-Computer Interaction.
key_points: Accessibility (a11y) serves people with permanent, temporary and situational limits; accessible apps work better for everyone.
Screen readers (TalkBack, VoiceOver) need meaningful labels: Semantics, tooltip and semanticLabel in Flutter, contentDescription and accessibilityLabel natively.
Touch targets should be at least 48×48 dp (Android) or 44×44 pt (iOS); text contrast at least 4.5:1, and never use colour alone.
Respect system text scaling with flexible layouts; test with the largest font size and with screen readers.
i18n prepares the app for many locales; l10n adapts it to one, such as Bangla.
Use string resources (strings.xml, values-bn) or Flutter ARB files with placeholders and plural rules, never concatenation.
Format numbers, dates and currency with locale-aware tools like intl, accept Bangla digits, test Bangla rendering, use start/end for direction, and offer an in-app language choice.
lessons.tip: Turn on TalkBack or VoiceOver for ten minutes and try to send a message or make a payment in an app you use daily. Then try your own app. You will immediately see which buttons have no labels.
lessons.task: Take one screen from your project and make an accessibility and localization checklist: list every icon button and its label, check touch target sizes, find any text with poor contrast, move all strings into an English and a Bangla resource file, and replace any concatenated sentence with a placeholder message.

quiz.q: A delete button shows only a trash icon. What should a screen reader announce?
options: A meaningful label such as Delete note
quiz.explain: Screen reader users need the purpose of the control, provided by a label or tooltip.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum touch target size on Android?
quiz.explain: Material guidance recommends at least 48 × 48 dp; Apple recommends at least 44 × 44 points.

quiz.q: What is the difference between internationalization and localization?
options: Internationalization prepares the app to support many locales; localization adapts it for a specific locale
Internationalization means publishing in many countries' stores
quiz.explain: i18n is the engineering groundwork; l10n is the per-locale translation and formatting.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid building messages like 'You have ' + count + ' new messages'?
options: Word order and plural rules differ between languages, so translators need whole messages with placeholders
Dart does not allow string concatenation
quiz.explain: Placeholder messages with plural rules let each language express the sentence naturally.

quiz.q: A user has set the largest system font size and your button text is cut off. What is the right fix?
options: Disable text scaling in the app
Tell the user to reduce the font size
Use a smaller font for that button
Change the layout to be flexible so the button grows and text wraps
quiz.explain: Respect the user's setting; layouts must adapt rather than block scaling.

lessons.title: Publishing, Monetization and Course Wrap-Up
lessons.content:
A home baker in Chattogram makes excellent cakes for family and friends. Turning that into a business takes more than baking: a proper kitchen that passes inspection, labels with ingredients and expiry dates, a page where customers can order, a price that covers costs, and a way to hear complaints and improve. Publishing an app is the same step from hobby to product. The code from the previous 24 lessons must be built for release, signed, described honestly in a store listing, reviewed, rolled out carefully, monitored and earned from. This final lesson walks through that path and then connects everything you have learned in this course.

Debug builds versus release builds: During development you run debug builds, with hot reload, extra checks and debugging information, which make them larger and slower. Users must receive a release build: compiled with full optimisation, without debugging tools, shrunk and obfuscated as lesson 22 described. In Flutter, flutter build appbundle produces an Android App Bundle, and flutter build ipa prepares an iOS archive. Always test the release build on real devices before uploading, because some bugs, such as code removed by shrinking or missing permissions, only appear there.

App signing on Android: Every Android app must be digitally signed. The signature proves that updates come from the same developer; Android refuses to install an update signed with a different key over an existing app. You create an upload key and keep it safe, outside version control. With Play App Signing, Google holds the final app signing key, and you sign uploads with your upload key; if you lose the upload key, it can be reset, which is far safer than losing the only signing key. Never commit keystore files or their passwords to a public repository.

Signing on iOS: Apple controls signing through the Apple Developer Program, which needs a paid membership. You use certificates, identifiers for your app's bundle ID, and provisioning profiles that tie them together. Xcode can manage much of this automatically. Builds are uploaded to App Store Connect through Xcode or command-line tools. The details change over time, so follow Apple's current documentation rather than old tutorials.

Versions: Each release has two version values. A user-facing version name, such as 1.4.2, often follows semantic versioning: major for big changes, minor for new features, patch for fixes. And an internal build number that must increase with every upload: versionCode on Android and the build number on iOS. In Flutter both live in pubspec.yaml as version: 1.4.2+37, where 37 is the build number. Forgetting to increase it is a common reason uploads are rejected.

Google Play Console: You publish Android apps through the Play Console after paying a one-time registration fee. The console offers testing tracks: internal testing for your team, closed testing for invited testers, open testing for anyone who joins, and production. Google has introduced requirements for some new personal developer accounts to run a closed test with a number of testers for a period before production access; check the current rules when you register. You upload an Android App Bundle, from which Play generates optimised APKs for each device.

The store listing: Users decide in seconds. The listing includes the app name, short and full description, icon, screenshots, an optional video, category and contact details. Write clearly in the languages your users read, including Bangla; show real screens, not misleading mock-ups; and state honestly what the app does. You must also complete the content rating questionnaire, the Data safety form from lesson 19, a privacy policy link and the target audience. Inaccurate declarations are a common cause of rejection.

App Store Connect and TestFlight: For iOS you create the app record in App Store Connect, upload builds, and use TestFlight to distribute beta builds to internal testers and to external testers, who receive builds through the TestFlight app. External testing requires a lighter beta review. When ready, you submit a build for App Review with screenshots, description, privacy details, and, if login is required, a demo account for the reviewers.

Store review: Both stores review apps against their policies. Apple's App Review is known for being thorough and checks functionality, design, privacy, payments and content. Google Play uses automated and manual review. Common rejection reasons include crashes, broken links, placeholder content, missing demo accounts, misleading descriptions, privacy declarations that do not match behaviour, unnecessary permissions, and payment rules violations. Read the policies before building features, not after rejection; designing around a rule is cheaper than rewriting.

Staged rollout: Even a well-tested release can break on some phones. Play Console lets you release to a percentage of users first, such as 5 percent, watch crash and ANR rates for a day or two, then increase to 20, 50 and 100 percent. If problems appear, you halt the rollout. iOS offers phased release for automatic updates over seven days. Combined with crash reporting from lesson 23, staged rollouts turn potential disasters into small incidents.

Updates and old versions: Not every user updates quickly; some keep old versions for months. Your backend must keep supporting older app versions, which is why API versioning from lesson 15 matters. For critical changes, apps can check a minimum supported version from the server and ask users to update; Android also offers an in-app updates API through Play. Use forced updates sparingly; forcing a large download on a limited data pack frustrates users.

Ways to make money: Paid apps charge once to download; this is rare in Bangladesh, where most users expect free apps. In-app purchases sell digital items or features inside the app, such as extra lessons or game items. Subscriptions charge regularly for ongoing access, such as a monthly premium plan. Advertising earns from showing ads, through networks such as Google AdMob, at the cost of user experience and privacy concerns. Freemium combines a free core with paid upgrades. Many apps, such as e-commerce, ride-sharing and fintech, earn from their real-world service, not from the app itself.

Store billing rules: Both stores require that digital goods and services consumed inside the app, such as premium features or digital content, use the store's own billing system, Google Play Billing or Apple's In-App Purchase, and the store takes a commission. Physical goods and real-world services, such as groceries, rides or food delivery, can use your own payment gateway, including local mobile wallets and cards. These rules have been changing in some regions due to regulation, so check the current policy for your situation. Getting this wrong is a classic rejection reason.

Payments in Bangladesh: For physical goods and services, Bangladeshi apps commonly integrate mobile financial services, cards and cash on delivery through payment gateways. Verify every payment on the server using the gateway's server-side confirmation, never trust the app's success screen alone, as lesson 22 taught. For digital subscriptions sold through the stores, check which payment methods each store supports for Bangladeshi users, because store payment options in a country may be limited, which affects how many users can actually pay.

Measuring after launch: Analytics tools, such as Firebase Analytics, show how users move through the app: how many finish onboarding, where they drop off in checkout, and which features are used. Track key metrics: daily and monthly active users, retention after 1, 7 and 30 days, conversion, crash-free users and ANR rate. Collect only what you need and disclose it, as lesson 19 required. Read store reviews and reply politely; a helpful reply to a one-star review often turns into a better rating.

Real-life example 1, a student's first app on Play: A CSE student builds a Bangla dictionary app in Flutter. She creates an upload key and stores it safely, sets version 1.0.0+1, builds an app bundle, tests it on her old phone, writes a Bangla and English listing with real screenshots, fills the Data safety form honestly declaring that no personal data is collected, and runs a closed test with friends. After production approval she releases to 20 percent, sees no crashes, and goes to 100 percent. Small banner ads on the word detail screen bring modest income.

Real-life example 2, a coaching platform's subscription: An online coaching app sells monthly access to video lessons. Because these are digital services consumed in the app, the in-app purchase goes through Google Play Billing and Apple's In-App Purchase. The server verifies purchases with the stores before unlocking content. The team uses staged rollouts for every update, watches retention by week, and notices that students who finish the first free lesson are far more likely to subscribe, so they redesign onboarding to start a lesson in under a minute.

Course wrap-up, how it all connects: You began with platforms and the sandbox, then learned Dart and Flutter's declarative UI, layout, navigation and state. You organised code with MVVM and repositories, loaded lists and images efficiently, handled async work, talked to REST APIs, and stored data in preferences, files and SQLite. You made apps work offline with sync, asked for permissions respectfully, used sensors, location and camera, sent notifications and scheduled background work. You secured data, tested and profiled, made apps accessible and bilingual, and finally learned to ship and sustain them. Each topic is one layer of a real product.

Where to go next: Build one complete app and publish it, even a small one; the experience teaches what no course can. Read the official Flutter, Android and Apple documentation, which change often. Explore deeper topics: native Kotlin with Jetpack Compose or Swift with SwiftUI, backend development with Firebase or your own server, CI/CD to automate builds, animations, and on-device machine learning. Join local developer communities and contribute to open-source packages. And remember the related courses: Web Engineering for APIs and web security, and Human-Computer Interaction for design.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Uploading debug builds; losing or leaking signing keys; forgetting to increase the build number; misleading listings or inaccurate Data safety forms; missing demo accounts for review; releasing to 100 percent at once; dropping support for old app versions too early; using your own payment gateway for in-app digital goods; and trusting the app's payment success screen. Exams ask: steps to publish an app on Play and the App Store; why apps are signed; version name versus version code; testing tracks and staged rollout; monetization models and their trade-offs; and store billing rules.

Recap: Ship release builds, signed with keys you protect, with an increasing build number. Use testing tracks and TestFlight, write honest listings in your users' languages, complete privacy and content declarations, and read store policies early. Roll out in stages while watching crashes and ANRs, keep backends compatible with old versions, and use forced updates rarely. Choose monetization that fits your users: in-app purchases and subscriptions through store billing for digital goods, your own gateway for physical goods and services, ads with care. Measure, listen to reviews, and keep improving. That is the full journey of a mobile app, from idea to the hands of real users.
key_points: Users get release builds: optimised, shrunk and obfuscated, and tested on real devices before upload.
Android apps must be signed; protect the upload key and use Play App Signing; iOS uses certificates and provisioning profiles via the Apple Developer Program.
Version name (e.g. 1.4.2) is for users; version code / build number (e.g. +37) must increase with every upload.
Play Console offers internal, closed, open and production tracks; iOS uses TestFlight before App Review.
Store listings and privacy declarations must be honest; common rejections include crashes, missing demo accounts and mismatched Data safety.
Staged rollouts (Play) and phased release (iOS) limit damage; keep backends compatible with older app versions.
Monetization: paid, in-app purchases, subscriptions, ads, freemium; digital goods used in-app must use store billing, physical goods and services may use your own gateway.
lessons.tip: Before your final-year project ends, publish it to at least an internal or closed testing track on Play. Going through signing, the listing and the Data safety form once will make your CV and your skills far stronger.
lessons.task: Write a release checklist for your own app: build command, signing steps, version number, testing track, listing items (in English and Bangla), privacy declarations, rollout plan with percentages, the two metrics you will watch after release, and your monetization model with the reason it fits your users.

quiz.q: Why must Android apps be signed?
options: So the system can verify that updates come from the same developer as the installed app
To translate them into other languages
quiz.explain: Android only installs an update over an existing app if it is signed with the matching key.

quiz.q: In pubspec.yaml, version: 1.4.2+37. What is 37?
options: The build number (versionCode), which must increase with each upload
quiz.explain: The part after + is the build number; 1.4.2 is the user-facing version name.

quiz.q: What is a staged rollout?
options: Releasing different apps in different countries
Releasing an update to a small percentage of users first, then increasing while monitoring problems
Asking users to update in stages manually
quiz.explain: Staged rollout limits damage: if crashes rise, you halt before most users are affected.

quiz.q: A food delivery app charges for meals inside the app. Which payment approach is generally allowed?
options: It must use only Google Play Billing
It must use only Apple In-App Purchase
Payments are not allowed in apps
Its own payment gateway, because meals are physical goods and real-world services
quiz.explain: Store billing rules apply to digital goods consumed in-app; physical goods and services can use other payment methods.

quiz.q: Why should the backend keep supporting older app versions for some time?
options: Many users do not update immediately, and breaking old versions would break their app
quiz.explain: Update adoption is gradual, so API compatibility and versioning protect users still on older releases.
